stories.title: The library
stories.description: The library is where one project's records live: the plan of work, how healthy each piece is, and what the project has learned. Every later storytree 0.3 story reads and writes the library, and only through its API. People never browse it directly; they see it through the forest and the arc surface, while agents reach it through the agent link.

capabilities.title: 1 · Project libraries
capabilities.description: Each project gets its own library, a separate database on one Postgres server, created the first time the project is opened, with its tables set up automatically, and brought up to date by the next open after storytree adds to them. Opening a project whose tables are already current touches no table, so an account let only read, or write a few kinds of record, can open it too. Storytree can list the projects on the server, and nothing written in one project can ever show up in another.

contracts.title: 1.1 · `openProject("site")` on a server with no storytree databases creates the project's database and its tables.
1.2 · Opening the same project again succeeds and changes nothing (no error, no second database, its records are untouched).
1.3 · After opening "site" and "app", `listProjects()` returns exactly `["app", "site"]`. Databases on the server that are not storytree projects are never listed.
1.4 · A record saved in "site" cannot be read from "app".

1.5 · A project name that is not lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens (1–40 characters, starting with a letter or digit) is refused before anything touches the server, and the error names the rule.
1.6 · `snapshot("site")` returns every record of the project and its whole history, as they stood at one moment, while writes go on.

1.7 · `restore("copy", snapshot)` into a project with no records and no history gives back the same records and the same history, sequence numbers, actors and times included, and the next write continues after them.
1.8 · Restoring into a project that holds any record or any history is refused, naming the project, and writes nothing.

1.9 · A local database that accepts TCP but never completes a fresh handshake is refused at a 3-second connection deadline by default, for both the server and project pools, with an actionable "storytree isn't reachable" answer. This includes library opens made by the CLI. A later call recovers once the database answers.

1.10 · Opening a project whose tables are current runs no table setup and writes nothing, so an account that may only read its tables (not their owner, no right to create in its schema) opens it and reads its records.

1.11 · Opening a project whose tables are not current, as an account that may not set them up, is refused with a ConnectionError (`project-owner`) naming the project and the account and saying that only the role owning its database may set them up; its owner's next open sets them up as before.

1.12 · `dropProject(name)` deletes the project's database, with every record and all its history, for every machine using the server; it is listed no more, other projects are untouched, and an unknown project is refused. An open that only reaches an existing project (`openProject(name, { create: false })`, how a folder that names a project opens it) refuses a deleted one as gone and never makes it again.
contracts.description: The library call under deleting a project (ADR-0831). Irreversible: a snapshot taken first is the only way back. Others' connections to the database are ended (DROP DATABASE … WITH (FORCE)).

capabilities.title: 2 · Library transactions
capabilities.description: The only data actions the library allows are: save a record, fetch it, list records of one type, change only named fields, or retire a record with a reason. Every change is all-or-nothing, and is written first to a permanent, append-only history, so nothing is ever truly erased.

contracts.title: 2.1 · `save` creates a record. Saving the same id again replaces it, and each save appends one history entry.
2.2 · `edit` changes only the fields it names; every other field keeps its stored value.
2.3 · `edit` merges onto what is stored NOW, not onto a copy the caller read earlier. If two edits of different fields race, both survive.
2.4 · `edit` of a missing record returns `null` and creates nothing.
2.5 · `get` of a missing record returns `null` and never throws.
2.6 · `list(type)` returns only that type's current records (none retired), and `[]` when there are none.
2.7 · `retire(id, reason)` removes the record from `get`/`list`, keeps the reason in the history, and retiring an already-retired or missing record is a harmless no-op.

2.8 · `history()` returns every change in the order it happened, with strictly increasing sequence numbers. `history({ id })` filters to one record, and `history({ since })` returns only entries after that sequence number.
2.9 · A `validate` check passed to `save`/`edit` sees the merged result. If it throws, nothing is written (no record change and no history entry).

2.10 · A write naming an `actor` keeps it in history. A write without one is accepted and its history entry has no actor; an edit or retirement never inherits an earlier write's actor. Refused writes and harmless no-ops add no history entry.

2.11 · Save, edit and retire accept an optional abort signal. If aborted before write admission, including while waiting for the project write lock, they reject without changing records or history. After admission, cancellation does not interrupt the write or undo its history. The in-memory twin applies the same boundary at write entry.

capabilities.title: 3 · Data schema
capabilities.description: Every record has a declared type with a fixed set of fields, and a badly filled-in record is refused with a message naming the problem field. Every record is stamped with the schema version it was written on, so a later change to a type is handled deliberately rather than silently misread: an older record is upgraded automatically, step by step, and stored upgraded the next time it is written, because every user's library is their own database and nobody else can repair it.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Saving a `story` with no `title` is refused, the error names `title`, and nothing is written.
3.2 · An unknown field (for example `titel`) is refused and named.
3.3 · An unknown type is refused.
3.4 · Every stored record carries its schema version (1 today).
3.5 · Reading a record stamped with a version NEWER than this code knows is refused with an error saying so. It is never guessed at.
3.6 · An `edit` that would leave the record invalid (for example blanking a required field) is refused, and nothing is written.
3.7 · A record written on an OLDER version of its type is read (`get`, `list`) upgraded to the current version, its upgrade steps applied in order. Reading it writes nothing.

3.8 · An `edit` of such a record merges onto its upgraded fields and stores it on the current version, in place, in the same all-or-nothing write. If the upgraded result does not fit, nothing is written.
3.9 · An older record that no upgrade step brings to the next version is refused by `get`, `list` and `edit`, with an error naming the missing step. It is never guessed at.

capabilities.title: 4 · Work model
capabilities.description: The library holds each project's plan of work: arcs (initiatives), stories (what a user can do), capabilities (the parts that make a story work) and contracts (single testable promises). Capabilities and contracts point at their parent. Stories belong to the project directly, and an arc *may* list the stories it grows, though a research arc may list none. The library refuses broken structure. A capability carries a proposed flag, on from its birth until the agent says it is built (`setProposed`, ADR-0744 D2); switching it says nothing about health, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed.

contracts.title: 4.1 · Add a story, a capability under it and a contract under that, and `projectTree()` returns them nested: story › capability › contract.
4.2 · An arc listing that story is returned by `arcsFor(storyId)`. An arc listing no stories is accepted.
4.3 · A capability naming a missing (or retired) story is refused, as is a contract naming a missing capability and an arc listing a missing story.
4.4 · A capability depending on another capability that does not exist is refused.
4.5 · A dependency loop between capabilities (A → B → A, or longer) is refused, and nothing is written.

4.6 · A capability is born proposed. The agent switches the flag off, and back on, and history names the writer; only a live capability has the flag, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed.

4.7 · A contract planned without a number is given its capability's next free one (after the highest its live contracts carry); a title whose number another live contract of the capability carries is refused, on planning and on correcting, and nothing is written. A capability with no number numbers nothing.

4.8 · A capability planned without a number is given its story's next free one (after the highest its live capabilities carry), so the contracts planned on it are numbered from the start; a number given is kept.
contracts.description: Regression for a contract planned moments after its capability that stayed unnumbered (2026-10-01): contract numbering keys off the capability's stored number.

capabilities.title: 6 · Knowledge artifacts
capabilities.description: Alongside the plan, the library keeps what the project has learned: decisions and definitions of terms, and principles, guardrails, patterns, processes, agent roles, friction, re-steers and tech stack, each with 0.2's fields. Each can link to the other artifacts it relates to, and you can find them again by searching their words; an edit keeps the old wording in history. An artifact never links straight to the work: capability 9 is how the work reaches its knowledge.

contracts.title: 6.3 · Editing a decision keeps its old wording in history.
6.4 · A link to a record that does not exist is refused.
6.1 · An artifact is found by `search` on any word it contains (case-insensitive).
6.2 · `relatedNotes(noteId)` returns every artifact that links to that artifact.

6.5 · `definitions()` returns every live definition, and nothing else, in creation order. Added for the agent link's definition lookups at each prompt (ADR-0636 D1, b2), which adds `definitions` to 7's list of functions.

6.7 · Friction with no evidence is refused, and so is a re-steer marked a defect with no failure mode. Friction stores the optional dischargedBy reference to the remedy that landed, alongside its route and reason; editing other fields preserves the reference.
6.6 · Each of the eight kinds is saved with its required fields, and refused, naming the field, without one.
6.9 · Opening an older project converts an explicitly classified memory once, keeping its id, links and history, and reports an unclassified memory while preserving its original record.
6.8 · Saving a `memory` is refused with the reason that memories belong to the harness, and nothing is written.

6.10 · `related(noteId)` ranks the other live artifacts by likeness to one, saying of each whether a link joins them in either direction; with `unlinked`, only those no link reaches. An artifact sharing no word with it is never listed.

capabilities.title: 5 · Health record
capabilities.description: Every story, capability and contract has a health record with two separate columns: what the agent **reported**, and what storytree **verified** by seeing it for itself. Each column is one of three states: `passing`, `failing` or `not-checked`. A missing entry always reads as `not-checked`, never as `passing`. A capability also has a word, as its card says it (ADR-0744 D1, D3): `proposed` while its flag is on; once the agent switches it off, `healthy` when every contract is verified passing, `unhealthy` when any is verified failing, and `untested` otherwise. Only the verified column counts: the agent's report never makes a capability healthy.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A node with no health entries reads `reported: not-checked, verified: not-checked`.
5.2 · After an agent reports a contract `passing`, it reads `reported: passing, verified: not-checked`.
5.3 · After storytree records the same contract verified `failing`, both columns are kept and shown side by side (`reported: passing, verified: failing`).

5.4 · A capability or story's health is rolled up from its contracts, column by column: `failing` if any contract is failing; `passing` only if it has at least one contract and every one is passing; otherwise `not-checked`. A single never-checked contract keeps its story `not-checked`.
5.5 · Every health entry is kept in history with who wrote it and when. A health entry for a node that does not exist is refused.

5.6 · A capability's word is proposed while its flag is on, even with every contract verified passing. Once the flag is off, it is healthy when every contract is verified passing, unhealthy when any is verified failing, and untested when any has no verified result or it has no contracts; reported passing alone reads untested.

5.7 · A verified entry can carry the kind of skip that left it not checked (owner, platform:<os> or other) and the earlier verdict it did not reproduce with that verdict's time; both read back from the contract's health and in the annotated tree, and an entry without them reads as before.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D2: a skip is data, not silence. The recorder writes these; the library keeps them and derives the reason from them (5.8).

contracts.title: 5.8 · A capability that is not healthy carries one reason and who moves it: not built while proposed; otherwise, from its contracts' verified columns, failing, then not re-run, then no test names it, then out of CI's reach, then needs owner; with the contracts carrying it and the earliest time one was recorded so. Only needs owner is the owner's; a healthy capability carries none.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D1: every card that is not healthy says why, and who moves it. The agent's work is ranked before the owner's, so the owner is asked only once nothing an agent can do remains.

contracts.title: 5.9 · The health worklist lists every capability that is not healthy with its reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when (the earliest time one was recorded so, or else when the capability was recorded), oldest first; one an open increment touches is routed and left off until that increment closes.

5.10 · In a project whose health nothing verifies (no verified entry anywhere), a built capability carries no reason and is marked as shown by the agent's report; its line says what the agent reports and that storytree does not check this project's tests yet, and it is off the health worklist
contracts.description: ADR-0630: a user's project shows what the agent reports, labelled as the agent's; nothing writes its verified column, so 'untested, no test names it, the agent's to move' is false there (increment_ef066f718a63).

capabilities.title: 7 · Library API
capabilities.description: One small, fixed list of functions is the only way anything outside the library reads or writes it. The agent link, arc surface, forest and desktop app all call these, and `changesSince` lets them see what just changed without re-reading everything.

contracts.title: 7.2 · `changesSince(n)` returns only changes after `n`, in order, each carrying the new cursor to pass next time.

7.3 · The package's public entry exports exactly this API and nothing else, and its internals cannot be imported through the package. At runtime it exports `connect`, `ConnectionError`, `DependencyLoopError`, `LifecycleError`, `LinkLoopError`, `MissingReferenceError`, `MissingUpgradeError`, `NewerSchemaError`, `NumberTakenError`, `ProjectNameError`, `RetireRefusedError`, `SchemaError`, `SupersessionLoopError`, `UnknownTypeError` and `WaitLoopError`. Everything else exported is a data type, including `WriteOptions`, `HistoryEntry` and `HistoryFilter`. The connection offers exactly `openProject`, `listProjects` and `close`. A project library offers exactly `name`, `get`, `list`, `history`, `addStory`, `editStory`, `createArc`, `editArc`, `addCapability`, `editCapability`, `addContract`, `editContract`, `projectTree`, `arcsFor`, `addIncrement`, `advanceIncrement`, `closeIncrement`, `editIncrement`, `parkArc`, `unparkArc`, `arcView`, `addWait`, `removeWait`, `waitHolds`, `raiseQuestion`, `settleQuestion`, `questions`, `heldOnQuestion`, `checkQuestion`, `renewQuestion`, `lapsedQuestions`, `reportHealth`, `recordVerified`, `health`, `healthHistory`, `recordDecision`, `writeKnowledge`, `defineTerm`, `editNote`, `search`, `rank`, `relatedNotes`, `related`, `definitions`, `frontCovers`, `decision`, `composeStatement`, `retire`, `changesSince` and `close`.

7.1 · An end-to-end "agent's day" against a real local Postgres: open a project, create an arc, add a story, a capability and a contract, report passing, record verified, record a decision as the capability's front cover and write a definition inside it, then read `projectTree()` and `changesSince(0)`. Every step is visible where the next step expects it.

7.4 · `editStory`, `editContract` and `editArc` change only the fields they name, merged onto what is stored now, and check a new reference as adding does (a contract's capability, an arc's stories). Each gives `null`, writing nothing, for an id that is not a live record of its type.

7.5 · `get`, `list` and `history` return whole records through the public API, agreeing with the in-memory twin. Live reads upgrade old records; history preserves original writes, including actors and retirement reasons, and can filter by id and sequence. Reads write nothing.
7.6 · Every public write carries its optional actor to history, as in 2.10. Health can name a writer separately from its reporter; omitting the writer preserves its existing `by` attribution.

7.7 · A connection hands its caller one named database of its own beside the projects, on the same server, local or Cloud SQL: created the first time (borrowing a granted creator role where the user may not create databases), never listed as a project, closed with the connection.
7.8 · `arcViews()` returns every live arc's view in a few reads, not one per arc
contracts.description: The same answer as calling arcView on each live arc, read from the library in a bounded number of record reads whatever the number of arcs, so a surface that needs every arc (the sessions list) costs a handful of queries per change instead of one batch per arc (ADR-0836 D3).

capabilities.title: 8 · Cloud connection (GCP)
capabilities.description: Instead of the local Postgres, a user can point storytree at a Postgres database in Google Cloud (Cloud SQL) and sign in with their Google account rather than a stored password. Everything above works the same, and each project still gets its own database, now on the cloud server.

contracts.title: 8.1 · Capability 2's behaviour suite, unchanged, passes against a real Cloud SQL instance reached with Google sign-in.

verified.note: not re-run at commit 43653675e1d355573215b3873b10070984fb3dd2: 1 of 14 tests skipped (owner: live Cloud SQL proof needs STORYTREE_TEST_CLOUDSQL_INSTANCE/USER and a database user that may create databases, itself or through a granted role)

contracts.title: 8.2 · A missing or bad Google sign-in is refused with a message saying what to fix, never a hang.

8.3 · Two accounts sharing the role that creates project databases (a laptop owner and a machine's service account on one instance) both open, write and read one project and a connection's own database: each connection signs in as its account and acts as the database's owning role, so every table either makes is the role's and neither needs the other's ownership.

8.4 · An account granted exactly infra/ci-health/grants.sql (CI's health account, ADR-0747) opens the project, records a contract's verified health, and is refused any other kind of record (a new one is refused by row-level security; one it may not change is not there for it to change) and any change to the tables; the owner's accounts are unaffected and read what it recorded.
8.5 · On a shared server, a library call waits for a free connection slot instead of failing, and each Cloud SQL pool holds at most three slots.
contracts.description: A server refusing a new connection for want of a slot (SQLSTATE 53300) is asked again with backoff for up to 30 s, so a read under a moment's slot pressure succeeds; each pool on a Cloud SQL instance opens at most three connections and queues busier work, so parallel sessions fit the instance (47 non-superuser slots when measured 2026-09-30). Tests: packages/library/src/project/shared-server.test.ts and cloud-connection.test.ts, "8.4".

capabilities.title: 9 · Knowledge entrances
capabilities.description: Every story and capability has its own shelf of front-cover decisions, and a decision can be a front cover of one of them at most. Artifacts link only to other artifacts, so the only way from the work into the knowledge is through a front cover.

contracts.title: 9.1 · A decision can be the front cover of a story or a capability, and `frontCovers(nodeId)` returns that node's live covers, founding (oldest) first, and nothing else.
9.2 · A front cover that names anything but a live story or capability is refused, and nothing is written. Only a decision can be a front cover.
9.3 · An artifact that links to a story, capability, contract, arc or health entry is refused, and nothing is written. Artifacts link only to other artifacts.

9.4 · A link that would close a loop between artifacts, an artifact linking to itself included, is refused with the chain it would close named, and nothing is written. The knowledge is a DAG under its covers (ADR-0647 D2).

capabilities.title: 10 · Work in flight
capabilities.description: Each arc is whole: its intent, its end state and its increments. An increment moves from proposal to ready to active to closed. An arc reads closed when its last increment closes, and reopens when new work is parked on it, unless the owner has parked the arc. A closed increment stays, as the arc's log entry: its date, pull request, note, and whether it landed, failed or was withdrawn.

contracts.title: 10.2 · An increment moves only forward. Closing records the date, pull request, note and outcome (landed, failed or withdrawn), and a close with no pull request needs a note.
10.1 · An increment belongs to one live arc. It is created as a proposal, stamped with the date it was parked, or born closed.

10.3 · An arc with increments reads closed exactly when none is open and none of its questions waits on the owner, and active otherwise; an arc with no increments yet reads active. A parked arc reads parked until it is unparked.
10.4 · An arc's intent and end state are required, and an arc written before they were is upgraded to carry them.

10.5 · An open increment moves to another live arc keeping its id, status and waits, its history recording the move and why; a closed increment, or a move to a closed arc, is refused and nothing is written.
10.6 · An arc parked until a day reads parked before that day (UTC midnight) and as if unparked from it on, worked out on read with no write in between
contracts.description: The owner's timed park (increment_6440942f1960): `arc park <arc> --until <YYYY-MM-DD>` holds an arc for a known date, and it comes back by itself, with no scheduler. A plain park still holds until unparked; unpark clears the date.

capabilities.title: 11 · Waits
capabilities.description: An arc waits on an arc, and an increment on an increment on any arc, each with a reason. A loop across both kinds is refused when it is written. The library alone answers whether a wait holds (`waitHolds`), naming its blockers and saying when one can never release.

contracts.title: 11.1 · An increment wait holds until the blocker closes as landed. A failed, withdrawn or missing blocker holds for good, and says it will never release.
11.3 · A wait that would close a loop across arcs and increments is refused, naming the loop, and nothing is written.
11.2 · An arc wait holds until that arc closes.
11.4 · `waitHolds(id)` returns the blockers still holding, each with its reason.
11.5 · `holds()` answers every live arc's and increment's wait holds, and every increment's owner holds, in one reading, each the same as `waitHolds` and `heldOnQuestion` give.

capabilities.title: 12 · Owner questions
capabilities.description: A question is raised on an arc, with its stakes, statement, context and options, and settled with the owner's answer, which stays on the arc. An increment held on an open question reads as waiting on him (`heldOnQuestion`), and the library alone answers that.

contracts.title: 12.1 · A question is raised with its required fields, and is open.
12.2 · Settling needs an answer and keeps it, with the date and the decision that carried it. A settled question stays readable on its arc.
12.3 · An open increment held on an open question reads as waiting on the owner. Settling the question releases it, with no write to the increment. A question that does not exist holds nothing.
12.4 · A question an increment is held on cannot be retired.

12.5 · An open question carries a review date and a lease, 7 days unless given. It checks fresh until the lease runs out and lapsed after, it is listed as lapsed until renewed, and renewing re-stamps it.
12.6 · Renewing a settled question is refused and nothing is written. A settled question checks settled and is never listed as lapsed.

12.7 · An open question's wording (title, stakes, statement, context, options, analogy, diagram, recommendation) can be corrected in place, changing only the named fields. Its arc, lifecycle, answer and lease are not edited this way, and editing a settled question is refused with nothing written: its answer stands.
12.8 · A question raised on a parked arc is refused, naming the arc, and nothing is written; once its wake day passes, it is raised
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D1: what a session would have asked goes into the arc's residue instead, to be raised when the arc is unparked.

capabilities.title: 13 · Decision log
capabilities.description: Decision numbers do not collide, even across concurrent writers, and history reserves every number a decision has held. Other projects start at 1. In the project named exactly `storytree`, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any record has ever held; automatic numbering is refused if that setting is absent. An explicit free number remains accepted. The N1 move is complete: the 29 Full record decisions retain their 0.2 numbers, the floor is 662, and the 53 founding books are ADR-0663..0715. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number. A decision's status is proposed or accepted, and it can be superseded: the superseded decision is kept, and reads as superseded. A decision carries the load-bearing mark, who decided it, in their own words, and one composed statement.

contracts.title: 13.1 · In projects with automatic numbering, decisions recorded at once from separate connections get distinct numbers, each higher than any before. A number held by another decision is never reused, including retired decisions and old numbers kept in history. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number and a refused edit writes nothing.
13.2 · A decision is superseded exactly when an accepted decision names it in `supersedes`. It stays readable, and a supersession loop is refused.
13.3 · Status and the load-bearing mark are stored and read back, and a decision written before status was is upgraded to carry one.
13.4 · A decision may carry one composed statement. A read returns it marked stale when the decision's text changed after it was written, and the full text is always readable.

13.5 · Only in the storytree project, numberDecision repairs a live decision once to the number in its own single Full record: ADR-NNNN line. Missing or ambiguous lines, mismatches, retired records, previous repairs, and numbers any record has ever held are refused without writing. Concurrent repairs cannot share a number or repair a record twice. The old number stays in history; editNote still refuses number. decisionNumberPlan lists proposed old → new numbers and refusals, including duplicate targets, without writing. Decisions without a Full record line are untouched.

13.6 · Only in storytree, setDecisionNumberFloor previews by default and apply: true stores 0.2's final number once as a positive safe integer project setting, retained in history and snapshots. Repeated or lower floor settings are refused, including concurrent attempts. Recording without an explicit number is refused while the floor is unset; afterwards, automatic numbers exceed the floor and every number any record has ever held, with concurrent writers receiving distinct numbers. An explicit free number remains accepted; other projects still auto-number from 1.

13.7 · numberDecisionsFromFullRecord previews by default; apply: true applies every eligible proposal through numberDecision and returns each refusal. Decisions already matching their Full record number are omitted. Duplicate targets are refused, the write checks history again under the project lock, and repeated bulk application writes nothing once all eligible repairs are complete.

13.8 · Only in storytree with its floor set, numberFoundingDecisions previews live decisions that existed at switch-on and have no Full record line, in first-creation history order. Targets exceed the floor and every number any record has ever held. Preview writes and reserves nothing; apply: true rechecks every write and returns each refusal. The record keeps its identity, other fields and old number in history. Concurrent moves cannot share numbers or move a book twice. Completed moves, Full record decisions and decisions created after switch-on are omitted; a repeat can finish a partial run without renumbering completed books.
13.9 · `decisions()` gives every live decision's view in one reading, oldest first, each the same as `decision(id)` gives.

capabilities.title: 14 · Ranked search
capabilities.description:
A library search ranks the live artifacts by how close their meaning is to the question, using an embedding model (bge-small) run on this computer, with no LLM, paid API or extra service, as the owner directed (0.2's ADR-0664). An artifact written or edited is embedded again before the next search ranks it, and with no model to hand the search falls back to word matches and says why.

As built: Windows delivery stages the locked Transformers Node distribution, ONNX Runtime CPU binding and DLL, and the Sharp runtime dependency beside the CLI and MCP entrypoints for x64 and arm64. No model weights ship. The existing lazy loader downloads bge-small on first use into <storytree home>/models. The installed-layout check imports Transformers and runs a weight-free ONNX Identity graph on the native CPU backend without a source checkout. Windows x64 execution is checked by installer CI; ARM64 PE headers are inspected, with ARM64 execution awaiting a native Windows acceptance run.

contracts.title: 14.1 · `rank(query)` orders the live artifacts by meaning, best first, with each one's score, and finds an artifact that shares no word with the question.
14.2 · An artifact scores by its best chunk (its rendered text packed into chunks of at most 3000 characters on paragraph boundaries), and at most `limit` artifacts come back, ten unless told.

14.3 · An edited artifact ranks by its new words at the next search; a chunk already embedded is not embedded again, and a library opened afresh on the same project reads the kept vectors, embedding only the question.
14.4 · With no embedding model to hand (switched off, or it cannot load), `rank` gives the word matches of `search` and says why, rather than failing.

14.5 · The installed Windows CLI and MCP tools resolve their bundled Transformers and native ONNX CPU runtime without a checkout or npm installation, on x64 and arm64. The installer ships runtime code and target binaries, never model weights; the embedding model remains a first-use download into <storytree home>/models.

14.7 · A ranked search puts first the records it names by title: one whose contract number (such as 7.17) is a word of the search, then one whose title (a definition's term) holds every word of it, ignoring case; each group, and the rest, keep their meaning order.

14.8 · rankAll ranks live stories, capabilities and contracts by their own wording alongside knowledge artifacts, labels each hit with its type, and finds a contract whose meaning matches even when it shares no query word.

14.9 · With no embedding model, rankAll returns word matches including a contract holding every query word, reports why it fell back, and never treats a plan record’s parent identifier as searchable words.

capabilities.title: 15 · Connection by address
capabilities.description: Instead of the local app's Postgres or Cloud SQL with Google sign-in, storytree reaches any Postgres by its address (Neon, Supabase, RDS, self-hosted, Cloud SQL with an ordinary user), its password resolved as a key.

contracts.title: 15.1 · A library at a Postgres address, with its password saved as the `postgres` key, opens, writes and reads a project as a password-authenticated role.
contracts.description: Proven against the throwaway test server with a role that must give its password (scram-sha-256).

contracts.title: 15.2 · With no password saved for the library (no `postgres` key and no PGPASSWORD), connecting is refused saying so and how to save one, before anything reaches the server.
15.3 · A password the server refuses and a host that cannot be reached are each refused as their own problem, with what to fix, and never show the password.

stories.title: The agent link
stories.description: The agent link lets the user's own Claude Code or Codex use storytree by itself, through two layers that share one base. A passive layer of hooks records what every agent does, so even an agent that ignores storytree shows up as unplanned activity. An active layer, an MCP tool server, is what the agent chooses to call to plan, claim, report red, green and landed, and write artifacts, taught by a short habits card. A setup check at every session start keeps it all set up. Red-green is a convention the card teaches, not a loop storytree runs.

capabilities.title: 1 · Project routing
capabilities.description: The first time an agent session starts in a folder that isn't a storytree project, storytree asks the user (through the agent) whether to set one up; if they say yes, this leaves a small marker in the folder naming the project, and from then on it routes everything an agent does anywhere in that folder to that project, whichever project the user happens to be looking at in the app. It never picks a project by itself: a folder the user hasn't said yes to is ignored, and when storytree isn't running it says so at once, so everything built on it quietly does nothing.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Setting a folder up as project "site" leaves a marker in it naming "site", and asking from the folder, from a sub-folder of it, and from a git worktree of it all give "site".
1.2 · A folder with no marker, in it or above it, gives "not a storytree project".
1.3 · A project name the library would refuse is refused when setting a folder up, and nothing is written.
1.4 · With the app's database stopped, asking where to send activity answers "storytree isn't running" in well under a second.
1.5 · A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: it answers in well under a second and never hangs.

1.6 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, a project folder routes to that instance (its connection name and user) whether or not the app's local database is running, and no local address is tried; with it local, routing is exactly as in 1.1 to 1.5.

1.7 · Routing reads only the library setting: damage elsewhere in settings.json (an unusable context guidance, say) does not stop it, while a damaged library setting, or a file that is not a JSON object, refuses naming the file and is never read as local nor rewritten.

1.8 · A folder that is a project's trunk, is inside one, is a git worktree of one, or holds one is refused when set up as another project, even with its marker gone, and nothing is written (ADR-0757 D3).
1.9 · A second folder for a project that already has a trunk on this machine is refused, joining or not, saying to work in a git worktree of the trunk; the trunk keeps routing (ADR-0757 D1, D3).

1.10 · A new folder given an existing project's name is refused unless it joins on purpose, on any machine, and the refusal suggests the first name no project has (name-2, name-3…); a matching folder name never joins (ADR-0757 D3, D4).

1.11 · A machine with no trunk for an existing project adds its checkout only on purpose (join), after which a git worktree of that checkout routes to the project, one project shared by both machines; joining a project that does not exist is refused (ADR-0757 D2, D4).

1.12 · A project set up before trunks were recorded keeps routing, and the first time the agent link reaches the library from it (a git worktree included) its main checkout is recorded as its trunk on this machine, never refusing and never moving a live one (1.13); a second trunk is then refused (ADR-0757 migration).

1.13 · A trunk whose folder is gone from this machine (moved or deleted) is forgotten when the project is set up, joined or seen: a moved folder becomes the trunk on first sight, and a new folder can join in place of a deleted one. A folder still there keeps its trunk, marker or not (1.8).

1.14 · Setting a new project up seeds its library with the starter roles, an orchestrator and a librarian, and the principles they stand on; joining it from another machine, or setting it up again after a failed try, adds no second copy
contracts.description: The starter pack (owner, question_6d10bcae0b9d): a new user's library starts with slim orchestrator and librarian roles drawn from storytree's own, so a first build is guided rather than improvised. The pack's text lives in one versioned place in the agent link's source (routing/starter-pack.ts).

capabilities.title: 2 · Agent activity log
capabilities.description: The agent link's own logbook of what agents do, one per project and kept beside the library rather than inside it, with one line for each thing that happens: a session starts or ends, a file is edited, a command runs, an artifact is read, work is claimed, released or landed. Lines are only ever added, never changed, and can be read back in order as "everything since line N", including lines that other processes wrote.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Two separate processes write lines for two sessions, and reading from the start returns every line once, in the order written.
2.2 · Reading "since line N" returns only the lines after N, in order, each carrying the number to pass next time.
2.3 · Lines written for project "site" never appear when reading project "app".
2.4 · The log never shows up in the library's list of projects, and writing lines leaves the library's own records and change feed untouched.

2.5 · The log opens on whichever server the library resolved to, reached through the library's connection: lines two machines write for one project on one Cloud SQL instance are both read back from either, in order (live, opt-in).

verified.note: 1 of 2 tests skipped (owner: live Cloud SQL proof needs STORYTREE_TEST_CLOUDSQL_INSTANCE/USER), at commit 43653675e1d355573215b3873b10070984fb3dd2

contracts.title: 2.6 · A line may name the earlier line of its own project's log that caused it (`causedBy`, ADR-0746 D2), and reads back naming it. A line naming a line its project's log does not hold (another project's, or none) is refused, whether appended alone or under the project's lock, and nothing is written.

capabilities.title: 3 · Hooks
capabilities.description: Small commands that Claude Code and Codex run by themselves when a session starts, after every file edit, before and after every shell command, at the end of each turn, and when it ends, each adding one line about that session to the agent activity log, so an agent that never calls storytree still shows up. At each prompt, one more adds the project's definitions for the terms the prompt names, for the agent to read: every matching term not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (3.7). The cap of five that 0.2's ADR-0201 set, never measured and never chosen by the owner, is removed by the owner's named choice ("turn the cap off.", 2026-09-28; ADR-0739 D3, ADR-0633); the once-per-session and harness-notice rules, which 0.2 did measure, stay. The same prompt hook carries capability 9's fresh-session nudge to a Claude Code session past its context guidance (9.9). At a session's start in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet, the harness waits for one more (Codex's own start hook, a second one for Claude Code), which has the agent ask the user whether to set storytree up there before the task it was given, and sets nothing up itself (8.12). Every hook also records the transcript path the harness named for its session, so capability 9 can work out any session's tokens used when asked, never from a transcript found by folder (ADR-0725, ADR-0728). They run in the background and always exit cleanly, so they can never slow down or break the agent, and when storytree isn't running they do nothing.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Real, recorded Claude Code hook inputs (a start, a file edit, a shell command, an end) are fed in, and four lines appear on that session, carrying the file path, the command and the machine's name.
3.2 · The same holds for real, recorded Codex hook inputs, where the edited files are read out of its patch text.
3.3 · With storytree stopped, with garbage input, or outside a storytree project, the command exits cleanly in under half a second and writes nothing.
3.4 · It runs on Windows without a Unix shell, and it never prints anything the agent would see.

3.5 · Real, recorded hook inputs for starting a subagent, for a storytree tool call made inside it, and for one made by the orchestrator make three lines: the subagent's id, type and task; the subagent asking, by its id and type, with the call's id; and the orchestrator asking, with its call's id. The same holds for Claude Code and for Codex.

3.6 · Real, recorded hook inputs from before a shell command, after one that failed, and at the end of a turn make three lines: the command started and the command finished, both under the call's id, and the turn ended. For Codex, whose hooks the agent waits for, the hook hands its line to one in the background and exits.

3.7 · At each prompt, the project's definitions for the terms it names are added for the agent: whole words in any case or plural, every one not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (a prompt naming six gets all six), each once a session, each meaning's first line cut to 200 characters. A harness's own notice gets none, and with storytree stopped nothing is printed.

3.8 · The status line shows what this session holds, how many other agents are working, and a warning when another is editing a file it edited. With storytree stopped it says so, and outside a project it shows nothing.

3.12 · Real, recorded Claude Code and Codex hook inputs record on their session the transcript path the harness named (`transcript_path`), and a session's transcript reads as the latest one recorded for it. For a `claude -p` run whose transcript sits under a project directory unrelated to its `cwd`, and for a session whose `cwd` is now worktree B while its transcript sits under the project directory of folder A where it started, it is exactly the named path; no folder is searched.

3.13 · Each hook streams its session's new transcript records, and each subagent's (from <transcript>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl) under its parent session by the subagent's id, into the shared log, secrets scrubbed (9.12), from where the last hook left off (a cursor read from the store), only whole records, never twice, and at most 2 MB per hook (ADR-0749 D3, D4).

3.14 · Lines a hook writes while storytree cannot be reached (not running, or the store refusing) wait on this machine under the storytree home, each with the time and machine it was written at; the next hook that reaches the log uploads them before its own, oldest first, at their own times, and each line exactly once, however many hooks try (ADR-0749 consequences).

3.15 · Real, recorded prompt inputs make a prompt line on their session (without the prompt's words), for Claude Code and Codex alike, and a Claude Code Stop always makes a turn-ended line carrying how many background tasks are still running (ADR-0754 D5).
3.16 · Every line a hook writes records the git branch its folder is on (even one with no commit yet), beside the folder; a folder on no branch records none (ADR-0754 D4).

3.17 · When a turn ends with its session's work resolved and no standing close-out, the Stop hook's output reminds the agent to close out; a session that is idle or has exited is never prompted (ADR-0758 D4).

3.19 · A Claude Code session's end is recorded even though Claude Code stops its end hook after 1.5 s and the store takes longer than that to answer: run as setup registers it (with `--background`) and cut short at 1.5 s, the hook hands its line to a copy of itself that outlives it, and the session-ended line lands.

3.18 · A Codex hook that runs, in any folder, notes on this machine that Codex runs storytree's hooks; they read as waiting while registered and not yet run since, and a later registration reads as waiting again.
contracts.description: Codex runs a hook only once the user trusts it, which storytree cannot read (Codex keeps it as its own hashes), so a hook that has run is the proof the connect step, the setup check and the app show.

reported.note: codex-trust.test.ts: red first (expected running, got waiting: no hook noted it), green after runHook notes Codex hooks.

capabilities.title: 4 · Sessions
capabilities.description: Reads the agent activity log as a list of agent sessions, one per Claude Code or Codex window, each showing which of the two it is, which folder it works in, when it started and when it was last seen. A session is working from a prompt until its turn ends, or while a command it started runs, and waiting otherwise (ADR-0754 D5); ended once its end line arrives. A session whose hooks report no turns (no prompt line: hooks not running, or installed before D5) is working while its lines keep arriving and waiting after the quiet time, the user's `idle-after` setting (capability 10, 10.10; ADR-0739 D2), 30 minutes when unset. So it never reads as working just because nobody said otherwise.

contracts.title: 4.1 · A start line makes a working session labelled "Claude Code", with its folder, when it started and when it was last seen.
4.2 · A session whose hooks report no turns reads as waiting once no line has come for longer than the quiet time, and after its end line it reads as ended.
4.3 · A resumed window continues the same session instead of starting a second one.
4.4 · A Codex session whose hooks never ran, but which calls a storytree tool, still appears and is flagged "hooks not running", so a missing hook never looks like an agent doing nothing.

4.5 · A command that started 40 minutes ago and has not finished keeps its session working. Once it finishes, or its turn ends with no background task left running, it no longer counts, and one started longer ago than the longest a command may run no longer counts.

4.6 · A session is its harness session id, never a folder: one whose lines name two folders reads with both as its worktrees, in the order it first worked in each, while its folder stays the one it started in (ADR-0749 D2).

4.7 · A session with no line for longer than a command may run (12 hours) and no end line has stopped reporting: it reads as gone, never as ended, since nothing said it ended; up to that limit it reads as idle (ADR-0749 consequences).

4.8 · Working comes from turn state (ADR-0754 D5): a prompt makes its session working until its turn ends, however long the turn writes no line, and compacting mid-turn does not end it; its end makes it waiting at once; a turn that ends with background tasks still running leaves their command running, so the session stays working until it finishes.

4.9 · Who is listed (ADR-0754 D4): a session whose branches (every branch other than main its lines name, a merged line's excepted) still hold open work stays listed whatever its end line or silence says; once its work resolves (the latest branch-state line for each branch says resolved), a session leaves on its end line or after the leave-after quiet time, counted from its last line or the resolution, whichever is later; a session the Claude or Codex app keeps (a session-archived or session-unarchived line names it) shows done instead of leaving, is removed at once when archived, and comes back when un-archived.

4.10 · Each branch a session worked on is marked resolved once a pull request from it merged (asked of GitHub from any machine), or, on the machine it was worked on, once it has nothing ahead of the main line or is deleted (a branch with no commit yet is neither); one still ahead stays open, and one worked on again after it resolved is looked at again and reads open when it is ahead. A branch-state line is written only when the state changes, on the session that saw it (ADR-0754 D4). The hooks take this look once a minute through a copy of themselves that may run longer than a hook, so a merge is recorded though GitHub answers later than a hook may run. A claim's `merged` line resolves its branch as a branch-state line does, until a later look reads it open.
4.11 · Closing out records whether the session says it is safe to close, and why, and the session carries it (ADR-0758 D2).

4.12 · A yes is checked, never trusted: it leaves the list at once when its branches are resolved and nothing of its own runs; otherwise it stays and needs you, naming the disagreement; a no stays with its why; a later prompt or new admitted claim voids it (ADR-0758 D3). Closing out first asks whether the project’s branches have merged, so a merge no hook recorded still bears a yes out.

4.25 · The sessions the Claude desktop app and Codex keep are read, read-only, from their own files on each machine (Claude's claude-code-sessions/<account>/<org>/local_*.json: cliSessionId and isArchived; Codex's state_5.sqlite threads: id and archived, headless runs and subagents excluded), and each session the project's log knows gets a session-archived or session-unarchived line when its state there changes, never otherwise. Absent files read as absent and damaged ones as unreadable, and neither writes anything (ADR-0754 D4).

4.13 · The sessions listing (`storytree session list`) first asks whether the project's branches have merged, so it never waits on a hook to have recorded a merge, then shows each session the list shows, one block each, with its state, listing, folder, open and resolved branches, close-out and what needs you; a hidden one (a verified close-out) only with --all; --json gives the same sessions as data.

4.18 · The hooks reap a worktree once it can go (ADR-0790): a clean linked worktree whose head is in the main line, whose every session (at least one) has a verified close-out or is archived, which is not locked and holds neither the hook's folder nor a registered hook script, is removed and unregistered and its branch deleted; a dirty, unmerged, locked, unused, still-used, protected or hook-running one stays; its folder is moved to a trash folder first and the trash emptied out of the hook's way.

4.19 · How the app that keeps a session names and describes it reaches the log: for each session this project knows, the Claude desktop app's title and its post-turn summary's status, or Codex's thread name (else its title), are written as one `session-described` line (by whichever session read the records, never on the session it is about), scrubbed as transcripts are and held to 120 and 300 characters, and written again only when those words change. Each session read from the log carries the latest title and status.

4.20 · A line about other sessions (a claim's merge, a branch's state, what an app keeps or how it names a session) never makes its writer a session: a person, or the app, that only looked is not listed, and an agent's look does not count as its own work.

4.21 · The app looks at each project's branches itself, once a minute while it runs, asking from the latest folder this machine still has and writing under app:<machine>, so its sessions list never waits on a hook to have recorded a merge.

4.22 · A session reads, for each folder its lines name, the branches recorded there, in the order first recorded, with whether each still holds open work and, while open, its pull request as the latest look read it (4.24). The main line is no branch; a branch with no folder is placed in the folder the session last worked in.

4.23 · A session reads the commands it started and has not seen finish, each with its command text and start time, background ones a turn left running included: the same reading that keeps a session working (4.5, 4.8).

4.24 · The branch look reads every open pull request of the project's repository in one GitHub call, alongside its merged-pull-request call, under the same once-a-minute stamp and fail-soft rules: for each open branch, its number, whether it is a draft, its head commit's checks taken together (pending, passing or failing; none when it has none), and whether it waits in the merge queue. The branch-state line carries these and is written again only when one changes; GitHub not answering erases nothing; a pull request closed unmerged leaves the branch open with none. The Session reading carries them on each open branch in branchesByFolder.
contracts.description: Lets the sessions list label a worktree with where its pull request stands (ADR-0824 D2), from the same once-a-minute branch look that resolves merges.

capabilities.title: 5 · Claims
capabilities.description: Before building a capability, the agent claims it with a one-line reason, so the user and the other agents can see who is on what, and every edit its session makes while holding the claim counts toward that capability. Only one live session can hold a capability: a second agent is refused with the holder's name and picks other work instead of queueing, and a claim ends when the agent lands or releases it, when its session ends, or when another agent takes it over after the holder has gone idle.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Session A claims "email form", and the claim shows A and the reason.
5.2 · B's claim on it is refused, naming A. Once A has been idle past the quiet time, B's claim succeeds.
5.3 · When A reports it landed, the claim ends and a "landed" line is written. A release, or A's session ending, also ends it.
5.4 · A claim on a capability the library doesn't have is refused, and when two agents claim at the same instant exactly one wins.
5.5 · An edit made while A holds "email form" counts toward it, and an edit from a session holding nothing counts as unplanned activity.
5.6 · While a command A started is still running, past the quiet time, B's claim on A's capability is refused, naming A.

5.7 · Session A claims a proposed increment, and the claim shows A and the reason while the library shows the increment active; B's claim on it is refused, naming A. A ready one starts the same way, an active one is not started again, and a closed one is refused.

5.8 · Claiming an increment whose own wait holds, or whose arc's wait holds, is refused, naming each blocker and its reason, and one held on an open question is refused as waiting on the owner. Nothing is written and the increment is not started. Once the wait releases, the claim succeeds.

5.9 · A claim on a capability is refused when every open increment naming it is waiting, naming what they wait for. It succeeds when one of them is not waiting, and a capability no open increment names is never refused.

5.10 · A claim taken on branch `feature/signup` ends with a "merged" line once GitHub shows a pull request from that branch merged after the claim was taken, found at the next tool call or hook line; a pull request merged before the claim, or still open, ends nothing.

5.11 · The public readings list current capability and increment claims and find the holder of one unit, with the same live or idle result on the terminal and the board. Released work and a unit in another project have no holder.

5.12 · Claude Code session A makes a workspace for a proposed increment: a new folder where its harness keeps worktrees, on a fresh branch cut from `origin`'s main as just fetched (a commit pushed after the clone is in it), and A holds the increment there, the claim naming that branch, and the increment is active. For Codex, preparation fetches main and returns its exact commit and a work-derived name for the app's `create_worktree`, without creating a folder, branch or claim. The agent then attaches the app's returned directory: Storytree verifies it is a linked worktree of this repository with HEAD at that exact commit, names a detached HEAD `codex/<name>` (keeps an existing named branch), and claims the work for that session on that branch. Moving `origin/main` after preparation does not change the expected commit.

5.13 · Making a workspace for work another live session holds, or for waiting work, is refused naming the holder or the blocker, and no folder, branch or line is made; for work the session already holds it is refused naming the branch it holds it on. Codex checks before app creation and again when attaching; a claim lost to another session between the steps is refused naming that holder, leaving the app's worktree untouched.

5.14 · When main cannot be fetched fresh, as from a folder with no `origin`, it is refused saying why, and nothing is claimed or started. Attaching a directory from another repository, the main checkout, a subdirectory, or a worktree at the wrong commit is refused without claiming or changing it. If attaching fails after taking the claim (including naming a detached branch), that claim is released; the app's worktree is never removed (a started increment stays active).

5.15 · A claim cancelled while waiting for the activity lock or the increment activation write lock leaves no claimed line, activation or activation history. A capability or already-active increment claim checks cancellation before its claimed line too. Once admitted, a claim completes normally; a workspace claim creates or attaches its workspace only after admission.

5.16 · A claim's reason is its session's name in the running-sessions list, so it is held to 40 characters (measured from the list's label column at its default width): a claim, or a workspace, whose reason is longer is refused naming the limit and the reason's length, nothing is written and nothing is started; a reason of 40 characters or fewer is claimed as before (ADR-0737 D2).
5.17 · A holder last seen on this machine before it restarted is taken over at once
contracts.description: A session whose lines name this machine and were last written before this machine last started cannot still be running: its claim reads idle at once, so the lane resuming its work claims it (logged as taken over from the dead holder) instead of waiting out the idle-after window. A holder last seen after the restart, or on another machine, stays protected until idle-after, as before.

capabilities.title: 6 · Agent tools (the MCP server)
capabilities.description:
The toolbox the agent calls, served as an MCP server: plan work (arc, story, capability, contract), see the plan and who is on what, claim or release a capability, report a contract red or green, report a capability landed, say a capability is built so it is no longer proposed (`mark_built`, ADR-0744 D2), and search, read and write artifacts (plus list and add a node's front covers, once the library has them). Each tool is a thin wrapper over the library API and the claims above that answers in a short plain sentence the agent can act on, and every artifact read is logged in the agent activity log (ADR-0624); a new artifact with no place named goes onto the claimed capability's shelf of front covers (ADR-0627 D4, which redirected ADR-0624's default link).

As built: the 6.21 MCP cancellation checks cover claim, make_workspace and attach_workspace before and after library admission. They wait for their blocking and observing database connections to disconnect before removing the throwaway project. An admitted claim still finishes normally; this corrects the test teardown, not the cancellation contract.

contracts.title: 6.1 · A test client talks to the server inside the test itself, with no real agent and no network. It lists the tools, then plans an arc, a story, a capability and a contract, which then appear in the library's tree, the story and the capability each with its founding decision as the first book on its shelf, and it can correct each of them.

6.2 · It claims the capability and the increment it drives, sees both named with their holders in the plan and its data, reports the contract red and then green (the library shows the agent's report going from failing to passing, while the verified column stays "not checked"), and reports the capability landed, which ends the claim.
6.3 · Every call is recorded against the session that made it, using the session id the harness passes, and the machine it ran on.

6.4 · A bad call, such as an unknown capability, gets a readable refusal rather than a crash, and with storytree stopped every tool answers "storytree isn't running, carry on without it". If the database accepts TCP but never completes a fresh handshake, a tool call gives up at the 3-second connection deadline, including its library open, and says storytree is not reachable with what to check before retrying. A later call on the same tool server recovers when the database answers.

6.5 · An artifact written with no place named while holding a capability claim goes onto that capability's shelf as ADR-0627 D4 says, even with a newer increment claim; one with no capability claim gets no default place.

6.6 · Searching and opening an artifact leaves a log line saying which session read it, how it was found (a search result, a link from another artifact, by id, or from a shelf) and whether it took a peek or the whole artifact.

6.7 · Each read also names the agent that made it: a subagent by its id, type and task, or the orchestrator, as the harness revealed them (Claude Code through the hook's line for the call, Codex on the call itself), and "unknown" for a call the harness said nothing about.

6.8 · After Claude Code's `/clear`, which gives the window a new session id the tool server never sees, each call is recorded on the new session, as the hook before it named it; a call no hook saw keeps the id the tool server was started with.

6.9 · The test client parks an increment on an arc, readies it, starts it by claiming it, and closes it landed with its pull request, which ends the claim; the library shows each step and the arc reads closed. It records a landing that was never parked, parks a new increment on the closed arc, which re-opens it, and parks and unparks the arc.

6.10 · It sets a wait with a reason, and a claim on the waiting increment is refused naming it; it clears the wait, and the claim succeeds. A wait that would close a loop gets the library's refusal as a readable answer.

6.11 · It raises a question on an arc and holds an increment on it, which a claim then finds waiting on the owner; it settles the question with his answer, which releases the increment, and retiring a question an increment is held on is refused.

6.12 · It records friction with concrete evidence and a re-steer with the owner's quoted words, the agent's account kept apart; friction whose evidence is vague prose, a re-steer whose evidence quotes nobody, and a defect with no failure mode are each refused as a readable answer, and nothing is written. Shared capture stamps the calling branch and UTC date, and refuses a fourth friction report on that branch that day, counting routed reports too; the refusal names the cap and points to friction reinforce.

6.13 · It corrects an artifact's wording in place: the artifact keeps its id and takes the new words, only the fields given change, and an artifact that is not there, or a field its kind does not have, gets a readable refusal.

6.14 · It retires a contract and then a capability with a reason, and each is gone from the plan, its history keeping it. An id that is not a capability or a contract gets a readable refusal, and nothing is retired.
6.15 · Reinforcing friction through the tool or public capture function appends dated concrete evidence to the same item and preserves its route. Invalid recurrences write nothing.

6.16 · Every library write made by the tools names the calling session in history, including every record a compound call writes, increment starts, Claude Code's session after `/clear`, and Codex calls made by a subagent. A refused write leaves history unchanged, including a question whose requested holds include a missing increment or another record kind.
6.17 · Another story registers tools on this server beside its own, sharing project routing and the session log, and its short instruction line reaches the agent with the habits card.
6.18 · Another story supplies `land`'s final next line when needed, with none when it is not. A refused landing asks for none, and a failed follow-up keeps the successful landing explicit.

6.19 · It makes a workspace for an increment (`make_workspace`, 5.12): a worktree on a fresh branch from `origin`'s main, where Claude Code keeps its own, with the claim held by the calling session and the way into it named (`EnterWorktree` with its path); for work another session holds it gets a readable refusal naming the holder. For Codex, `make_workspace` instead returns instructions and the exact `ref` and `name` for the app's `create_worktree`, then `attach_workspace` takes that returned folder, ref and name and claims its verified branch. The agent uses the returned directory explicitly; an app registration error with a returned worktree is not a reason to create another. Attachment refusals say the app's folder is kept.

6.20 · An edit_plan call cancelled by MCP while its library write is still queued for the project write lock leaves the record and its history unchanged. A write already admitted completes normally and remains attributed to the calling session.

6.21 · MCP claim, make_workspace and attach_workspace calls cancelled before claim admission leave no held claim, claimed activity line or increment activation. A cancelled make_workspace creates no worktree or branch; a cancelled attach_workspace leaves the app worktree unchanged. Calls already admitted complete their claim, activation and workspace operation with the calling session retained in activation history.

6.22 · A test client calls `read_context` as session S and gets S's reading (session, harness, tokens used, when, source) worked out at the time of the call (9.5), including after S's transcript has grown with no turn ended; after a `/clear` whose hook named session T, the same call returns T's.
6.31 · `search_notes` answers with the library's ranked search (capability 14 of the library story), taking an optional `limit`, and says why when it fell back to words.

6.23 · `mark_built` switches a capability's proposed flag off once the agent considers it built, and back on (built: false), with the session as its writer; anything but a capability gets a readable refusal.

6.24 · A tool call a hook saw writes its `tool-called` line and every `note-read` it records naming that hook's `tool-requested` line as their cause, joined by the harness's call id. A call no hook saw names no cause, and nothing is guessed from timing (ADR-0746 D2).
6.26 · `open` on a contract shows it whole: its title, its description and the capability it belongs to, as it shows an artifact; an arc still gets a readable refusal.
contracts.description: An agent that finds a contract with search_notes can open it and read it whole (increment_c4b9051ec2de).

reported.note: Test 6.26 in agent-tools.test.ts; landed in PR #305.

contracts.title: 6.27 · `correct_question` corrects an open question's wording in place through the library's editQuestion (12.7): only the wording fields given change and it keeps its id; a settled question is refused with its answer standing, and a missing question or no words given get a readable refusal, with nothing written.
contracts.description: A session using only the agent link's tools can fix an unanswered question's wording, as `storytree question` / library edit can since PR #296 (increment_2d3b0027b274, friction_0805d54752f9).

reported.note: Test 6.27 in agent-tools.test.ts; red pushed, green on the increment_2d3b0027b274 branch.

contracts.title: 6.28 · `move_increment` moves an open increment to another arc through the library's moveIncrement, keeping its id, with the session as writer and the reason in its history: the target arc then lists it and the old one does not. A closed increment, a closed or missing arc, and a missing increment get a readable refusal, with nothing written.
contracts.description: The move gets both front doors (ADR-0793): the command line landed in PR #313 (storytree arc increment move); this is the agent link's half (increment_5e88ebc83dde).

contracts.title: 6.29 · `show_plan` gives each capability's word, and for one that is not healthy its reason, who moves it and the contracts carrying it, in its text and its data.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D1, through the agent link.

contracts.title: 6.30 · health_worklist gives the oldest three capabilities on the health worklist, each with its reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when, and how many more wait; a capability an open increment touches is not offered.
6.32 · name_session names the calling session, latest call wins
contracts.description: A session names its own row in the sessions list with a short one-line title (40 characters or fewer, as a claim reason is held), and renames it by calling again when its work shifts. A longer title is refused naming the limit. The command line's `storytree session name` does the same.

contracts.title: 6.33 · The built storytree-mcp command, started as a harness starts it, serves the agent's tools over stdin and stdout, and exits when stdin closes.
contracts.description: ADR-0838 D4: the tool server's entry point, which harnesses start for each session, proved as built.

contracts.title: 6.34 · A tool call a hook saw works in the folder that hook was run in, the session's worktree, not the folder the harness started the server in: a claim it takes carries that worktree's branch, so its merge ends it. A call no hook saw, or one whose hook named a folder of another project, works in the server's own folder.

6.35 · A re-steer whose evidence is the user's exact words without quotation marks is refused with the step that passes, putting those words inside double quotation marks, and the same words inside them are then recorded (regression: Conduit 3 on the reset laptop, 2026-10-02).
contracts.description: In Conduit 3 (packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build/runs/conduit-claude-turn-31.txt) an agent gave record_resteer the user's sentence verbatim, without quotation marks, was told to "quote what the owner actually said", retried with a shorter exact excerpt, still without them, and gave up: the re-steer was never recorded. The check is syntactic (a quoted excerpt), so the refusal says what it checks. increment_9f9bf0367bf5.

capabilities.title: 7 · Instructions (the habits card)
capabilities.description: One short text, a screen or less, that teaches the agent storytree's habits: plan the story first, claim a capability and open the knowledge it needs before touching it, write the failing test and report red, make it pass and report green, report it landed, and record an artifact for anything worth remembering. The tool server hands this text to the agent at the start of every session, as its instructions; Claude Code reads it from there. Codex (0.158 on) does not: it shows the model neither a tool server's instructions nor its tools until the agent searches for them, so connecting Codex also writes one short marked section into the AGENTS.md in Codex's home that sends the agent to check_setup before its first change in a storytree project and keeps it silent elsewhere (7.4; measured 0 of 3 without, 3 of 3 with, packages/app-setup/evidence/codex-first-session).

contracts.title: 7.1 · The text names every tool the server has, and no tool the server lacks.
7.2 · The text is no longer than 60 lines.
7.3 · The tool server hands the text to the agent at the start of every session.

7.4 · Codex, which hides a tool server's instructions and tools until the agent searches for them, is told through the AGENTS.md in its home to call check_setup before its first change in a storytree project, and to ignore storytree in any other folder: one marked section, written again changes nothing, the user's own text kept, removed exactly.
contracts.description: Codex 0.158 always defers MCP tools and does not show a server's instructions, so the habits card never reaches a Codex session; its home's AGENTS.md does, trusted hooks or not. Measured on the owner's Windows laptop: 0 of 3 untrusted first sessions called check_setup without the section, 3 of 3 before their first change with it (packages/app-setup/evidence/codex-first-session).

reported.note: codex-agents.test.ts passes; connect writes/removes the section (connect.test.ts 2.2). PR storytree-ai/storytree#320.

contracts.title: 7.5 · The card says who decides what
contracts.description: The card handed at session start names the kinds of decision the agent makes and records, the kinds it asks the owner about, that it checks the owner's standing delegations first, that the user's own instructions file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) overrides that split either way, and the honesty promises no file moves: it never signs off its own output, never skips tests, and writes a question rather than only asking in chat (ADR-0842 D1, D2).

contracts.title: 7.6 · The app shows who decides what, read-only, from the card's own lines
contracts.description: The owner sees, without asking an agent, the same split the habits card hands every agent (the kinds the agent decides, the kinds it asks about, that the user's instructions file overrides them, the promises no file moves), with nothing on it to edit, and the project's standing delegations when its library defines them (ADR-0842 D4).

capabilities.title: 8 · Setup check
capabilities.description:
The only thing the user installs is the storytree tool server, once, with the one-line command Claude Code or Codex already uses for any MCP server, and after that every session start checks storytree's setup and fixes whatever is missing on the spot. It opens storytree if it is closed, registers the hooks if they are missing (walking Codex users through Codex's one-time approval), and in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet it asks the user, through the agent, whether to set one up. It also says whether Claude Code or Codex is signed in and whether git and a usable Node are there, naming the fix for each that is missing, and never waits on a tool that does not answer (ADR-0716). It registers hooks for each harness home it finds except a harness the user disconnected from storytree (the app setup's contract 2.5), which gets its hooks back only when it is connected again. It also puts the `storytree` command on the user's path (contract 8.9): a shell script, or on Windows a small program of its own that hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it (ADR-0854).

As built (increment_e0065ed16d5a, PR #452, contract 8.20): check_setup asks the agent to write .storytree-check with its own file-editing tool. Once this session's edit hook has arrived, each check file it names is deleted at the recorded path, resolving relative paths against that hook line's folder, including a worktree different from the tool server's folder, even while other hooks are missing. A file the operating system refuses to remove stays for the agent. The repository deliberately does not ignore .storytree-check: a leftover remains visible as evidence that the edit never arrived or cleanup failed.

contracts.title: 8.1 · In a throwaway home with only the tool server installed, the first session start registers the hooks for Claude Code and for Codex without touching any other setting.
8.2 · A second start changes nothing, and removing storytree takes out exactly what it added.
8.3 · With storytree closed, a session start opens it.

8.4 · In a folder that is not a project, check_setup says the folder is not a storytree project and that the user can add it (Add project in the app, `storytree doctor --set-up <name>`, or asking their agent), without telling the agent to offer setup (ADR-0752 D3), and nothing is created until the user asks. A successful yes creates the project and folder marker, then durably records that project as the user's choice for the app. A refused or failed setup does not report success or change the remembered choice; if saving the choice fails, the folder marker is restored to its previous state so the explicit setup can be retried. An ordinary session start, an existing-project setup check, or a repeated setup tool call in an already configured folder records no choice. The setup tools' input and output shapes remain the same (ADR-0657 D3).

8.5 · The agent fires a test of each hook (a session start, a call to a storytree tool, a file edit, a command), and the connection shows as verified only when storytree has received every one. Until then it names the missing hook and the fix, such as Codex's one-time approval.

8.6 · Live check: a real Claude Code session and a real Codex session, each in a new empty folder set up as a project by the installer's folder step (or `storytree doctor --set-up`), with nothing else configured by hand, and told "add a sign-up form, with tests", show up live, plan, claim, report red then green and land, and the agent activity log and the library show all of it. A second session that ignores storytree and only edits a file shows up as unplanned activity. *Subscription-billed: run once, as the final proof.*
