contracts.title: 8.7 · A status line of the user's own is kept: storytree's is installed only where there is none, and removing storytree leaves theirs.
8.8 · With `gh` missing, signed out or signed in, the check never asks the agent to install or sign in to it; a person running the check in a terminal sees a note of what gh is for (ADR-0751).

8.9 · In a throwaway home, the first start puts a `storytree` command on the path, a second changes nothing, and removing storytree takes it out. On Windows, where the command is a program of its own (ADR-0854), `storytree setup remove` run through it exits 0 with the command off the path when it returns, its file deleted once it has exited, and the user's own settings kept (regression: storytree-ai/storytree#83; proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason on other systems).

contracts.title: 8.10 · A terminal runs the shared check without an agent session and gets diagnostic lines and fixes, including when the app is stopped. Checking creates no project; an explicit setup request creates it, and the next check reports it ready. Where hooks are present, a `transcripts` line says each session's transcript streams into the shared log, obvious secrets are scrubbed before they leave the machine, the scrub is best-effort, and raw records are kept 180 days (ADR-0749 D4).

8.11 · The check says whether Claude Code or Codex is installed and signed in, naming the fix when neither is ready; a missing or old git or Node is a note, never a fix (ADR-0751); a tool that does not answer is reported as not answering within seconds, never waited on.

8.12 · At the start of a session in a folder that isn't a storytree project, no hook adds anything to the agent's context, for Claude Code and for Codex, an older install's asking start hook included; nothing is set up (ADR-0752 D3).

8.13 · The setup check has an archives line: ok, naming how many sessions the Claude desktop app and Codex each keep, when either record can be read; otherwise a note (never a fix) that says why and that sessions on this machine leave the running-sessions list after the leave-after time instead of when archived (ADR-0754 D4).

8.16 · Until one of Codex's hooks has run, the check says Codex waits for the user to trust them, with the one step in plain words (type /hooks in Codex, or answer "Hooks need review"), also where it registers no hooks (the app's folder check); once one has run, it says they run.

capabilities.title: 9 · Context readings
capabilities.description:
How many tokens a session's own context window holds, worked out when it is asked for from what the hooks recorded (ADR-0725, ADR-0728; 0.2's `storytree context`, ADR-0716 O2). The hooks record each session's transcript path (capability 3). A reading is computed at ask time from that transcript as it stands, so it is fresh mid-turn, and in a `claude -p` run whose turn has not ended. On the session's own machine (the status line, `storytree context`) that means the transcript file itself. The app reads no transcript file: its readings and windows are parsed from the transcript records the hooks stream into the shared log (3.13; ADR-0749 D3), so an app on any machine reads every machine's sessions. Those records have obvious secrets scrubbed on the way in (9.12) and are kept 180 days, after which what was worked out from them is kept instead (9.13; ADR-0749 D4). A reading is a plain record: the session, its harness, tokens used, when it was read, and its source (the transcript it was read from). It carries no window size and no fraction (ADR-0728 D1). The guidance a session judges against is a token figure the user sets on the agent link settings surface (capability 10, `context-guidance`; ADR-0728 D2, D3). A reading states that guidance and whether tokens used are past it or under it (9.7); it is a soft line, never enforced. The same figure is the line past which a Claude Code session is nudged, through the prompt hook (capability 3), to hand off and start fresh (9.9; ADR-0739 D1): one setting, no second figure, and 0.2's separate 850,000 hard mark is not brought across. The nudge is advice; nothing stops the session. Codex sessions get no nudge until Codex matures (ADR-0739 D5). This capability owns the nudge because whether a session is past its guidance is this capability's reading (9.7); the prompt hook only carries the words. Built with advice once per session; later prompts in the same session do not repeat it.

For Claude Code, tokens used are the latest request of the session's own conversation: `input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens`, counted once per `requestId`, with subagent (`isSidechain`) and `<synthetic>` lines left out. A transcript with nothing to count is an absence with its reason, never 0. For Codex, tokens used are the rollout's last token count. Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking, so the board can later show one per session; that display is not built here. It reads and never enforces: the session still decides whether to take on more work.

The transcript is always the one the hooks recorded as named by the harness (`transcript_path`, on every Claude Code and Codex hook input). Nothing ever looks for a session's transcript by folder. That is what fixes 0.2's two blind spots. 0.2 worked out who was asking from the `.claude/worktrees/<name>` folder the command ran in, then matched transcripts whose recorded `cwd` sat inside it. A batch (`claude -p`) session run from a main checkout or from outside that folder was refused or matched nothing (0.2 friction `storytree-context-cannot-read-a-batch-sessions-own-window`). A session that moved into a fresh worktree kept writing its transcript under the project directory of the folder it started in, so the new folder matched nothing. And because worktree folders are reused, the fallback could read another session's window (0.2 friction `context-verb-blinded-by-the-fresh-worktree-its-own-rule-mandates`: no reading from the new worktree, 506,097 tokens from the old one in the same minute).

As built (guidance-reading): `contextReading` and `readContext` add `guidance` without changing the existing session, harness, tokens, composition, at or transcript-source fields. Guidance is `{ value, source: "default" | "set", position: "under" | "at" | "past" }`, read afresh through capability 10's `readSettings`; its default is 600,000 tokens (ADR-0739 D1). An unusable settings file gives `{ absent: <the reader's reason> }` while retaining an available token count. No transcript remains an absence with no token count. `storytree context` and `read_context` state the guidance in their text and include it in their data; a count under, at or past guidance is never refused. Contract 9.7 is pinned in `packages/agent-link/src/context/context.test.ts`, and the existing 6.22 MCP test checks guidance output.

Remaining integration for 9.7: the current library-location routing reads the same settings file before it can open the activity log (ADR-0735). If that file is already unusable when `storytree context` or `read_context` starts routing, the call cannot reach the transcript record; the reader's token-preserving guidance error is therefore not reachable through those entry points in that case. This lane does not guess a local library or bypass the settings reader. Resolving that routing dependency is outside its context/tools-output file fence. Contract 9.7 must not be marked fully proved until that end-to-end case is resolved. `packages/agent-link/evidence/guidance-reading/captures.txt` records both the successful reader case and the route refusal.

As built (fresh-nudge): the Claude Code prompt hook calls the existing `readContext` for the session named by the recorded hook input. It adds advice to hand off and start a fresh session at the next safe boundary only when that reading is past its current guidance, naming both tokens used and the guidance. Definitions and context advice use separate per-session ledgers through the definitions hook's extracted `notYetGivenIds` helper; each nudge is given once per session across separate hook processes. Under or at guidance, absent readings, unreadable settings, and Codex inputs add no nudge. No threshold or switch is added: the existing reading supplies the sole setting, including the default change owned by capability 10. The built-hook contract 9.9 test covers boundaries, changed settings, repetition, definitions alongside advice, Codex, and absence/recovery; every prompt exits 0 with no blocking decision. The existing 9.7 routing qualification above remains.

contracts.title: 9.1 · A recorded Claude Code transcript whose last own request used 12,000 input, 300,000 cache-read and 5,000 cache-creation tokens reads 317,000 tokens used; a request repeated across lines with one `requestId` counts once, and a later subagent (`isSidechain`) or `<synthetic>` line does not change the figure.
9.2 · A transcript that is empty, unreadable, or holds only subagent or synthetic requests reads as an absence naming which, never as 0 tokens.
9.3 · A recorded Codex rollout reads its last token count as tokens used (ADR-0728: no window size).

9.5 · A session's reading is worked out when asked, from the transcript last recorded for it (3.12) read at that moment (9.1, 9.3), and carries the session, harness, tokens used, when it was read and its source, with no window size or fraction (ADR-0728). Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking. A session with no recorded transcript gives an absence, and another session's transcript is never read.

9.6 · `storytree context`, run with the harness's session id in its environment, prints that session's tokens used, worked out at that moment (9.5), even mid-turn with no turn ended since the transcript grew, and `--json` prints the record; it exits 0 whatever the figure, states no window size or fraction, states the guidance as 9.7 says, and with no reading it says so and prints no number.

9.7 · A reading states the context guidance in effect (capability 10: set, or its default) and whether tokens used are past it or under it; with 400,000 set, 317,000 reads under and 450,000 reads past, and the command still exits 0. With the settings file unusable (10.4), the reading gives tokens used and says the guidance could not be read, and why.

9.8 · A Claude Code or Codex reading carries its composition: estimated tokens in four groups, sorted from the labels the harness put on each record, never from a body's words. Injected: the system prompt and tool list (the tokens of the first request, or Codex's first token count, less what the transcript recorded before it), Codex's base instructions and developer messages, project guidance, catalogues, hook output, reminders, file-change notices and harness-authored messages (for Codex, a user message it never recorded as the user's own). Grounding: what reading calls returned (file reads, searches, web and library reads, subagent digests, a shell command that only reads, such as a grep; a Codex exec cell whose every tool call only reads). Implementation: what changing calls returned (edits, writes, any other shell command, such as a test run; a Codex exec cell with any changing call, and a wait on it) and every call the session authored. Other: its own prose and reasoning, the human's words, and any label nothing sorts, named. Subagent lines and harness bookkeeping are left out; sizes are bytes at 3.8 characters per token, except an image (a screenshot read, a pasted picture), which counts at its pixels ÷ 750 tokens, at most about 4,800, as the model pays for it, never at its base64 length.

9.9 · A recorded Claude Code prompt hook input, for a session whose reading (9.5) is past the context guidance (9.7), makes the prompt hook add for the agent advice once per session to hand off and start a fresh session, naming its tokens used and the guidance; under or at the guidance it adds none. Later prompts in that session add no more advice, even if its reading crosses the guidance again; a fresh session may receive its own. It is advice: the hook still exits cleanly and the prompt is never refused. The same input from a Codex session past the guidance adds no advice (ADR-0739 D5), and with the guidance unreadable (10.4) or no reading, none is added.

9.10 · A session's window is read from its transcript (ADR-0746 D1, ADR-0756): the tool results it holds now (after the last compaction, with the segment Claude Code says it kept; never a subagent's side chain), each joined to the call that brought it by the id the harness wrote; each note or file it opened (the agent link's open, a shell's storytree library read, a file-read tool, a shell cat, head, tail or sed -n), in order, with whether that read is still in the window; and the notes it only glimpsed: named in a result it holds now but never opened, each once, in the order first named. Claude Code transcripts and Codex rollouts both read; nothing is inferred from timing or wording.

9.12 · Before a transcript record is stored, obvious secrets in it (API keys, bearer and OAuth tokens, private keys, connection-string passwords) are replaced by a marker naming what was removed ("[scrubbed: API key]", "[scrubbed: bearer token]", "[scrubbed: OAuth token]", "[scrubbed: private key]", "[scrubbed: password]"), and the record still parses; ordinary text passes untouched. The scrub is best-effort for obvious shapes, never a guarantee (ADR-0749 D4).

9.13 · The retention pass (the app runs it at each start) deletes raw transcript records older than 180 days; before they go, the session's context reading and window worked out from them are kept, and are what is read for that session from then on (ADR-0749 D4).

capabilities.title: 10 · Settings
capabilities.description:
The user's own settings for the agent link: read and written by this package, set from the command line and from the app's settings panel (ADR-0728 D2, D3; ADR-0729; ADR-0739; ADR-0649). Per user only: one file, `settings.json`, in the storytree home (`STORYTREE_HOME`, else `[home], capability 1) beside `project-choice.json`. Each setting has a name, a type, a default and a plain-language meaning. An unset setting reads as its default, marked as the default. A value of the wrong type, or a name that is not a setting, is refused with its reason and nothing is written. A settings file that cannot be read or is not valid is reported, naming the file and the problem; it is never silently replaced, and a set refuses to overwrite it.

The settings (ADR-0739, owner's choices of 2026-09-28):

- `context-guidance`, tokens, default 600,000. The owner changed it from 700,000 (ADR-0729's default, which matched 0.2's last soft mark): "can we change the context guidance to be 600k." A context reading states it and whether tokens used are past it (capability 9, 9.7). It is also the line past which a Claude Code session is nudged, through the prompt hook, to hand off and start fresh (9.9): one setting, no second figure, by the owner's words "Can we make the context guidance cover the nudge as well - should be one setting." 0.2's separate 850,000 hard mark is not brought across, by that named choice (ADR-0633). The reader defaults to 600,000 (packages/agent-link/src/settings/settings.ts); the existing 10.1 and context-reading tests pin that value.
- `idle-after`, a duration, default 30 minutes: the time before a session is considered idle (the owner: "Idle after sounds like something we should have a configurable setting for maybe just rename it to time before session considered idle."). Node session liveness (capability 4), claim readings and locked claim takeover (capability 5) read the configured duration (10.10). The MCP server reads it once per call that needs liveness, so a running server sees a saved change without restarting; independent context readings still return tokens and explain unusable settings. The browser-safe readers accept an explicit quietMs and otherwise retain the 30-minute default; the forest display still uses that default until its bridge is updated in a separate step.
- `library`, where the library lives (ADR-0734 D1, ADR-0735): `local` by default, or `cloudsql` with the Cloud SQL instance's connection name (project:region:instance) and the Google account to sign in as: `storytree settings set library cloudsql <instance> <user>`, or `storytree settings set library local`. Stored in the same file as `{ "location": "cloudsql", "instance": …, "user": … }`. Routing (capability 1) reads it to say where a project's library is; the app (the app story's lifecycle) reads it to decide whether to start its local Postgres at all.

Not settings, by the owner's choice (ADR-0739):

- Storytree's Claude Code status line is always installed when the user has none of their own; it is not a switch: "since its built we can keep it but dont think it belongs as a configurable surface it should just be on."
- Term definitions per prompt: the cap of five is removed, not made a setting ("turn the cap off."; capability 3, 3.7).
- The longest a command may keep its session live (12 hours, LONGEST_COMMAND_MS) stays a fixed value, not exposed; so do the hook deadlines, database waits and merged-PR polling.
- Codex: no Codex nudge and no control over Codex's auto-compaction, deferred until Codex matures: "Dont add a setting to turn on and off codex nudge, lets not worry about building this feature for codex, when codex matures more then we will build it atm it feels like we need to let them sort out their bugs and user experience more." Codex has a PreCompact hook that could cancel auto-compaction, but hooks are reported unreliable in the Codex desktop app, and it offers no public off switch.

As built (settings panel, PR #182, #183): Settings in the app's shared gear overlay mounts the agent link's panel through @storytree/agent-link/view. It lists every reading with its value, meaning and default or set-by-you source, and saves through this capability's writers over desktop IPC. Context guidance uses a numeric text field; Library offers local or Cloud SQL with its instance and account fields; a newly listed setting of a plain type needs no panel change (10.7), so `idle-after` appears there once the reader lists it. Refusals appear inline verbatim; a read failure offers Retry. The app's overlay owns dismissal and the shared focus loop, including its sections and gear; closing returns keyboard focus to the gear. The reader, writer and update-on-next-open semantics are unchanged. Earlier panel evidence: packages/agent-link/evidence/settings-panel/. Current owner-review captures: packages/app/evidence/top-bars/. Appearance awaits the owner's acceptance.

As built (idle setting): `idle-after` is a duration string in the same per-user settings.json, default `30m`. Positive whole seconds (s), minutes (m), hours (h) or days (d) are accepted within the safe millisecond range. Invalid values such as `soon`, `0m` and `-5m` are refused with a reason through the command line and gear panel, leaving saved bytes unchanged. Settings show derives its list from readSettings. The gear labels the duration “Time before a session is considered idle” and uses a text input. The status line uses the setting for its session, claim and shared-file windows. A command still running keeps its session and claims live. Contract 10.10 covers default live/refused and configured idle/takeover after 15 quiet minutes, the running-command exception, and a setting change observed by the same MCP server. Component captures under packages/agent-link/evidence/idle-setting show the real gear/settings components in a preview page; native desktop smoke and owner appearance acceptance remain with the supervisor. The forest display's 30-minute default is the known remaining limit.

contracts.title: 10.1 · In a throwaway storytree home with no settings file, `context-guidance` reads 600,000, marked as the default, with its type (tokens) and its meaning.

10.2 · `storytree settings set context-guidance 400000` writes it to `settings.json` in the storytree home, and `storytree settings show`, and a fresh read by the agent link, give 400,000 marked as set.
10.3 · Setting a name that is not a setting, or `context-guidance` to a value that is not a positive whole number, is refused naming why, and the settings file is left as it was.

10.4 · A settings file that is not valid JSON, or holds `context-guidance` of the wrong type, is reported on read naming the file and the problem, never read as the default; a set refuses to overwrite it, and the file is left byte for byte.

10.5 · With no library setting, `storytree settings show` reads the library location as `local`, marked default; `storytree settings set library cloudsql <instance> <user>` saves the Cloud SQL instance's connection name and the Google account to sign in as, and reads back as set; `storytree settings set library local` returns to local.

10.6 · `settings set library` with anything but `local`, or `cloudsql` with an instance not written project:region:instance or a user that is not an email, is refused with the reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte.

10.7 · Settings in the app’s gear opens a panel headed Settings, with “Yours on this computer · all projects”. Every setting returned by the reader has its current value, meaning, and default or set-by-you source; values can be saved with capability 10’s writers. A newly listed numeric setting needs no panel change.

10.8 · A refused value shows the writer’s exact reason beside its row, leaves the settings file byte for byte, retains the saved source, and can be corrected and retried. A successful save reads back when the panel reopens. Library location uses the same local/Cloud SQL writer and reports that changes apply when the app next opens.

10.9 · A failed read of the Settings panel shows the failure's reason and Retry, never fabricated defaults in place of the rows, and Retry reads again; a save whose transport fails shows its reason and leaves Save available for retry. The overlay that holds the panel (its focus loop with the reachable gear, Close or Escape returning focus to the gear, and its fit at narrow window sizes) is the app frame's: The app 2.6 and 2.7.

10.10 · With no settings file, `idle-after` reads 30 minutes, marked as the default. With `storytree settings set idle-after 10m`, a claim whose holder was last seen 15 minutes ago, with no command running, reads idle and can be taken over, and a session whose hooks report no turns reads waiting, where unset the claim cannot be taken over and the session reads working; a session whose hooks report its turns is never judged by it (ADR-0754 D5). A value that is not a duration (such as `soon`, `0m` or `-5m`) is refused with its reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte.

10.11 · With no settings file, `leave-after` reads 1 hour, marked as the default; `storytree settings set leave-after 2h` sets it, and a value that is not a duration is refused with its reason and the settings file left byte for byte (ADR-0754 D4; default from ADR-0758 D5).

10.12 · `storytree settings set library postgres <address>` saves a postgres:// address (host, port, database, user, sslmode) and reads back as set; an address carrying a password is refused, saying to save it as the `postgres` key with `storytree auth set postgres`, and the settings file is left byte for byte (ADR-0846 D1).

10.13 · Routing reads a Postgres-address library as the library's connect options for that address, and the settings panel offers it as a third library location beside local and Cloud SQL, saved through the same writer.

stories.title: The app
stories.description: The app is storytree 0.3's desktop window. It starts and stops the database that holds every project's library, lists the storytree projects on the computer and shows one at a time, and hosts the surfaces that show the project on show: the forest, with the arc surface as an overlay the forest hosts. The page inside it cannot reach the database, so the app carries everything a surface reads. It keeps itself up to date (capability 4, added 2026-09-27, ADR-0637).

capabilities.title: 1 · Lifecycle
capabilities.description: When the app opens it starts the database that holds every project's library, and it keeps it running until the app is quit: closing the window leaves both running in the background, with a tray icon whose Quit stops them, so agents' work is still recorded. The app can also be controlled from outside (ADR-0656 D0): asking it to quit from the command line stops it as the tray's Quit does. There is one owner at a time: opening the app again brings its window forward, another program holding the database is named, and while it runs the app leaves records saying where the database is and how to open the app, which is how an agent's session finds it or opens it.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Starting runs the database on the app's data folder, it answers at the address handed back, and stopping stops it.
1.2 · A second start on a data folder that a live process holds is refused, naming that process, and its database is left running.
1.3 · A database left running by a process that died is stopped and replaced, and a dead owner's record alone is cleared.
1.4 · With the app's database stopped, an agent's session asking where to send its activity is told "storytree isn't running" in well under a second.
1.5 · A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: the answer comes in well under a second and never hangs.
1.6 · With storytree closed, an agent's session start opens it.

1.7 · Closing the window leaves the app and its database running; the tray's Quit, or asking the app to quit from outside (`storytree app quit`), stops them: it stops the database once, and the app exits only after it has stopped. Quitting, including smoke teardown and restarting into an update, stops the page's polling before closing the library, without logging a closed-library error.
1.8 · When the app starts, and once a day while it runs, it writes a snapshot of each project to `[home]<project>/`, keeping that project's newest 14 (ADR-0641 B1).
1.9 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, the app starts no local Postgres and opens its projects, surfaces and snapshots on the instance; quitting leaves the instance alone.

1.10 · With the library set to Cloud SQL and the instance unreachable (no Google sign-in, a refused account, or no answer in time), the window says so in the refusal's own words and what to fix, and the app never falls back to the local library.

1.11 · With the library on Cloud SQL, where the app starts no local database, the running app is still found (its launch record carries its process id): storytree app quit quits it, a stopped app reads as not running, and a delivery waits for the app itself rather than for a database it never starts.

1.12 · The installed app opens at sign-in, straight to the tray with no window, unless the user has turned that off in the gear's Updates section; a development copy, a portable build or a runtime slot never registers itself
contracts.description: So its release updater runs all day and the hooks it installed follow each release (question_44555a5ee60d, option A). On by default for an installed app; a development copy, a portable build or a runtime slot never registers itself. The off switch sits in the gear's Updates section and is remembered across starts.

reported.note: apps/desktop/src/main/sign-in.test.ts, merged in #372

capabilities.title: 2 · Storytree projects
capabilities.description: The app lists the storytree projects in its database and shows one at a time. Its always-visible, full-width top app bar holds only a gear at the right. The gear opens a large centred overlay with Projects, Settings, Updates and Help sections. Projects moves the whole app to another project in place; Settings mounts the agent link's per-user panel, Updates mounts the app's existing update status, and Help mounts app-setup's existing help surface. The separate arcs-only bar sits below the app bar and the forest starts below both. This capability also decides which project is on show when the app opens.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Projects in the gear overlay lists every project, with the one on show selected. Choosing another project switches the forest and closes the overlay; a failed choice shows its reason inside Projects and leaves the list available for retry.
2.2 · The list is read again every three seconds, including while empty; a first project appears without restarting, unchanged reads leave the surface alone, and closing the page stops polling.

2.3 · Reopening follows the latest successful explicit project choice, whether made in the picker or by saying yes to setup. A newer picker choice supersedes an older setup choice, and a newer setup choice supersedes an older picker choice. `--project` wins on launch and becomes the remembered choice when that project exists. A remembered project that has gone falls back to the first; an unknown explicit project is named as missing.

2.4 · After a successful setup yes, the chosen project is durably recorded and becomes the project on show on the next refresh, or on reopening. The last successfully recorded yes wins even when several setups complete between reads or while the window is closed. A project-list read never overwrites an explicit choice, including one recorded while that read is in flight; discovering a name alone does not count as choosing it (ADR-0657 D3).
2.5 · With no projects, the app tells the user to start Claude Code or Codex in a folder and say yes when asked to set it up.

2.6 · The gear opens a full-size centred overlay below the always-visible app bar, with space around it at wide and narrow window sizes. Clicking the gear again, pressing Escape, the Close button or clicking the backdrop closes it and returns keyboard focus to the gear. While open, keyboard focus stays within the overlay and its reachable gear, and the app behind it is inert; dismissal does not also activate the forest or close the arc drawer.

2.7 · The gear overlay has Projects, Settings, Updates and Help sections. The app owns the overlay frame, project switcher and existing Check for updates surface; the agent link mounts its existing per-user Settings panel; app-setup mounts its existing Help surface, including its first-run offer. Settings and updates retain their existing reader, writer and action behaviour. The section navigation has room to grow as settings are added.

2.8 · An always-visible full-width 48 px app bar holds only a 36 px gear at the right. A separate full-width 48 px arcs-only bar sits directly below it, with no project name. The forest and its controls start below both bars at 96 px, and the arc drawer opens below them. With the overlay closed, the forest receives pointer input below the bars or open drawer. The backdrop click that closes the overlay is consumed; subsequent forest input works. The existing data-state and data-drew smoke readings remain valid.

capabilities.title: 3 · Surfaces
capabilities.description: The app's window hosts the surfaces for the project on show: the forest, which the app opens on (until it lands, today's plain list), with the arc surface as an overlay that the forest hosts. The page cannot reach the database, so the app carries everything a surface reads to it, and tells the surfaces when the project changes.

contracts.title: 3.1 · The page can ask the app for the library's changes and the agent log's new lines since a point, for the project on show, and only newer ones come back.
3.2 · A name that is not a project is refused, and never created.
3.3 · The smoke check, pointed at the surface on show, passes only if that surface says it drew every story and capability of the project.
3.4 · The page can ask the app for a story's or capability's shelf of front covers, and for the artifacts that link to an artifact, for the project on show.

3.5 · The page can ask the app for the context readings of named sessions in the project on show (agent link 9.5, 9.8), each parsed from the transcript records in the shared log, with no access to the machine the session ran on (ADR-0749 D3); a session with none named reads as an absence, and a name that is not a project is refused.

3.6 · The page can ask the app for a session's window in the project on show (agent link 9.10), or several sessions' in one ask that reads the log once, parsed from the transcript records in the shared log, with no access to the machine the session ran on (ADR-0749 D3); a session with none named reads as an absence.

3.7 · The Surfaces menu lists every surface with its switch and its settings; a surface switched off is saved to the settings file and reads back off, and one that follows it goes off with it; switching an always-on or unknown surface, or to an unknown choice, is refused with its reason and the file is untouched.
contracts.description: ADR-0750's Surfaces menu: what the menu shows and how a switch persists. ADR-0838 D4: its view and switches gain a contract their existing tests carry.

contracts.title: 3.8 · The page can ask the app for the project's standing delegations
contracts.description: For the project on show, the page can ask for the register its library keeps as the definition "Standing delegation"; a project without one answers with none (agent link 7.6).

capabilities.title: 4 · Updates
capabilities.description:
The app keeps itself up to date by itself: on the owner's machine it runs from its own copy of merged main, notices new merges within a few minutes, and rebuilds and restarts itself in the background, so it never runs unmerged work and nobody rebuilds it by hand. Check for updates in the top-right gear asks that same merged-main updater to check now and shows the running build and its progress or failure. A ready build restarts once no seed is writing the library. A checkout explains that it does not update itself. Before first users, an installed app does the same from published releases. As built (increment_aca4e6853237): an installed app's downloaded release waits for a quiet moment (packages/app whenToInstall: ten minutes after launch, ten minutes without window input or agent activity from a session that has not ended), because a first install was replaced 17 seconds after setup said the app was open (packages/app-setup/evidence/acceptance, F1). The gear answers from the release updater in an installed app, marks itself with a dot while an update is pending, and its Restart to update installs at once. A seed still holds any restart. The owner accepted contracts 4.4 and 4.7's wording for this on 2026-09-29 (question_df551985ad62).

As built (increment_c3e1441890f9, contract 4.12): installed release updates read named, independent run holds under the app home/update-holds before each automatic installation. packages/app/src/updates/hold-run.mjs wraps a foreground command, publishes its hold before launch, removes it on return and preserves its exit code. Holds expire after the requested positive duration, at most six hours; overlapping runs do not release one another. Downloads continue, the pending status names the run, and the user's Restart to update still overrides holds while respecting seed writes. The standalone wrapper and usage/proof are in packages/app/evidence/update-hold. No laptop acceptance run is part of this implementation.

contracts.title: 4.1 · When merged main moves, the app is built at main's new commit beside the one running, and work not merged to main is never run.
4.2 · A build that fails leaves the running app as it is.

4.4 · An installed Windows app checks for a newer published release, downloads and verifies it, and installs it only at a quiet moment: not in the first ten minutes after a launch, not while the window has been used or an agent session has worked in the last ten minutes, and never while a library seed writes; the user can install it at once from the gear, which shows a pending update. Installing stops its database and restarts through the installer into the new app using the same lifecycle handoff as the development updater.
4.5 · A failed release check or download leaves the app running and can be retried; equal and older releases never replace it, concurrent checks share one download, and quitting stops updates.
4.6 · Releases contain only work merged to main and verified on all three systems; every later main build has a higher version, and a rerun cannot replace a newer published release.
4.3 · After each update, the app that follows merged main checks its own verified health
contracts.description: After restarting into a new merged-main build, the app runs `pnpm check:own-health` from that running slot in the background, against its own library. Its window and database remain available. The check joins the running app's database through `appLibraryServer` with `writes: true`, holding the writing lock so an update cannot restart the app while the check runs. The check's output and failures go to `[home] (or the same file under `STORYTREE_HOME`). A failed check never stops the app and is tried again at the next update. Reopening the same build does not repeat the attempt. When the `library` setting names a Cloud SQL instance, the app runs no check and records nothing: CI's run on main is the one writer of the shared library's verified health (ADR-0744 D3), and the app's log says so in one line. This contract applies to the app that follows merged main; installed releases do not run checkout scripts.

contracts.title: 4.7 · Check for updates in the gear checks now, using the same updater as the automatic check: merged main where the app follows main, published releases where it is installed. Concurrent requests share the work. If no newer build is needed, the menu says the app is up to date and identifies the running build.

4.8 · The menu shows when a new build is building, ready or restarting. A ready build updates and restarts the app through the existing lifecycle, waiting while a seed writes the library; waiting neither rebuilds the ready commit nor starts a second restart.
4.9 · A failed manual update check or build shows its reason, leaves the running app alone, and can be retried from the gear.
4.10 · When the app was started from a checkout rather than a runtime slot, Check for updates explains that it does not update itself; the request neither fetches a build nor restarts the app.

4.11 · Setting up the app that follows main refuses while the app is running, naming its process; otherwise it builds merged main in the runtime folder and starts the app from that build, in the background unless asked to show its window
contracts.description: `pnpm app:follow-main` (ADR-0637 D2): the one-off setup of the app that follows merged main never replaces a build a running app may be using; "running" is the app's database owner process being alive.

contracts.title: 4.12 · A named acceptance run can hold automatic release installation until it releases its hold or a finite ceiling expires; overlapping runs keep independent holds. Downloads continue, and an explicit Restart to update still installs once no seed is writing.

stories.title: The forest
stories.description: Each project is its own 3D forest that grows as its agents' work lands, and any story opens to explain itself in plain words. Every story is a story node carrying a grove, one tree per capability: a tree grows as its capability lands, and its leaves show what the agent reports about its tests. The agents at work show at the capabilities they hold, and work done while holding no claim is listed beside the forest.

capabilities.title: 1 · Story nodes
capabilities.description: The forest keeps one story node for every story in the project: where the story sits in the forest, with its title and its overall health. Nodes follow the library, so a new story appears as a new node and a retired story's node goes, with nothing arranged by hand.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Three stories give three story nodes, each with its title and its overall health as the agent reports it.
1.2 · Adding a story to the library adds a node, and retiring a story removes its node.

1.3 · A story's place is its row by dependency depth and its slot in the row: the bottom row has the story most depended on in the middle and the rest outward, a higher row is ordered by where its dependencies sit, each row is packed round the globe's front with the sea gap between neighbours, and a loop in the dependencies never stops the layout (ADR-0839).
1.4 · A story's island sits north of every story it depends on; stories that depend on nothing share the bottom row; the rows run evenly from about 42° south to 42° north (ADR-0839).
1.5 · Adding a dependency moves the dependent's island up a row (ADR-0839).

1.7 · A growing island moves its row's neighbours along the row and nudges islands in other rows aside, each staying within a bound of its row position and clear of the rest; islands in other rows that fit never move (ADR-0804 D7, ADR-0839 D3)
1.8 · When a row no longer fits round the globe or nudging cannot make room, the globe's radius grows until no island overlaps another (ADR-0804 D7, ADR-0839 D3)
1.9 · Where the code survey names stories' package dependencies, a story's row is by those, not by its capabilities' dependsOn; a project without them keeps the roll-up (ADR-0840 D2).
contracts.description: A code edge the plan never recorded still places the island. Protected by packages/forest/src/story-nodes/story-nodes.test.ts.

contracts.title: 1.10 · A five-story forest opens with every nameplate readable, in a row and in a chain
contracts.description: At the app's default view, a five-story project whose stories depend on nothing (one row) and one whose stories each depend on the last (a chain) show every story's nameplate: none hidden, no two overlapping on screen, and every island facing the eye at least half on, not squeezed at the rim.

reported.note: settlePlates steps crowded plates down (ADR-0855 D1), plates wrap to 112 px (D2), opening faces the islands' middle (D3). In-page: row 5/5, chain 5/5, storytree 14/15 (Keys turned away), 0 overlaps.

capabilities.title: 2 · Capability tree
capabilities.description: Each story node carries its capability tree: the story's capabilities, which ones build on which, and where each one stands, from planned through built to landed, and it grows as they land. Where a capability stands comes from two records kept side by side: the arc surface's rule for planned, in progress or landed, and the health the agent reports for its tests, always labelled as the agent's own.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A story with four capabilities, planned, being built, landed and reported passing, and landed with a failing report, gives a seedling, a seedling, a full green tree and a dead tree, in build order, each with the capabilities it builds on.
2.2 · A capability the agent reports red while it is being built stays a seedling.
2.3 · A landed capability with nothing reported is a pale tree.
2.4 · A story with no capabilities yet shows one seedling, so a new story is never invisible.

capabilities.title: 3 · Story node render
capabilities.description: The page opens in Forest mode, drawing every story node and its capability trees on the globe with the library core beneath them. Forest / Library switches this one globe (ADR-0660 D4): Library hides the story nodes and shows the knowledge points alone. You can turn and zoom in either mode, hover a visible artifact dot to see its title, and click a dot to read its summary in the right-hand story-panel slot (ADR-0661 D1/D2). Forest also lets you open a story by clicking its island. An artifact card and a story panel replace one another; Close and Escape dismiss the card. Switching modes preserves the scene, camera, rotation and zoom. Each launch defaults to Forest, with no saved mode. The flat forest and separate Look-inside view remain unavailable (ADR-0655).

contracts.title: 3.1 · The app opens a seeded project on the globe in Forest mode; its smoke check finds one story node per story, each drawn with its capability tree.
3.2 · A capability landing redraws just its story node, without a reload.
3.3 · Clicking a visible story node selects it, opens its story panel and closes any artifact card.
3.4 · Each near-side story node shows its story's name, readable as the globe turns and zooms (ADR-0636 D4: in 0.2 the names lived on the 2D map the owner cut, so the 3D forest carries them).
3.5 · The globe’s glass shell has a nearly clear middle, admitting at least 80% of the far-side contribution through both faces, with a bright rim and one soft highlight; there is no opaque sea.
3.6 · Every recorded "builds on" link has exactly one continuous trail chain; shared trunks are drawn once and their width counts the original links.
3.7 · A cross-story link docks at both actual clipped shores and continues to its capabilities.

3.9 · Choosing Library hides every story node, including trees, names, claims, failure markers, selection rings, pathways and island overlays; only the core points at their computed depths and the separated no-shelf artifacts are drawn. Choosing Forest restores the surface.

3.10 · Switching either way preserves the canvas, scene, core, camera, rotation and zoom. Library remains orbitable; choosing it clears story selection and its panel, and hidden islands cannot be picked. A new launch defaults to Forest.

3.11 · In Forest mode a failing island (one with a capability storytree verified unhealthy, never the agent's report alone) is never hidden: opening faces a failure; a far-side failure has an edge marker whose click reveals it, including after returning from Library. Library is the viewer's explicit choice to hide story nodes (ADR-0660 D4, ADR-0825 D3).

3.12 · In Forest and Library, hovering an eligible artifact dot shows its title and a pointer cursor, and clicking within 8 CSS pixels picks the nearest projected dot. Forest rejects far-side dots behind the shell and dots behind land; Library admits every on-screen drawn dot. Off-screen or clipped dots cannot be picked, and movement of 5 CSS pixels or more is a drag rather than a click.

3.13 · Clicking an artifact dot opens its summary card in the right-hand story-panel slot and closes the story panel. Opening a story replaces the card. Close and Escape dismiss the card, and none of these actions writes to the library.

3.14 · Each capability is one connected, bordered territory on its story's island, its share of the island following its share of the lines of code (the island may grow to fit its files' circles, 3.19); Unclaimed code is its own territory (ADR-0804 D2, D3)
3.15 · Clicking a capability's territory selects that capability, as picking it in the story panel does (ADR-0804 D2)

3.16 · Every surveyed code file is one flat circle lying wholly inside its capability's territory and on the land, never overlapping another or stacked, spread over the territory's room; its diameter grows gently with its lines, 1.2 + 0.14·√lines (a 1,000-line file about 5.6 across), with no per-island scaling (ADR-0804 D3)
3.17 · Pointing at a file circle names the file, its lines and its capability (ADR-0804 D3)

3.18 · The land wears the session's traversal (ADR-0804 D5): the forest hands the knowledge core each file circle's place on the globe, and the surveyed imports between files, and a file circle the selected session opened is lit in the session's colour with the in-view ring (a compacted one lighter, no ring), and a capability's territory it opened is filled in the session's colour; everything else stays as it was.

3.19 · A surveyed island's land follows its story's lines of code, with a floor so a tiny story stays visible, and grows beyond that until its files' circles all fit at full size (3.16), its neighbours making room as any growing island's do (1.7, 1.8); an unsurveyed island keeps its capability ratio (ADR-0804 D3, D7)

3.20 · Each capability's territory is filled by its word (ADR-0744), in three colours only: healthy green, unhealthy red, and yellow while it is proposed or untested; a claim never changes the fill, and no territory is grey (grey is kept for mapped). Unclaimed code stays neutral (ADR-0825 D3)
contracts.description: The land says what storytree verified about each capability, not an index tint and not the agent's report.

capabilities.title: 4 · Drill-down
capabilities.description: Clicking a story node opens a panel that explains the story in plain words: its sentences, and its capability tree, each capability pointing at the ones it builds on, including any in other stories, named with their story. The tree has a space of its own inside the panel, where the user drags it around and zooms it; it opens zoomed out to fit the whole tree, as far as the least zoom allows, and an icon in that space's corner opens the same tree in a larger window over the forest, which opens fitted too. Each capability's card says proposed, healthy, unhealthy or untested on a strip coloured as 0.2 coloured those words, with the agent's report and storytree's as labelled marks (ADR-0743, ADR-0744). Clicking one of the story's own capabilities, in the panel's tree or in the larger window, shows it below the panel's tree: its sentences, its health as the agent reports it, and its contracts on request (ADR-0659).

contracts.title: 4.1 · A story whose third capability builds on the first two gives its sentences, its capabilities in build order each with its sentences and its health as the agent reports it, and a diagram with exactly two arrows.
4.2 · A capability that builds on a capability in another story shows an arrow to it, named with that story, and that capability's card says its word.
4.3 · A capability with no description says "no description yet" instead of leaving a blank.
4.4 · A contract the agent reported red, then green, shows "red, then green"; one reported only green says so.
4.5 · Storytree's own column shows beside the agent's report only where something wrote it.

4.6 · The panel shows the story's sentences and its diagram, and below the diagram only the capability selected: its word, its sentences, its health as the agent reports it, and its contracts folded until asked for. No front cover shows in it.
4.7 · When a story opens, the capability shown is the first in build order that has not landed, or the first if all have; one clicked stays shown, and a choice outside the story falls back.

4.8 · Each of the story's capabilities is a card you can click, marked when selected and tinted by its word (a healthy card edged green, an unhealthy one red), never by the agent's report; another story's capability is in the tree but cannot be clicked.

4.9 · The capability tree is a graph of fixed-size cards: each capability sits above the ones it builds on, and another story's capability sits one row below the capability that builds on it, not in one row with every other outside capability.

4.10 · Each card, another story's too, has a strip across its top saying its word, proposed, healthy, unhealthy or untested (ADR-0744), coloured as 0.2 coloured it (proposed amber, healthy green, unhealthy red, untested grey), and the agent's report and storytree's as marks labelled "the agent reports" and "storytree saw", storytree's only where something wrote it. The work state (planned, in progress, landed) is not on the card.

4.11 · The capability tree has its own space inside the panel, moved by dragging and zooming, with no scroll bars and never out of reach. It, and the larger window, open with the whole tree fitted in the frame and centred, never above full size nor below the least zoom; the larger window's "Fit" puts that view back. An icon in the panel space's corner, labelled "Open in a larger window", opens the larger window.

4.12 · The capability selected, when it is not healthy, says why under its word and who moves it (the agent, or you), naming the contracts that carry it; a contract whose last verdict was not re-run says "last seen failing <date>, not re-run since"; a healthy one says nothing more.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D1 and D2 on the card: the library's derived reason (library 5.8) and the verdict an entry did not reproduce (5.7).

contracts.title: 4.13 · In a project whose health nothing verifies, a built capability's card and detail lead with what the agent reports, labelled as the agent's, and say storytree does not check this project's tests yet, never untested or who moves it
contracts.description: ADR-0630 in the story panel, for a user's project: a first user is not told tested work is untested and the agent's to fix (increment_ef066f718a63).

capabilities.title: 5 · Agent capability claims
capabilities.description: Draws each session that has a row in the running-sessions list (capability 7) as one wisp orbiting the island of each story it holds a claim in (ADR-0736), replacing the claim dots of ADR-0730. Each session has its own stable colour, the same on its wisps and on its row; hovering a wisp highlights its row and hovering the row highlights its wisps. A wisp carries no visible agent name, reason text or hooks warning. It follows the agent link's claims and sessions, so a holder whose hooks have reported fades after the quiet time; a holder whose hooks have never reported is never faded as idle. Subagents and supervised lanes folded under a parent get no wisp of their own, nor does a session with no row; there are no build wisps, exploring hovers or waiting queues (ADR-0635). Missing hooks are reported by the agent link's setup check (capability 8, contract 8.5).

contracts.title: 5.1 · Session A claims "email form", and one wisp in A's colour orbits that capability's island, with no visible agent name or reason text; when A also claims a capability on a second island, a second wisp of A's orbits that island.
5.2 · For a holder whose hooks have reported, after the quiet time with no new line its wisps fade; when A reports the capability landed and holds nothing else on that island, its wisp there goes.
5.3 · A session seen only through its tool calls keeps its wisps unfaded even past the quiet time; the map draws no hooks warning.
5.4 · None of this changes how a capability's state is drawn.

5.5 · A session's colour is the same on every read, on its wisps and on its row in the sessions list, and is never the proven-green colour; hovering its wisp highlights its row, and hovering its row brightens its wisps. A subagent folded under its parent, and a session with no row, draw no wisp.

5.6 · A capability a running session claims has its territory's border outlined, inset, in that session's colour, fainter once the session is quiet; the territory's fill still says its word (ADR-0825 D3, narrowing ADR-0804 D9)
contracts.description: A claim is drawn on the border so the fill stays free for health.

capabilities.title: 7 · Running sessions
capabilities.description: A full-height, see-through panel at the forest pane's left lists one plain row per session that has not ended, claimed or not (ADR-0749 D1; ADR-0737 D1's removal of off-plan rows and their evidence stands, and capability 6 stays retired), showing facts as labels and no prose on the owner's behalf: anything that needs the owner is an open question on the arc surface (ADR-0824). An unclaimed row is named from its harness and what it works in; a session working in several worktrees says so (D2). Each row shows what it is doing, its context bar and its available context total. Explicitly related subagents and supervised lanes fold beneath their parent behind “+N”. Each row has one expander (the same control as “+N”), closed at first; expanded, it lists each worktree the session works in (full path on hover) labelled unmerged or merged, the commands it started and has not seen finish, and the files in its window, read from the agent link's window reading (9.10) only when expanded, then its children. No row uses a state colour; each root row wears its session’s own colour, the colour of its wisps on the forest (capability 5, ADR-0736), and a hovered wisp highlights its row. Hovering or focusing a row lights its claimed islands and dims the others. Waiting rows stay plain, working and waiting read from each session's turns (ADR-0754 D5); rows neither working nor waiting fold into one idle row by their state alone; ended sessions are hidden. Parent relationships and totals are read only when recorded or supplied by the agent link; missing values are not guessed.

contracts.title: 7.1 · The list includes once each session the agent-link reading lists (agent link 4.9, 4.12), whether or not it holds a claim: a session holding unmerged work stays even after it ended, while a verified close-out, or an ended or quiet session with no open work past the user's leave-after setting (1 hour by default, read as idle-after is), is excluded (ADR-0754 D4, ADR-0758 D3, D5, narrowing ADR-0749 D1 and ADR-0737 D1). Sessions at work come first and the rest fold into the idle row (7.10). A waiting row stays plain; working and waiting come from the session's turns (agent link 4.8), and only a session whose hooks report no turns is judged by the user's idle-after setting. A row's task uses its claim reason or held increment title; a session with neither is named from its harness and what it works in (its latest claim's branch, else its last folder), held to 40 characters, and never labelled off plan. A session whose lines name more than one folder shows how many worktrees it works in, naming them on hover (D2).

7.2 · An explicit parent relation or subagent-started record folds that child under its parent behind the row's “+N” expander (7.8), closed at first as every row is (7.8); expanding reveals its task and collapsing hides it again. No child is duplicated at the top. A recorded subagent lacking its own session reading is shown as observed, without inventing a live state; absent parent relations are never inferred from claim wording.

7.4 · Hovering or keyboard-focusing a row lights the forest islands containing its held capabilities and its descendants’ held capabilities and dims the other islands. Leaving the row restores the ordinary forest appearance. With no held island the row does not arbitrarily select one.

7.5 · Every row reserves an empty context-bar slot. When an agent-link context total is supplied the row displays that total; when absent it displays an unavailable mark, never zero. This increment draws no composition segments, thresholds or estimated totals.

7.6 · Each row's bar is its session's tokens used (agent link 9.5), read again every 10 seconds, on one scale for every row: 1,000,000 tokens across the full width (the display's choice; a reading has no window size, ADR-0728). A Claude Code reading's bar is split into Injected, Grounding, Implementation and Other in proportion to its composition (9.8), and hovering gives the tokens and each group's estimated share; a Claude Code row marks its reading's context guidance (the user's setting, 600,000 by default; ADR-0739 D1), one mark; a row whose reading carries no guidance has none; a Codex row is one raw segment with no marks. With 400,000 tokens split 2:2:3:1, the segments are 10%, 10%, 15% and 5% wide. The list's header names the four groups in bar order, each beside a swatch in its segment's colour.

7.7 · The list hands the knowledge core its rows as the core's roster, each row with its children in the row's colour. Clicking a row selects its session in the core and marks the row (a child's row selects its parent); clicking the selected row again goes back to every session. The list and the core share one selection (ADR-0738).

7.8 · Every row has one expander, an arrow at the row's start, closed at first, opening only when the user expands it; a row with children counts them as “+N” after its name (7.2's control, not a second one). Expanded, a row lists, under a small “Worktrees” label, every worktree it works in, oldest first, each by its folder's own name with its full path on hover and its merge label (7.15); then its “Running” block (7.16); then, under a small “Files” label, the files in its window (agent link 9.10), each once, in the order first opened, with files no longer in the window muted; then its children. Files are read from the agent link's window reading only when a row is expanded, never from a second reader; a session without a window reading says why and lists no files. Collapsing hides the detail and the children again.

7.9 · The running-sessions list shows facts as labels and prints no prose about a session: no 'needs you' chip or line, no close-out why, no 'holding unmerged' line. A row folds as idle, and counts in the header, by its state alone (working, or waiting within the idle-after time). Owner decisions surface only as open questions on the arc surface (ADR-0824 D1, D2, narrowing ADR-0758 D1).

7.10 · Listed sessions that are neither working nor waiting within the idle-after time fold into one "N idle" row, collapsed at first, which expands to list them, whatever their close-out or unmerged work; a finished desktop window its app keeps unarchived counts there, never hidden (ADR-0758 D5, superseding ADR-0754 D4's dimmed "done"; ADR-0824).

7.11 · A session whose close-out is unverified (a no, or a yes the facts disagree with) stays listed, and its row folds and counts by its state alone, showing neither a mark nor a reason for its close-out (agent link 4.12; ADR-0758 D3 as narrowed by ADR-0824 D1).

7.12 · A session holding unmerged work (agent link 4.9's open work) stays listed, even after it ended, wherever its row sits; its row prints no line about it, the fact showing only as its worktrees' "unmerged" labels (7.15) (ADR-0754 D4, ADR-0824 D2).

7.13 · When the listed sessions run on more than one machine, each row names the machine its session runs on (the latest its activity lines name), beside its name; when they all run on one machine, no row names one.

7.14 · A row whose session holds no claim is named by its app's title (agent link 4.19), held to the label limit, before falling back to its harness and place. Expanding any row opens with up to three lines describing it, from recorded words only: the app's title where the row's name is not it, the objective of the increment it holds, and the app's latest status. A row with none of these shows no description.

7.15 · Each worktree in a row's detail carries one short label from the branches its session recorded there: "merged" when none still holds open work; for an open branch with a pull request, "PR #n" and what it waits on (in merge queue, draft, failing, or in CI while its checks run), or "PR #n" alone when its checks pass or it has none; "unmerged" when no open branch there has a pull request read. The main line, or no branch, carries no label; a branch recorded with no folder is folded under the folder last worked in, and none is dropped.

7.16 · An expanded row's Running block lists the commands its session started and has not seen finish, background ones included, each by its first words (one line, ellipsised, full command on hover) and how long it has run.

7.17 · The list is a strip along the forest pane's bottom, spanning its width (up to 40% of the pane tall, scrolling vertically inside, never horizontally), see-through so the globe shows behind it. Its header (name, count, colour legend and a caret) hides and expands the whole list like the arcs bar's handle: it starts expanded, collapsed leaves only the header, and the choice is kept per project in the page's storage (a missing or foreign value reads as expanded). Every row starts collapsed and its expander opens it (7.8), with no expand-all control; an expanded row lays its Worktrees, Running and Files side by side, in one column when narrow. The strip keeps clear of an open story panel and of the stale-forest mark.
7.18 · A session that has named itself is listed by its own name
contracts.description: A row is named by the session's own name (its latest, from the agent link's name_session or `storytree session name`) ahead of its claim reason, its held increment's title and its app's title; until it names itself the row reads as before, ending at harness · folder. Eventually consistent: a rename shows on the next reading.

capabilities.title: 8 · Code survey
capabilities.description: Surveys each story's package (one package per story, ADR-0649) and reports its source files: each file's lines of code, test files excluded (ADR-0804 D3); the capability each file belongs to (ADR-0804 D4); and the relative imports between source files, which the island traversal draws as its solid steps (D5). Code outside every story's package (forest-world, local-postgres, scripts/) is not surveyed (D8). Founding decision: ownership is derived from the contract numbers the tests name, and capability records gain no file list (ADR-0804 D4). A test title naming contract "N.M" pins capability N of that test's story; a test file reaches the source files it imports, following relative imports and a package index's re-exports; a file belongs to the capability whose numbered tests reach it most. A file no numbered test reaches falls back to its top source folder when that folder's name matches a capability's title slug; otherwise it is Unclaimed ground on its story's island. Code lives in packages/forest; where the survey reads the repository (the app's main process or the command line) keeps the frame and the front door thin.

contracts.title: 8.1 · A source file a test titled "N.M …" reaches belongs to capability N of that test's story, whether the test imports it directly or reaches it through any number of further ordinary imports and re-exports. When tests of several capabilities reach it, the capability whose tests reach it nearest (fewest ordinary imports away; a re-export adds none) owns it, then the one whose tests reach it that near most, then the lower number.
8.3 · A file's lines of code are counted for source files only: a test file, or a test helper under a testing/ folder, adds no lines to any file, capability or story.
8.4 · A relative import from one source file to another is reported as a link from the importing file to the imported one.
8.5 · Surveying the checkout again reads no file that has not changed since the last survey (same path, size and modified time), and reads a changed file again.
contracts.description: The survey may lag the checkout but must not re-read every file on every tree read (ADR-0836 D2): an unchanged story returns the same survey, a changed file is read and surveyed again.

contracts.title: 8.6 · A source file a numbered test's runs executed, in its own process or one it started, belongs to the capability whose tests executed it most (the package's coverage map); a direct import outranks it, and it outranks a file reached only through further imports.
contracts.description: ADR-0838 D3: where import tracing cannot reach because a test runs the code in a process it starts (the command line's tests spawn the built binary), coverage allocates it.

contracts.title: 8.7 · A source file a numbered test reaches only through type imports (a file of types, or one imported only for its types) belongs to the capability whose tests reach it so nearest, then most; any reach by a value import or by running it outranks a reach by types.
contracts.description: ADR-0838 D4: a file of types has no code a test can run, so the imports that name its types allocate it, after every other reach.

contracts.title: 8.8 · Each surveyed story names the stories whose packages its package depends on, through any dependency field of its package.json.
contracts.description: ADR-0840 D2: the code's story edges, for the forest's rows. Protected by packages/forest/src/code-survey/read-survey.test.ts.

stories.title: The arc surface
stories.description: Over the forest, one read-only top drawer shows the project’s arcs as dense two-line lanes, with queued arcs behind their blocker’s caret and a bar for each root lane’s increments: what has landed, what an agent is on right now, what is queued behind other work, and what is waiting on you. Picking an arc opens its briefing, with what the arc is about and the questions waiting on your answer, and every state is worked out from what storytree has recorded, never typed in.

capabilities.title: 1 · Work states
capabilities.description: Every part, increment and arc shows exactly one state, worked out by one rule from the records, so no two views, and no two lines of one view, can disagree. A part is planned, in progress or landed; an increment, once closed, is landed or not completed (failed, withdrawn, or closed with nothing recorded), and before that is waiting on you, queued, held by an agent or open; an arc is waiting, blocked, claimed, idle, quiet, parked or closed.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A part no line names is planned. A claim makes it in progress, a landed report makes it landed, and a new claim after landing makes it in progress again.
1.2 · A part that is released, or whose window closes, without landing stays in progress, with nobody on it.
1.3 · A story is planned while every part is planned or it has no parts, landed once every part has landed, and in progress otherwise.

1.4 · A closed increment reads landed only when a landing was recorded or it carries a pull request. Every other close, whether failed, withdrawn or closed with nothing recorded, reads not completed (red), with the hover naming which. Nothing reads landed merely because it closed.

1.5 · An open increment gets one reading, first match wins: waiting on you (held on a question you have not settled; it drops back the moment you settle it), then queued (its own wait, or its arc's, still holds), then held (an agent holds it, idle or not), then open. A proposal reads open, and never waiting on you. An active increment whose agent released it reads open, still in progress, with nobody on it.

1.6 · An arc reads one state, first match wins: closed or parked, as recorded; then waiting (a question on it you have not settled); then blocked (its own wait still holds); then queued (every open increment is held, on a wait or on you, and it names what it waits on); then claimed (an agent on its work is live); then idle (every agent on it is idle); then ready · N to take (N open increments nobody holds and nothing holds up); then quiet (nothing open). Queued, ready and quiet are read from its increments on every live reading (ADR-0760 D1).

capabilities.title: 2 · Agents on the board
capabilities.description: Every increment and part an agent holds shows which agent: Claude Code or Codex, when its window opened, the reason it gave when it claimed, and whether it is live or idle, and for how long. It reads the agent link's own claim reading, so the overlay and the claim tool always agree, and an idle holder still holds its work.

contracts.title: 2.1 · An increment Claude Code holds shows "Claude Code", when that window opened, and its reason. Two Claude Code windows are told apart by when they opened.
2.2 · After 30 quiet minutes the holder reads "idle for N min" and still holds the increment. Once it releases or lands it, its window closes, or its pull request merges, nobody is on it.
2.3 · A Codex holder whose hooks never ran is flagged "hooks not running".
2.4 · An arc's holders are the agents holding its increments, or a part its increments name, and nobody else: an agent on a part none of its increments names is not on the arc.

capabilities.title: 3 · Arc surface
capabilities.description: A full-width arcs-only bar sits below the app story's separate gear-only app bar and opens one read-only drawer over the forest. The bar carries no project name. Both bars reserve their space above the forest so its controls remain reachable, and the drawer opens below them. The drawer leaves the forest usable below and lists root arcs as dense two-line lanes (state chip and title, then small bars and count), with a bar for each increment, finished work first, each bar coloured by its work state, a count of what landed and what is open (never a percentage), and a chip with the lane's state and who is on it; Active, Parked and Closed each show their own arcs. It stays current while it is open: about every two seconds it asks for what changed in the library and the agent log, which the app carries to it, and it re-checks the clock once a minute, so an agent that goes quiet turns idle without any new record.

contracts.title: 3.1 · A full-width 48 px bar labeled Arcs sits directly below the app's separate 48 px gear-only bar, spans the whole window and carries no project name. Clicking either end opens or closes the drawer below both bars; the bar also works from the keyboard and Escape closes it, returning focus to the bar. The forest and its controls remain below both bars and receive input below the closed bar or open drawer while the app overlay is closed. The gear remains reachable above the arc bar and open drawer at wide and narrow window sizes. No action writes library data, and it carries no Library switch or artifact links. While its first read is on the way it says so, and a read that fails says so rather than drawing an empty board.

3.2 · Each root lane has a state chip and title on line one, then small separated bars and the count on line two. It has one bar per increment, finished ones first and then open ones, longest-waiting first. Its count reads like "3 landed · 1 not completed · 2 open", skips zeros, and is never a percentage.

3.3 · Lanes sort waiting, blocked, claimed, idle, quiet, then the most recently active. An idle chip carries its age on its face ("idle · 42 min"), and its hover names who holds what. Active shows on the first launch, then the saved scope is restored; Parked and Closed show only their own arcs, and there is no "All".
3.4 · In the app: a claim written while the overlay is open shows on it within about two seconds, without reopening.
3.5 · In the app: with no new line, a holder turns idle once the quiet time passes. The test uses a stand-in clock.

3.6 · In the app: the smoke check visits every scope and opens every root queue caret, then judges document.body.dataset.drew.arcSurface against the expected root lanes, expanded queue chips, root-lane increment bars and their agent marks. It does not count +N descendants or queued increments as drawn bars.

3.7 · Between launches, each project remembers drawer open/closed, scope and selected arc. A valid saved arc is restored; if it disappears the normal briefing fallback applies. Closing keeps scope and selection for the next open.
3.8 · The app's Surfaces menu lists the arc surface as Arcs, with no settings, on until the user switches it off; switched off, it is saved and reads off at the next launch (ADR-0750)
contracts.description: The arc surface's own declaration, read through the app's Surfaces menu: the user can turn the arcs bar off (the globe then gets the full height) and it stays off.

capabilities.title: 4 · Waits
capabilities.description: Every arc or increment that waits on other work says so and names what it waits for: an arc queued behind another arc folds away under that arc’s lane, behind a ▸/▾ caret in a fixed gutter; expansion shows chips, and an increment waiting on another increment, on any arc, draws yellow and names its blocker and why. A blocker shows what it holds up, a wait that will never release by itself says so, and an arc with something waiting on you is never hidden under its blocker.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An arc waiting on an open arc, or whose every open increment waits on work in another open arc, appears only as a chip under that arc's initially collapsed caret, not also at the top; waiting on several, it sits under the first on the board. Selecting the chip opens the queued arc's briefing. Once the wait releases, or it has work nothing holds up, it returns to the top, with nothing written. Waits that form a loop are cut at the loop's first arc on the board, so no arc disappears (ADR-0760 D1).

4.2 · A one-behind-one queue draws as a chain (A → B → C). Two arcs behind one blocker draw as a set, with a · separator and no arrow between them. A queued arc that holds up others carries "+N", one also waiting on another arc says "+1 other wait", and one queued by its increments names the increment it waits on in the arc above it.
4.3 · An arc with a question waiting on you stays at the top while it waits on another arc, and its other open bars still read queued.

4.4 · An increment waiting on another names it, its arc and the reason, and the blocker names what it holds up. If the blocker closed without landing, or cannot be found, the wait says it will not release by itself.

capabilities.title: 5 · Briefing
capabilities.description: Picking a lane, or a queued arc, opens its briefing: what the arc is about, then the questions waiting on your answer there, with the questions you have settled below, under their answers. “Open ↗” replaces the question list with the full reading, and “← back to questions” restores it. The reading is statement first, with its stakes, diagram, options as for and against, a recommendation marked not binding, and the longer parts folded with their word counts, so you can read it whole without leaving the overlay.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Picking an arc shows its intent, then its open questions under "Waiting on you", or "Nothing is waiting on you here", then a note that "blocked" comes only from waits. The drawer restores a valid saved selection; otherwise it opens on the first arc with a question waiting on you (or the first lane).

5.2 · “Open ↗” swaps the list for one full reading; “← back to questions” restores the list. The full reading is statement first, then stakes, the diagram or "no diagram stored", options split into for and against, the recommendation marked not binding, and analogy and context folded with their word counts. Each row in the list shows its word count and whether it has a diagram.
5.3 · A settled question moves under "Settled" with its answer, and stops counting as waiting.

5.4 · A parked arc's briefing lists its open questions under "Parked with the arc" (they wait for it to be unparked), never "Waiting on you", and a parked arc's question does not pick the drawer's first briefing
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D2: parking an arc parks its questions too, off the owner's list until the arc is unparked.

stories.title: The command line
stories.description: `storytree` is the command a person types in a terminal to read and change their project's records. It is a front door and nothing more: each command is handed to the function its owning story already has (the library, the agent link), so the command line and the agent's tools can never disagree.

capabilities.title: 1 · Front door
capabilities.description: `storytree <family> <verb>` works out which project the folder you are in belongs to, opens that project's library, and hands the command to the owning story's function, keeping no rule of its own. Every answer is a short plain sentence or listing; where it names records it may offer, under `next:`, the commands that open them, and nothing else (ADR-0786). A failure exits non-zero and says what to do; a command it does not have answers with the real one for that job.

contracts.title: 1.1 · In a project folder, `storytree library search <word>` finds an artifact written through the library.
1.2 · In a folder that is not a project, it exits non-zero with "not a storytree project".
