1.3 · With storytree stopped, it says "storytree isn't running" within a second.
1.4 · A record the library refuses reaches you as the library's own message, and nothing is written.
1.5 · `storytree` alone lists the families.
1.6 · `storytree <family> <verb> --help` (or `-h`) prints that command's usage and summary and exits 0 without running it, even when the command needs arguments it was not given.

1.7 · A command or verb it does not have is refused (exit 2) naming the command for that job when agents are known to guess the word, else the nearest real one by spelling, and listing what the family has (ADR-0786 D3).
1.8 · An answer's `next:` offers only commands that open a record the answer just named or listed; no stock hints (ADR-0786 D2).

1.9 · `storytree --version` prints the 0.3.<n> of the build it comes from, the number the desktop app shows for that commit (ADR-0753 D2): from a source checkout, with its short commit; from an installed build, the release and commit stamped into it at packaging.

1.10 · Through `pnpm storytree` in a storytree checkout, a word arrives as written, holding double quotes, >, &, |, ^, %, backslashes or backticks, and nothing else runs or is written on its way (ADR-0851 D1).

reported.note: Commit 399163ab (.npmrc shell-emulator=true): the pnpm route prints exactly the door's own answer for the word, and no stray file is written. Windows, pnpm 9.15.0.

contracts.title: 1.11 · A word the script shell still changes on its way (a $, a line break) is refused before the command runs: nothing is done, and the refusal names the word and says to pass that text from a file (ADR-0851 D2).

reported.note: Commit 399163ab (packages/cli/src/handed.ts): refused before dispatch, naming word 1 and @<file>; by hand, a --answer holding $HOME was refused as word 5.

contracts.title: 1.12 · On Windows, a word given to the installed command whose double quotes the caller's own quoting changed, as Windows PowerShell 5.1 hands on a word holding a space and a double quote, is refused before the command acts, naming the word and saying to pass it from a file; a line quoted by Windows' standard rules (Git Bash, a program) is never refused (proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere).
contracts.description: Windows PowerShell 5.1 wraps a word holding a space in double quotes without escaping the ones inside it, for every program it starts, so 'he said "x" ok' arrived as other words, in silence (increment_e95ceec15288, measured 2026-10-02). The installed command's launcher hands its line on, and the door refuses a line no standard quoter writes, as 1.11 does for pnpm's line.

reported.note: Green on the laptop and on CI's Windows runner for storytree-ai/storytree#492: from Windows PowerShell 5.1 the word is refused before the command acts, naming word 1 and @<file>; from Git Bash the same word reaches the command. Skipped on Linux and macOS with its reason.

verified.note: 1 of 1 tests skipped (platform:win32: only on Windows does the installed command's launcher hand the caller's line on, and only Windows PowerShell 5.1 leaves a word's inner quotes unescaped), at commit 132652ac4fbff8f0e1a0b5a76f060273c0c4d40f

capabilities.title: 2 · Who wrote it
capabilities.description: Every write made through the command line is recorded as the person who ran it (their computer user name), so the library's history can tell a person's change from an agent's. When an agent runs the command from its own shell, the write is recorded as that agent's session instead (A1).

contracts.title: 2.1 · An edit through the command shows in the record's history as the person.
2.2 · The same edit, run with an agent session's id in the environment, shows as that session.

capabilities.title: 3 · Library
capabilities.description: Read any record whole, list a kind (optionally filtered by a field), search the artifacts, see what links to an artifact, and see a record's history of changes, all through the library's own reads. Write a new record of any kind, or edit named fields of one, with long text taken from a file, and a bad record is refused with the library's own message. Retire a record with a reason and its writer through the library's existing retire, preserving its refusals.

contracts.title: 3.1 · `read` returns the whole body.
3.2 · `edit` changes only the named fields.
3.3 · `new` without a required field is refused, naming it.
3.4 · `history` lists every write with its writer.
3.5 · `list` shows only live records of the kind and filters by a field.
3.6 · `new memory` is refused with the reason that memories belong to the harness, and writes nothing (ADR-0650).
3.7 · `related <artifact> --unlinked` lists the artifacts most like it that no link reaches.
3.8 · `library retire <id> --reason <why>` retires any record the library permits, recording the reason and writer and returning the library's own refusals.
3.9 · `library search <words…> [--limit <n>]` shows the library's ranked answer (capability 14 of the library story), best first with scores, at most the limit; when it ranked by words it says why.
3.10 · `read <id> --field <name>` prints that one field exactly as stored and nothing else (a value that is not text, as JSON); a field the record does not have is refused, naming the fields it has.

capabilities.title: 4 · Arcs and increments
capabilities.description: See the arcs, and one arc whole: its intent, end state, increments and their states, the questions waiting on you, and what each waiting item waits for. Create, edit, park or unpark an arc; park an increment, record a landing that was never parked, close one with its outcome, and make an arc or increment wait on another with a reason, or clear the wait.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An arc with no intent is refused.
4.2 · A close with no pull request needs a note.
4.3 · A wait that would close a loop is refused, naming the loop, and nothing is written.
4.4 · `arc show` names what each waiting increment waits for.
4.5 · `arc list` names each live arc with the library's state.
4.6 · Closing an increment ends its claim for any holder and outcome; a refused close leaves it held.
4.7 · `arc increment move <increment> --to <arc> --reason` re-homes an increment to another arc, keeping its id and any claim on it; without a reason it is refused.

capabilities.title: 5 · Questions
capabilities.description: Raise a question for the owner on an arc (stakes, question, context, options, plus the analogy, diagram and recommendation 0.2 expected), optionally holding increments on it. Settle it with his answer in his words and the decision that carried it, retire one that was wrong, or list the open ones.

contracts.title: 5.2 · Settling needs an answer.
5.1 · A question with no stakes is refused.
5.3 · A held increment reads as waiting on you until its question is settled.
5.4 · A question an increment is held on cannot be retired. `question retire` retires questions only: another record kind is refused without a write and points to `library retire`.
5.5 · `question list` lists open questions across arcs, or on one arc.
5.6 · `question check` says whether a question's review is fresh or lapsed; `question renew` re-stamps it, and renewing a settled question is refused.
5.7 · `library edit <question>` corrects an open question's wording in place; editing a settled question is refused, pointing at its standing answer.
5.8 · `question list` leaves out a parked arc's open questions and says how many wait there until it is unparked
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D2: parking an arc parks its questions too, off the owner's list until the arc is unparked.

contracts.title: 5.9 · `arc show` on a parked arc lists its open questions as parked with the arc, waiting for it to be unparked, not as waiting on you
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D2: parking an arc parks its questions too; the arc's own view says so.

capabilities.title: 6 · Decisions
capabilities.description: List decisions (current, by status, load-bearing) and record a new one with an explicit `--number <n>` or the next number, its status, who decided it in their own words, and what it supersedes. In storytree, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any record has ever held; omitting a number is refused if the floor is absent. Other projects start at 1. All numbering rules belong to the library; the CLI parses and reports them. Pull a decision out as a markdown file, edit it, push it back, and write its composed statement (the owner's C2). The one-time number, renumber (both modes), and set-floor commands have been retired after the completed N1 move.

contracts.title: 6.1 · In projects with automatic numbering, two `adr new` run at once get different, increasing numbers.
6.2 · Pull then push with no edit changes nothing.
6.3 · A superseded decision drops out of `--current`.
6.4 · A composed statement reads stale after its decision's text changes.
6.5 · `adr pull` names a decision by id, number, or ADR number.

6.6 · `adr new --number <n>` preserves an explicit unused number and refuses a reused or invalid number. In storytree, omitting the number is refused while the persisted decision number floor is absent; when present, omitting the number allocates above that floor and every number any record has ever held. Other projects continue to auto-number from 1.

capabilities.title: 10 · Plan view
capabilities.description:
`storytree tree` prints the plan as an indented tree: stories, capabilities and contracts, each with the health its agent reported (labelled as the agent's) and any claim on it. Name a story to see only that story.
`storytree capability built <capability>` says a capability is built, so it is no longer proposed, and `storytree capability proposed <capability>` says it is proposed again (ADR-0744 D2); both call the library's `setProposed`.

contracts.title: 10.1 · A story with a capability and a contract prints in order with "agent says passing".
10.2 · An unknown story says so.
10.3 · `capability built` switches a capability's proposed flag off and `capability proposed` back on, each with its writer; an unknown capability says so.
10.4 · `storytree tree` prints each capability's word, and for one that is not healthy its reason, who moves it and the contracts carrying it.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D1, at the command line.

contracts.title: 10.5 · `storytree health worklist` prints the oldest three capabilities on the health worklist, each with its word, reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when, and how many more wait; with none it says nothing waits.

10.6 · In a project whose health nothing verifies, `storytree tree` gives each part the agent's report alone, and each built capability says storytree does not check this project's tests yet, never untested or a mover
contracts.description: ADR-0630 at the command line, for a user's project (increment_ef066f718a63).

capabilities.title: 7 · Board, read only
capabilities.description: Show who is on what right now: each claim on an increment or a capability, with its agent's harness, window and reason, and whether it is live or idle; or who holds one piece of work. Claiming and releasing stay with the agents' tools.

contracts.title: 7.1 · A claim made through the agent tool appears with its harness and reason.
7.2 · An idle claim reads idle.
7.3 · `noticeboard <id>` names the holder, or "nobody".

7.4 · `noticeboard log [--session <id>] [--limit <n>]` shows the activity log's latest lines (20 unless told), each with its number, time, harness, session and what happened. Each names the line that caused it ("caused by #n"), or says "cause not recorded", never "no cause" (ADR-0746 D2).

capabilities.title: 8 · Doctor
capabilities.description: Run storytree's setup check from a terminal, the same one every agent session start runs: is storytree running, are the hooks registered and last seen firing, is this folder a project, is `storytree` on the path, is `gh` signed in, is Claude Code or Codex installed and signed in, and are git and a Node of at least 24 there. It fixes what the check fixes by itself and names the fix for the rest, and it sets a folder up as a project only when you tell it to.

contracts.title: 8.1 · With storytree closed, it opens it.
8.2 · With `gh` signed out, it names `gh auth login`.
8.3 · In a folder that is not a project, it creates nothing unless told to.
8.4 · A second run changes nothing.
8.5 · Setup installs the full command beside its hooks; the launcher reads the library and runs `doctor`; `setup remove` through the bundled command removes it again.

8.6 · With Codex's hooks registered and none run yet, the doctor names the one step that lets Codex run them, and from an administrator terminal that Codex cannot run commands there (agent link 8.16, 8.17).
contracts.description: The doctor picks the setup check's lines one by one; the live laptop run on 0.3.358 showed it printing neither new Codex line.

reported.note: doctor.test.ts 8.5: red first (no Codex hooks line in the output), green once doctor prints the codex-hooks and elevated lines.

capabilities.title: 9 · Friction and re-steers
capabilities.description: File friction with concrete evidence, or a re-steer with your own quoted words, through the agent link's own capture functions, so vague evidence is refused from a person exactly as from an agent. Add a recurrence to a friction item when it happens again. List the friction due for a landing's pass and route it, through the librarian's own drain and route.

contracts.title: 9.1 · Friction with vague evidence is refused.
9.3 · `reinforce` adds a dated recurrence.
9.2 · A re-steer whose evidence is a paraphrase is refused.

9.5 · `friction route <friction> --to <route> --reason …` records the librarian's route and reason, with an optional --discharged-by stamp; the librarian's refusals (a tool route with no live remedy) reach the terminal unchanged and write nothing (ADR-0789 D2).
9.6 · `friction drain` lists the librarian's friction drain for the calling branch: up to three unrouted reports other branches filed, most recurrences first (ADR-0789 D2).

capabilities.title: 11 · Workspace
capabilities.description: `storytree workspace <increment> --reason <text>` makes a claimed Claude Code workspace, or prepares a Codex workspace by checking availability and fetching main. For Codex it prints the exact ref and name for the agent to pass to the app's `create_worktree`; the agent then runs `storytree workspace attach <increment> --folder <returned-directory> --ref <commit> --name <name> --reason <text>`. Storytree verifies the worktree and claims its branch; only the app creates the Codex folder. Both steps refuse held or waiting work, and only a running agent session may claim.

contracts.title: 11.1 · From a Claude Code agent's shell, `workspace <increment> --reason` makes a worktree on a fresh branch from `origin`'s main and claims the increment for that session on that branch, naming the folder to work in.
11.2 · Work another live session holds is refused naming its holder, and no worktree is made.
11.3 · From a shell no agent session runs, it is refused saying to run it from the agent, and nothing is claimed, for both preparation and attachment.

11.4 · From a Codex agent's shell, `workspace <increment> --reason` returns the exact freshly fetched commit and suggested name for the app's `create_worktree`, without creating a folder or claim. `workspace attach` with that ref, name and returned folder claims its verified branch for the same session and names the working directory. A bad directory is refused without a claim, explaining that the app's worktree is kept.
11.5 · `workspace release` ends the calling session's increment or capability claim without closing or landing the work.
11.6 · `workspace release` refuses another session's claim, an unheld target, and a shell without an agent session, without writing claim events.

11.7 · `session close-out --safe yes|no --why <text>` from an agent's shell records the calling session's close-out, which the sessions reading then carries; from a shell no agent session runs it is refused, and a --safe other than yes or no is refused as a usage error (ADR-0758 D2).

stories.title: The librarian
stories.description: The librarian keeps a project's library honest as a library: new artifacts are genuinely new, an artifact links to what it really rests on, every accepted decision stays true, durable lessons move to where agents read them, and the question and friction queues are drained. It is 0.2's `librarian-curator`, ported whole. In 0.3 storytree runs no agents of its own, so the librarian is a hat the user's own agent puts on for a few minutes at a landing, using storytree's tools.

capabilities.title: 1 · Links
capabilities.description: The librarian links one artifact to another only where the first really rests on the second. It finds neighbours no edge reaches with related-but-unlinked search, alongside plain search (ADR-0654). This is how the whole-project decisions come to sit behind the covers that rest on them.

contracts.title: 1.1 · `link(from, to)` makes artifact `from` rest on artifact `to`, keeping its other links. Linking it again writes nothing.
1.2 · A definition rests only on a decision, and a friction or re-steer rests on nothing: any other link is refused, naming the rule, and nothing is written.
1.3 · The worklist names each accepted decision on no shelf that no artifact rests on, and drops it once one does.

1.4 · For each live artifact written since the session's cursor, including edits, the worklist lists neighbours ranked by likeness that no link joins in either direction. It uses the library's related-but-unlinked search and writes no links; the agent decides which are real dependencies.

capabilities.title: 2 · Decision log
capabilities.description: Every accepted decision stays true in full. When a later landing overtakes something a decision says, the librarian corrects it in place if the decision did not change, and records a new decision that supersedes it if it did; finished business is retired or consolidated.

contracts.title: 2.1 · `supersede(olds, decision)` records a new accepted decision naming the old ones in `supersedes`. Each old one reads superseded and stays readable; the new one takes the shelf the first old one covered, and any old one's load-bearing mark.

2.2 · `correct(id, fields)` changes a decision in place (its text, title or load-bearing mark), and the old wording stays in its history. A correction that would turn an accepted decision back to proposed is refused, since only the owner does that, and nothing is written.

2.3 · `annotate(target, { by, note })` adds a dated annotation to the target decision's text, naming the decision that narrows it. A narrowing decision that is not a live decision is refused, and nothing is written.
2.4 · The worklist's health report names each link or supersession that points at a record no longer live, with both ends.

capabilities.title: 3 · Catalogue
capabilities.description: Every artifact that lands is either genuinely new or an edit to the artifact that already covers it, and never a near-copy. Guidance any capable agent would work out for itself is pruned.

contracts.title: 3.1 · `retire(id, reason)` retires an artifact nothing points at. An artifact that another live record points at (a link, a supersession, a process's hand-on, an agent role's reading, rules or anti-patterns, an increment's remedies, or a question it settled) is refused, naming what points at it, and nothing is written.
3.2 · The worklist lists each artifact written new since a cursor, with the live artifacts a plain search for any word of its title finds, so the agent can see what might already cover it.

capabilities.title: 4 · Graduation
capabilities.description: ADR-0650 keeps the built graduation functions, but graduation is not needed for the MVP. Harness memories remain outside the library; promotion writes a proper artifact kind.

contracts.title: 4.1 · The worklist lists each memory in the memory folders that is new, changed since it was parked, or parked more than 60 days ago. A memory parked unchanged within its 60 days is not listed.
4.2 · `park(memory, reason)` keeps the reason, the date and what the memory said when it was parked, beside the memory folder, never in the library.

4.3 · `graduate(memory, kind, fields)` writes the lesson as a principle, process or definition, and only then deletes the memory. A write the library refuses leaves the memory where it was, and any other kind is refused.
4.4 · The worklist lists each process that names none of the tools served, and each tool served that no process names.

capabilities.title: 5 · Queues
capabilities.description: Open questions whose review lease has lapsed and unrouted friction reports are looked at on the librarian's pass, and nothing is closed without a reason. The library owns the review date and lease; the librarian uses its lapsed-question drain (ADR-0654).

contracts.title: 5.1 · The worklist lists only open questions whose review lease has lapsed, across every arc, longest lapsed first. Fresh and settled questions are excluded; gathering the list neither settles nor renews a question.

5.2 · The worklist's friction drain holds at most three friction reports not yet routed that another session filed, never one filed from the session's own branch. Reports with the most recurrences come first, with oldest first on ties; no recurrences counts as zero, and missing provenance still counts as another session's report.

5.3 · route(friction, route, reason, options?) records the routing judgement with its reason and an optional dischargedBy reference to the remedy that landed. The reference is trimmed and must be non-empty when supplied; omitting it preserves an existing stamp. An already-routed report can receive its stamp later. A route with no reason or a blank delivery reference is refused without writing.

5.4 · A tool route requires a live, non-closed increment whose remedies names this friction, unless the report already carries a delivered-by stamp or receives one in this call. An unrelated or closed increment is insufficient; refusal writes nothing and explains the missing remedy or delivery reference.

5.5 · A report already routed is routed again only to the same route (a later delivery stamp or a clearer reason); routing it elsewhere is refused naming the earlier route and its reason, and nothing is written, so two librarian passes cannot silently replace each other's judgement.
contracts.description: Regression for two landing sessions that drained the same friction 23 s apart, the later route replacing the earlier with no warning (2026-10-01).

capabilities.title: 6 · Rounds
capabilities.description: When the librarian runs, and how an agent is told to put on its hat. At a landing where the session wrote to a curated kind of artifact, storytree asks for the librarian's pass before the landing is reported.

contracts.title: 6.1 · The trigger fires when the change feed since the session started holds a write to a curated kind, and when there is no start to read from; graduation is due at every landing either way.
6.2 · The worklist gathers each capability's list into one report: graduation's and the friction drain always (ADR-0789 D3), the rest only when the trigger fired.
6.3 · `land`'s answer ends with the "next" line "run the librarian's pass" when the trigger fired, and with none when it did not.
6.4 · A test client lists the librarian's tools on the agent link's one server, beside its own, and calls them.
6.5 · The librarian's subagent definition names every librarian tool the server serves.

stories.title: The knowledge core
stories.description: The knowledge inside the planet. The project's artifacts hang below the front covers on the stories' and capabilities' shelves, deeper the longer the chain of references that reaches them; replaced decisions sit as see-through ghosts beside the decisions that replaced them; and the artifacts one recorded session reached light up in each of its agents' colours. The owner looks inside the globe on purpose, pins an artifact to read it, and replays a session.

capabilities.title: 2 · Earlier decisions beside their replacements
capabilities.description: A replaced decision appears as a see-through ghost beside the decision that replaced it, and lights when its recorded reader reaches it. Its card tells an explicit supersession from an earlier cover found in write history. Proposed decisions stay out of this first slice.

contracts.title: 2.1 · An accepted decision that explicitly supersedes an old one makes a ghost, even when the old front-cover mark was never cleared. A proposal naming an old decision does not supersede it.

2.2 · For older records, a new cover on the same shelf linking to the old one, followed by clearing the old cover's mark, makes an "earlier cover" ghost when the replacement is unique. Clearing a mark alone, editing the wording, or merely linking to an old decision does not.
2.3 · A unique chain of replacements ends beside its current successor. A missing or ambiguous successor gets an outer ghost labelled "replacement not placed", rather than a guessed home.

2.4 · Depth and incoming-link sizes use only artifacts that are neither ghosts nor proposed; replacement relations are not support links. A ghost never changes that layout, and its own visit count stays inspectable.

capabilities.title: 1 · Knowledge under its shelves
capabilities.description: The project's artifacts hang below the stories' and capabilities' front covers, with depth counting the longest chain of references from any shelf. A shared artifact appears once, a loop is drawn as a labelled error, and an artifact no shelf reaches has "no depth". On the globe, shelf-placed knowledge is drawn beneath its islands. Story-text definitions are excluded from the drawing; the remaining no-shelf artifacts fill a ball within 0.55 globe radii, separated from one another and shelf points by at least 0.035 radii (ADR-0661 D3). Forest shows the core beneath the story nodes; Library shows it alone on the same globe (ADR-0660 D4). The separate Look-inside view stays unmounted.

contracts.title: 1.1 · With a cover A, links A → B → C and a shortcut A → C, C stays at depth 3: the shelf-to-cover step counts as 1. Visits and incoming-link counts never change that depth.

1.2 · An artifact reached by two shelves appears once, at its greatest depth, and names both entrances. A front cover keeps its own shelf as its home, and another shared artifact hangs under the oldest reachable shelf, with a stable tie-break.

1.3 · With A → B → C → B and C → D, B and C share a loop marked as an error at group depth 2, and D is at 3. An unreachable loop, like any unreachable artifact, is classified as no shelf, with no depth.
1.4 · Forty covers on their shelves and five artifacts on none, with no links, give forty artifacts at depth 1 and five with no shelf route, with no invented links. An empty shelf says it is empty.
1.5 · The globe draws every shelf-placed artifact once beneath its home island at its computed longest-chain depth. Ghosts, proposals, retired artifacts and story-text definitions add no points.

1.6 · No-shelf artifacts that are not story text fill a deterministic ball within 0.55 globe radii. Their centres remain at least 0.035 radii apart and at least that far from drawn shelf points, above the 0.012-radii dot diameter; every dot is wholly inside the shell. They gain no depth or invented shelf, and an empty corpus draws no points.

1.7 · Forest and Library submit the same complete set of eligible artifact points at the same positions and computed depths, with the same separated no-shelf artifacts; hiding story nodes leaves the live core mounted.

1.8 · isStoryText(record) is true only for a definition whose term or title starts with "Story text: stories/". Those records are excluded from the globe points whether loose or shelf-placed, while ordinary definitions, principles and decisions remain eligible and no library record is removed.

capabilities.title: 3 · Reads by session and agent
capabilities.description: Choose one recorded session and see which artifacts its orchestrator and named agents reached, each in its own colour, with visits counted across the project's captured sessions. A peek only lights its artifact, full reads advance as jumps, and an unknown agent stays pale with no path.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Repeated peeks and whole reads of one artifact by several agents in one session count as one visit; a second session makes two. The card gives peek and whole-read totals separately.

3.2 · Interleaved agents replay separately in recorded order, including equal timestamps resolved by log line number; no step crosses agents or sessions. A missing agent field behaves exactly like "unknown".
3.3 · A peek neither draws a step nor replaces the agent's previous full-read stop. A whole read found "through a link" stays a jump, because today's record names no source artifact.

3.4 · Receiving the same log lines twice does not count visits twice. Switching projects clears the old project's picture, and a read of an artifact no longer present is counted as a missing artifact, not dropped or reconstructed.
3.5 · With no captured reads the picture says "no recorded reads"; it never says the knowledge was unused.

capabilities.title: 4 · Look inside and inspect an artifact
capabilities.description: On the globe in Forest or Library mode, clicking an artifact dot pins it and opens its summary card in the right-hand slot used by the story panel (ADR-0661 D2). The card shows the artifact's kind, title and description or another summary field; when there is no summary it shows the whole text. It has no links list, read counts, depth figures or entrances. Close and Escape dismiss it. Opening a story replaces the card, and opening a card replaces the story panel. The separate look-inside view, with its replay and size controls, was removed after staying unmounted (increment_64a16707ff78); the notes are drawn under the islands, lit by the running sessions' reads and a selected session's traversal.

contracts.title: 4.1 · Clicking an artifact dot in Forest or Library opens the existing pinned-artifact card in the right-hand story-panel slot. It shows kind, title and description or another summary field; with no summary it shows the whole text. It contains no links list, read counts, depth or entrances.

4.6 · Opening an artifact card closes an open story panel, and opening a story closes the card. Close and Escape dismiss the card. The shared core pin and summary renderer serve both globe modes without writing to the library.

4.7 · With no session selected, every session in the running-sessions list lights the notes it has read since it started, in that row's colour (a subagent's reads wear its parent's), with no lines between them; a session with no row lights nothing, and a note read by more than one listed session is marked shared and wears its latest reader's colour (ADR-0738).

4.8 · Drilling into a listed session colours its orchestrator in the session's own colour and each subagent in a distinct shade of that hue; an unknown agent stays pale, and a session with no row keeps the fixed palette (ADR-0738).

4.9 · The globe's knowledge dots light exactly as the core does: every listed session with none selected, or the selected session alone in its agents' colours; with no running sessions nothing lights (ADR-0738).

4.10 · Each session's reading path draws as curved lines: from each full read to the same known agent's next, in recorded order, pointing to the later read, bowed away from the globe's centre. Every listed session's path draws in its colour with none selected; a selected session's draws in its agents' colours only when it has no window to read, a subagent's first read stepping from the session's latest full read before it (where it was spawned), and otherwise its window's traversal draws instead (4.16, ADR-0756). A peek, an unknown agent or an unlisted session draws none, and a curve never claims a followed link (ADR-0740).

4.11 · Each known agent of a drawn session has a reading path in its colour: its full reads' steps in recorded order, ending at its latest full read; a peek adds no step, and an unknown agent or an unlisted session has none (ADR-0742).

4.12 · A new step's line grows from its earlier read to its later one (one agent's new steps one after another, different agents at once); with no session selected each agent's grown path is replayed in a loop by a glow travelling its steps in recorded order, bright at its head, pausing after the last, and opening the view grows nothing. With a session selected one replay walks all its agents' steps in recorded order, growing each line and lighting each note as it is reached, holds the finished picture, then clears and replays (ADR-0797). Reduced motion neither grows, glows nor replays; paths carry no arrowheads and no wisp model (ADR-0742).

4.15 · A note lit by a new read stays unlit until the growing line into it arrives (including a line queued behind that agent's earlier steps), then lights in its session's colour; a note already lit, or reached only by steps read before the view opened, is never held (ADR-0742 D2).

4.16 · Selecting a session reads its window from the host and draws it on the knowledge dots (ADR-0756): one line per step from each note it opened in full to the next, in reading order (files between do not break the chain; a note gone from the library is stepped over; a step taken twice draws once), in the session's colour, solid where a stored link joins the two notes either way round and dotted where none does, growing toward the later note when new and then showing direction with a faint fill that runs from the earlier note to the later. A note whose read is in the window now has a ring; one compacted out since is lighter, and its lines fade with it; one only glimpsed is tinted faint with no line. An answer for a session no longer selected is dropped, and with none selected no window is drawn or asked for.

4.20 · A selected session's file opens join its traversal (ADR-0804 D5): each file whose path names a surveyed file (any path ending packages/<package>/src/…) is a stop on the code's surface, beside the notes it opened, in reading order; a step between two files is solid when one imports the other and dotted otherwise, a step between a file and a note dives into the core (or rises out of it), a compacted file's read fades with its steps, and a path that names no surveyed file is stepped over, never drawn. Opening a capability lights its territory; an arc, an increment or any other plan record is drawn nowhere and breaks nothing.

4.18 · With no session selected, the core reads every listed session's window, a child's too, in one ask to the host per round, never starting a round while one is out; a newly listed session is asked for at once when none is out; a session that leaves the list is no longer drawn. A selected session's window is never asked for again while its last ask is out.

stories.title: The app setup
stories.description: A new Windows user gets from one command in a project folder to a working storytree connection they can understand and ask for help with. The database, the yes-before-creating-a-project step, hooks, the project switcher and app updates belong to other stories; this story joins a fresh installation to them.

capabilities.title: 1 · Get storytree
capabilities.description:
One command gets the Windows app and the tools its agent needs onto the computer, ready to run without a storytree checkout. Running it again reuses a working installation or explains what failed and how to retry.

As built: the release publishes install-storytree.ps1, its PowerShell one-liner and a version-matched SHA-256 manifest alongside the existing combined Windows x64/arm64 NSIS installer. Desktop packaging ships a native pinned Node 24 runtime, the complete agent-link buildBins output including imported chunks, a delivery helper and Node's license in resources/agent-tools. Delivery verifies and reuses a working installation before contacting the feed, explicitly launches its executable to show a hidden window or establish the first app launch, and waits for the app-owned database. It records stable installed tool paths in the 0.3 home's delivery.json and puts its CLI wrapper on the per-user Windows PATH; unrelated storytree commands are preserved and named. Failed steps include a retry action, incomplete existing apps are retained with repair/update instructions, and delivery does not create projects, change harness settings, install a developer toolchain, or touch 0.2. Ordinary updates remain the app's existing NSIS update route and replace the tool payload at the same paths. setup install retains its existing hook/command meaning; capability 2 owns connection.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md. Linux tests use temporary homes, fake app launch/readiness and real PowerShell orchestration with injected effects; the actual built CLI, hook, setup, delivery helper and MCP server run outside a checkout. Both Windows runtime downloads match pinned SHA-256 values and their PE architectures. Windows CI additionally checks the installed x64 tool payload from a path with spaces. These proofs do not attest real first-ever/hidden-window startup, fresh-terminal registry propagation, interrupted NSIS installation, native arm64 execution, a live release update with active agent processes, or the agent-link 8.6 two-harness walkthrough; those remain the laptop acceptance lane.

As built: after delivery is ready, the one-liner prompts for Claude Code, Codex, both, or skip and calls the delivered Node/CLI directly with setup connect and the selected switches. This connects capability 1's installed paths to capability 2's existing registration functions through delivery.json. A connection failure does not reinstall the app or discard a successful connection; the command reports per-agent recovery. Tools registration is never presented as hooks verified. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/join/README.md.

As built (ADR-0854): on Windows the installed command is `storytree.exe`, a 5 KB program of its own built with LLVM from the agent link's launcher source and shipped in the payload as `storytree-launcher.exe`, so no shell reads its words: from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, each word reaches the CLI as the caller's command line spelled it (contract 1.9). The batch file it was before, `storytree.cmd`, is replaced by it in its folder. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/native-launcher/README.md.

contracts.title: 1.1 · On a clean Windows x64 machine and an arm64 machine, the PowerShell one-line command delivers the matching app, a bundled Node runtime and a runnable tool-server, hook, setup and command-line bundle, including its imported chunks.

1.2 · The first-run journey displays the app and reaches its database both without a previous launch record and when the app is already running with its window hidden, without a separate manual "open once" step.

1.3 · Repeating the command in the same or a second folder reuses the installation without replacing user settings or touching 0.2's installation or data; run from a folder that is already a project, its folder step says so and creates nothing.
1.4 · An interrupted or refused installation reports the failed step and a retry action, without announcing a working connection or replacing the last usable installation.

1.5 · After the app takes an ordinary release update, the next agent session still starts compatible tools from a durable location, without rebuilding a checkout or relying on a package-manager cache.
1.6 · The installed command runs from a fresh Windows terminal; an existing unrelated `storytree` command is preserved and the conflict is named.

1.7 · After connecting the agents, the one-line command asks for the project folder: Enter takes the folder it was run from (from the home folder or a drive root, Enter skips instead), a typed path is created if missing, and S skips, saying how to add a project later. The suggested name is the folder's and editable; a refused name is asked again. The chosen folder becomes a project exactly as the setup check's yes makes one (marker, library project, the app's project choice), and the app shows it (ADR-0752 D1).

1.8 · Uninstalling from Windows Apps & features (or `storytree setup uninstall`) removes everything storytree added. That is the app, its command and PATH entry, this installation's agent registrations, hooks and status line in Claude Code and Codex, the update cache and its home. It asks first whether to keep the local library (kept, only the library stays). The user's project folders, other agent settings and another installation's home stay untouched, and an app update removes nothing.
contracts.description: A first user who wants out can leave cleanly in one step (increment_3522f6c13cef; owner 2026-09-30: a smooth, pleasant experience makes advocates).

contracts.title: 1.9 · On Windows, the installed command hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it, through no shell: run by name from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, a word holding >, &, |, % or ^ arrives unchanged, as does an inner double quote from Git Bash or a program; nothing else runs and no file is written (ADR-0854; proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere).
contracts.description: Regression: the batch launcher (storytree.cmd) let cmd.exe read the words as its own syntax, before the batch's first line ran: a > after an inner quote cut the word and wrote a file, and & or | started a command (reproduced on the laptop 2026-10-02). Windows PowerShell 5.1's own quoting of a word holding a space and an inner quote is increment_e95ceec15288.

reported.note: Green on the laptop (Windows 11 arm64) and on CI's Windows runner (x64, LLVM 20) for storytree-ai/storytree#489: every word arrived unchanged from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell 5.1 and a program starting the command; no file written. Skipped on Linux and macOS with its reason.

verified.note: 1 of 1 tests skipped (platform:win32: only Windows starts a command's file through cmd.exe, which reads its words as its own syntax), at commit 42ef624440fb0937b0ceea96af0c76860684e717

capabilities.title: 2 · Connect an agent
capabilities.description:
The user chooses Claude Code, Codex or both, and storytree connects its installed tools to those agents. The next session uses the existing setup check to ask about the project and show whether the connection actually works.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/connect exports connectAgents and disconnectAgents for the chosen harnesses, with installedToolServerCommand(bundledNodePath, installedMcpScriptPath) as the delivery seam. Registration is per user, keeps unrelated settings and old entries, uses the existing storytree MCP name, and reports incompatible entries without overwriting. It captures no project or working directory. Repeating it leaves the compatible entry untouched. Missing harnesses, invalid settings, missing installed tools and failed writes produce separate recovery results for each harness.

As built: disconnect removes the selected registration and only hooks matching this installation, preserving other commands in mixed groups and any other installation's hooks. It keeps the shared command until no connection remains and removes only the matching launcher. A disconnected harness stays disconnected: disconnect records it in the storytree home (disconnected-harnesses.json), and the setup check, run from the other harness's sessions, registers no hooks for it until Connect connects it again. Installation results distinguish tools registration from hooks not verified; the existing setup check owns project consent and received-event verification. Connect also registers the chosen harness's hooks (and Claude Code's status line), never the unchosen one's, so the first session after installing already runs the start hook that asks the setup question; before this, hooks arrived only when that first session's tool server ran the setup check, too late for its own start. Registering is still not verifying: results keep saying "hooks not verified" until the setup check has received each event.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Choosing either harness or both registers the installed tool server per user for the chosen harnesses, preserving other servers, settings and any existing 0.2 entry.
2.2 · A new agent session in the invoking folder, and later in another folder, reaches that folder's existing setup check rather than a fixed installer directory or a hard-coded project.
2.3 · Repeating registration leaves one effective storytree entry per chosen harness; an incompatible existing entry is explained instead of silently overwritten.
2.4 · A missing harness or an invalid settings file gets a specific recovery action and no success claim for that harness; a successful registration for the other harness is reported separately.

2.5 · Disconnecting one harness keeps the other's connection and the shared command working; removing all connections cleans up only storytree-owned registrations, hooks and command, keeping project libraries and unrelated settings.

2.6 · The installation result tells "tools connected" apart from "hooks verified"; a missing hook stays named by the existing setup check until its event is received. For Codex it says whether its hooks run or wait for the user to trust them, naming the one step while they wait, and, from an administrator terminal, that Codex cannot run commands from one.

capabilities.title: 3 · First-run guide
capabilities.description:
A short in-app guide tells the user what to do next, what storytree will ask, and what a working first project looks like. They can reopen it when adding another project or recovering from a connection problem.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/view mounts one Help entry outside the project surface, available with no project, either forest or a library error. First launch offers the guide; dismissal is remembered locally and Help reopens it. The guide covers the chosen agent, explicit project consent, harness approval, received-hook verification, first visible work, a second project, the unsigned Windows installer and feedback. Check a folder calls the agent link’s public runSetupCheck and displays its diagnostic lines and fixes. The adjacent copy action prepares a check_setup request for the agent; this folder check does not install hooks or the command and cannot verify hook receipt. The app’s existing projectSelection/followProjects refresh remains responsible for the project list.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Headless Chromium exercises the actual renderer and isolated library, including two setup fixtures and both selectable forests. Contract 3.3’s real two-empty-folder/two-yes harness walkthrough and the final installer handoff remain Windows acceptance work.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Completing installation offers the in-app guide without requiring a project to exist, and its entry point opens it again later.
3.2 · From the guide, the user can reach the existing setup diagnostics and their recovery action when the connection is incomplete.

3.3 · The guide says how to add a project three ways (the app's Add project, `storytree doctor --set-up <name>` in a terminal, or asking the agent in the folder); a project added any of these ways appears in the running app and both forests are selectable.

3.4 · Add project in the app's Projects section opens the native folder picker; the chosen folder becomes a project under its own name (a name already taken by another project gets `-2`, `-3`…, so a second folder never joins an existing project silently), set up as the installer's folder step sets one up, and is shown. A folder already in a project is simply selected; cancelling the picker changes nothing (ADR-0752 D2).

3.5 · The first-run guide shows, each time it opens, that Codex waits for the user to trust storytree's hooks, with the one step, until one has run, then that it runs them; with no Codex hooks it says nothing of Codex.
contracts.description: The Help panel's guide is where a new user already looks; a half-connected Codex must not be silent there.

reported.note: help/agent-connections.test.ts: red first (agentConnections missing), green after. The look lands with its picture after the laptop run.

contracts.title: 3.7 · Remove, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project remove <name>`, takes a project added by mistake off this computer's list and frees its folder here (a marker git tracks is left and named); its records stay in the library, and a deliberate join brings it back. An unknown name is refused.
contracts.description: The non-destructive half of removing a project (increment_6bb0564567cb). Deleting its records waits on the owner's question on arc_cfc7db517fae; freeing the folder on this machine is increment_f600d1ee7b87.

contracts.title: 3.6 · Delete, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project delete <name> --confirm <name>`, drops a project's records for every computer using the library once its name is typed, after saying where they live and who loses them; a snapshot into this computer's backups is taken first unless skipped, and restores it. Its activity lines and transcripts go with it, and a computer that had hidden it forgets the name, so a later project of that name starts clean and is shown. capabilities.title: 5 · Send feedback
capabilities.description:
A button in the app lets the user describe a problem or suggestion and opens it as a draft GitHub issue on storytree's repository. They see what they are sending and submit it themselves.

As built: Help → Send feedback provides editable title and message fields and an explicit Open GitHub draft action. The package constructs https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/issues/new with only those two user-authored fields; the desktop carries the OS external-browser action. It attaches no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs. A failed handoff preserves the message and offers retry or copy, with an explicit copy failure and selectable original text. Success says “Opened a draft”, leaving GitHub submission to the user. Closing help sends nothing.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Fake-opener tests and the actual desktop renderer cover no-project and both-forest access, cancellation, editing, retry, copy, exact payloads and honest success status. No issue was submitted by the checks.

5.2 · Before submission the user can review and edit their message; the action sends no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs automatically.
5.3 · Failure to open the browser draft offers a retry or a copy of the prepared text.
5.4 · After opening the draft the app says it opened a draft, never that feedback was received.

stories.title: Process ledger
stories.description: A session can finish its work without leaving a process it started running unnoticed. It records who started each run, keeps sight of runs whose request ended or timed out, lists what remains on this computer, stops only the caller's own runs with their children checked, and tells an honest empty inventory apart from an incomplete one.

capabilities.title: 1 · Record who started each run
capabilities.description:
Every tracked run names the session that started it and the computer where it runs. Background shells and detached servers keep that owner after the request or launcher that started them has gone away.

As built (foundation): @storytree/processes supplies one launchOwned boundary for resolved Claude Code/Codex callers and explicitly session-bound manual callers, with ownerFromCall accepting the agent link's public caller and agent context. Each launch durably records its owner, machine, optional project, executable/arguments, folder, launch time, PID and native lifetime observation before reporting tracked. Explicit parentRun/parentSession/subagent links survive the launcher; no PID adoption or folder/time/command inference assigns ownership. Failed launches or registration return a named gap, including a surviving PID when known. Installed CLI/MCP inventory, stop and clear doors are wired through the own package. Existing command hooks alone still do not register runs; this landing does not add launch coverage.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A registered run keeps its resolved session, machine, project when known, process identity, command, folder and start time.
1.2 · Two sessions in the same checkout keep separate process ownership, including when their command text is identical.
1.3 · A detached child registered at launch remains attributed after its launcher exits.
1.4 · A background command launched through the supported Claude Code, Codex or manual launch path has a durable ownership record before its launch is reported as tracked.
1.5 · A launch without a usable owner or successful registration reports that gap instead of assigning an owner by folder, start time or command text.

capabilities.title: 2 · Keep sight of unfinished runs
capabilities.description:
A request ending or timing out does not mean its work has stopped. Each run stays visible until the computer confirms it has ended, with anything it cannot establish shown as uncertain.

As built (foundation): readLedger and observeRuns retain records independently of requests, turns, sessions, claims and age, without a library connection. Request outcomes stay unknown unless the caller records evidence; explicit timeout evidence never implies process death. Native probes distinguish live/gone/unknown and compare Linux boot/start ticks, macOS boot/native microsecond start time or Windows exact creation FILETIME before attributing the current PID to a recorded lifetime. Failed or partial reads stay visible alongside readable records. Only registered runs and explicit child links are covered; unregistered launch paths and descendants remain untracked. Stopping and closing consume these observations in later capabilities and must revalidate identity before any signal.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A surviving process or owned child remains visible after a request timeout, labelling the request as timed out only when the caller supplied that evidence; otherwise its request outcome is unknown.
2.2 · Ending a turn, restarting or ending a session, releasing a claim, or passing twelve hours does not erase a surviving process record.
2.3 · A probe reports live, gone or unknown; unknown is never treated as confirmed dead.
2.4 · If a recorded PID has been reused, the replacement process is neither attributed to the old run nor signalled under its authority.
2.5 · Unreadable records and failed inventory reads remain visible as observation gaps alongside the records that could be read.

capabilities.title: 3 · See what remains
capabilities.description:
The session can list its remaining work or inspect all recorded sessions' work on this computer with an owner beside each run. The answer identifies what is running, what ended without reporting back, and what the inventory could not observe.

As built (listing API): @storytree/processes/listing exports listRuns and renderInventory over the foundation's observeRuns. The self view requires an explicit resolved owner and includes explicitly delegated descendants; the all-session view needs no owner and grants no cross-session stop authority. Rows keep command/arguments, folder, age, owner, machine, run/PID/lifetime identity and independent process/request findings. Only the inspector's exact lifetime is excluded. Read gaps, uncertain readings, foreign-machine records and coverage remain visible offline. Optional shared lifecycle readings have no stop action. The API offers an action only when a surface supplies an installed stop entry point and the row has an owned local live identity; otherwise it explains the absence.

As built (scope alignment): inventory uses the same ownership and conflicting-registration checks as stopOwned. An explicitly unknown calling agent refuses self inventory with a pointer to all-session inspection rather than reporting an empty scope. A named subagent sees only its own runs in self scope; its siblings and parent have no stop offer. Session callers retain explicitly delegated descendants, including established multi-hop parentSession links. An unchanged ledger no longer offers an action that stopping refuses for scope or conflicting ownership. Stopping still revalidates at invocation, so changed ownership or lifetime can alter the outcome.

As built (installed doors): storytree processes / own --all and MCP list_own_runs / list_all_runs call the listing API outside a project and with the app/database absent. Each self view offers only its installed stop entry point (CLI command or MCP tool), retaining the API's scope checks and explicit coverage. Both doors include the public app/database lifecycle reading as shared work with unknown native identity and no stop action, pointing to storytree app status / storytree app quit. An unknown shared lifetime keeps the overall reading incomplete.

As built (caller identity, supervisor-directed): with the app/database down, a CLI caller's self is the harness session named by CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID or CODEX_THREAD_ID, using the workspace command's environment seam. Missing or competing harness signals refuse self inventory, stop and clear and point to read-only own --all. MCP uses Codex's per-call session/thread metadata offline. When the library is reachable, exact call-id hook records supply the corrected session and named subagent, limiting it to its own runs. Claude MCP's shared server environment cannot identify an offline calling agent, so unresolved self operations refuse and point to list_all_runs / own --all. No authority is inferred from folder, timing, commands or a synthetic MCP session.

As built (delivery): the shared agent-link builder bundles both installed doors and stages Koffi's physical loader plus the host native module in its supported build/koffi/<ABI> prebuild layout, accepted by the unchanged installer payload verifier; the standalone CLI uses the same staging function. Desktop packaging replaces the host native package with the exact win32-x64 or win32-arm64 target before hashing each payload. The desktop manifest explicitly copies the native dependency directory as an extra resource, because electron-builder excludes a root node_modules directory from its general resource copy. Missing native targets fail the build. The habits card teaches all four own tools. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/. Built CLI and stdio MCP tests execute native inventory/stop/clear on each CI host; Linux additionally assembled both Windows payloads and checked target PE architecture and manifest hashes. Real installed Windows x64/arm64 harness acceptance remains with the laptop supervisor.

contracts.title: 3.1 · The self inventory distinguishes live, unknown and gone runs with command, PID/run identity, age, owner and folder, excluding the inspecting command itself.
3.2 · The all-session view works without a current session identity and attributes every readable local run without granting cross-session stop authority.
3.3 · Self-scoped operations use the existing harness identity and refuse an unidentified caller rather than returning an apparently empty inventory.
3.4 · Inventory works while the app or database is unavailable and states its machine and launch coverage, including unsupported or unregistered paths.
3.5 · Live work is a normal inventory result, with a usable stop action for the caller's stoppable rows; shared or uncertain-identity rows explain why no such action is offered.
3.6 · The retained CLI forms and the MCP tools return the same ownership and process findings through the owning package's API.

capabilities.title: 4 · Stop the work I own
capabilities.description:
The session can stop the runs it names without stopping another session's work. It checks the run and its covered children after each attempt, and reports failure whenever their disappearance cannot be confirmed.

As built: `@storytree/processes/stopping` exports `stopOwned({ owner, targets, home?, graceMs?, forceMs? })`. Targets are registered run UUIDs. Parent sessions cover explicitly delegated sessions and registered `parentRun` descendants; a named subagent cannot stop its parent or siblings. Malformed/unregistered, foreign-machine and conflicting-owner targets are refused; uncertain or replaced lifetimes never authorize signalling.

Each result states its computer, registered membership, exclusions, gaps, attempts and final process readings. Ownership is reread before each delivery. Polite and forced phases each check the root and every covered child; survivors, unknown readings, ownership changes, late registrations and unreadable inventory make the result unsuccessful. All records remain for capability 5.

Coverage is explicitly `registered-runs-and-linked-descendants`, with `nativeTree: unconfirmed` and the foundation launch-coverage warning. A successful scoped stop is not proof that unregistered OS descendants or the whole computer are clear. Linux uses identity-checked pidfds; macOS uses combined birth/PID-version evidence and audit-token signals; Windows uses a FILETIME-checked handle, targeted WM_CLOSE when available, then bounded force. No process-group or PID-only fallback is used.

As built (installed stop doors): storytree processes stop <run…> and MCP stop_own_run call stopOwned directly. They preserve every per-target stopped, already-gone, refused or incomplete outcome, native-tree limits, exclusions and gaps; unsuccessful results exit nonzero / set MCP isError. Unknown callers receive no authority. CLI, bundled CLI, source MCP and bundled stdio MCP tests stop a real owned child while refusing another session or sibling. Online Claude hook attribution also retains the named subagent boundary after a session reset. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/stopping/ and packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 4.1 · A stop outside the caller's explicitly established ownership/delegation scope is refused with its owner, while an unregistered or malformed target is refused without receiving a signal.
4.2 · A target whose original process is confirmed gone receives no signal; a reused PID or uncertain target identity cannot authorise a stop.
4.3 · Stopping an owned tree/group never includes a process with conflicting or unestablished ownership, and the covered membership is stated.
4.4 · A bounded initial stop and, under C1, forced escalation are each followed by checks of the root and covered children; a surviving child prevents a stopped result.
4.5 · A live or unconfirmed survivor keeps its record and makes the stop unsuccessful, regardless of whether the operating system accepted the signal.
4.6 · Multiple named targets each receive an outcome, and any refusal or survivor makes the overall result unsuccessful.

capabilities.title: 5 · Finish with an honest inventory
capabilities.description:
The session can clear records of work confirmed gone without hiding work that may still be running. Its closing check distinguishes an empty observed inventory from an incomplete observation, so a tidy record cannot become a false claim that the computer is idle.

As built: `@storytree/processes/closing` and `@storytree/processes` export `clearOwned({ owner, home?, knownGaps? })`, `readClosing({ home?, owner?, knownGaps?, shared? })` and `renderClosing(reading)`. Clear removes only the caller session/harness's records, with named subagents limited to their own records; delegated sessions' records are untouched. Original lifetimes and all registered descendants must be confirmed gone. Live, unknown and foreign records remain; unreadable records and known gaps prevent unproved child clearance. Removal failures are reported separately from successful removals.

Clear rereads records and child membership after probing and before unlinking. Changed, disappearing, reparented or newly registered children retain the affected parent; only this call's confirmed removals may shrink its previously observed membership. It preserves request evidence and gap records, never signals processes, and changes neither claims, sessions nor increments.

The closing reading reuses the listing API in all-session scope, irrespective of the caller, session end or released claims. Its status is `empty`, `remaining` or `incomplete`. Live/unknown rows stay visible; persisted read/registration gaps and caller-carried gaps whose persistence failed make it incomplete and name missing evidence separately. An empty verdict says “no tracked session work remains on this machine”, with the launch coverage and an explicit remote-machine limit. Shared work remains separately visible and is never stopped automatically.

These are point-in-time observations, without a launch interlock. Only explicitly registered descendants are covered; neither whole-machine idleness nor remote clearance is claimed. Evidence: `packages/processes/evidence/closing/README.md`, `red.txt`, `red-membership.txt`, `green.txt`, `gate.txt`, and the PR's three native CI checks. As built (installed clear doors): storytree processes clear and MCP clear_own_runs call clearOwned without signalling, preserve removed, retained, failed and gaps as separate fields, then return an all-session readClosing. Read gaps from clear are carried as knownGaps into that closing reading. Failed removals or clear gaps exit nonzero / set MCP isError while retaining the full result. Remaining live work and unknown shared app identity remain visible in the closing verdict; clear success does not claim closure or whole-computer idleness. The current doors perform no launches and have no additional unpersisted launch-gap source. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Clear removes only the caller's records whose original processes and covered children are confirmed gone, leaving every other session's records untouched.
5.2 · Clear retains live, unknown and unreadable records and reports failed removals rather than claiming they disappeared.
5.3 · The closing reading cannot say that no owned work remains while live or unknown work survives, even if the session has ended or its claims have been released.
5.4 · A known registration/read gap makes the closing reading incomplete under G1, with the missing evidence named separately from known live work.
5.5 · An empty closing reading says “no tracked session work remains on this machine” with its coverage, and never claims a whole-machine census or remote-machine clearance.

stories.title: The website
stories.description: A visitor can decide whether storytree fits their work from its public website. The journey lives in packages/website: a plain introduction, the current Windows install command, the app engine drawing a saved public plan, license and contact, published as static files on here.now.

stories.title: The world
stories.description: The drawing engine a project's world is drawn with: it lays a project's stories out as islands, grounds and dresses them, and draws them in 3D on a globe the viewer can turn and point at. Its code lives in packages/forest-world (story id forest-world); the forest story draws with it.

capabilities.description: Turns a project's stories and capabilities into a forest scene: islands and parcels on a hex lattice, trails between them and the props they carry, then maps that scene to 3D descriptors (src/core, src/scene.ts, src/world-to-3d.ts).

stories.title: The local database
stories.description: storytree runs its own Postgres on this machine from binaries it ships, so nothing needs installing: the app's library database and the throwaway database the tests run against both start and stop through it, and a data directory has one owner at a time, recorded beside it. Its code lives in packages/local-postgres (story id local-postgres).

stories.title: The dev loop
stories.description: A session developing storytree gets from a change to a proven landing with one set of commands: its worktree is installed for it, the tests the change can reach run to an end that always says what passed, failed or never ran, the gate reports PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN, and the checks that keep the repo honest (package boundaries, agent guidance, the library's own health and backups) run the same way locally and in CI. Its code lives in packages/dev-loop (story id dev-loop), moved there from scripts/.

stories.title: Keys
stories.description: A user gives storytree a key once and every storytree process (the app, the command line, the MCP server) finds it: saved with `storytree auth set` into an auth.json in storytree's home that only the user can read, or pointed at the user's own store with a `!<command>` entry, with the vendor's environment variable as the fallback. storytree borrows a login the user already has wherever one exists and keeps a key only when nothing can be borrowed (ADR-0843). Its code lives in packages/keys (story id keys).

capabilities.title: 1 · Key store and resolver
capabilities.description: Keeps the keys storytree must hold in one auth.json in storytree's home, only the user can read and write it, and many processes can write it at once safely. It resolves a named key the same way in every process: an explicit value, then the file entry (a literal, or a `!<command>` run once per process), then the environment variable. `storytree auth set|list|remove` is its command-line front door: the cli family parses, calls this package and prints.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Saving a key creates `auth.json` in storytree's home (`STORYTREE_HOME` when set, else `[home], the folder `settings.json` uses), readable and writable by the user alone: on macOS and Linux the file's mode is 0600; on Windows it relies on the user-profile folder's own permissions, and nothing changes them.

1.2 · Two writers saving different keys at once both survive: reading `auth.json` back after they finish finds both entries, because every write holds a file lock and writes a temporary file that is then renamed over `auth.json`, so a reader never sees a half-written file.

1.3 · Resolving a key returns, first to last, an explicit value given by the caller, then its `auth.json` entry, then its environment variable: with all three present the explicit value wins; with no explicit value a saved entry wins over the environment variable; with neither, the environment variable is returned; with none, resolving says the key is not set.

1.4 · An `auth.json` entry `!<command>` resolves to the command's standard output, trimmed, and resolving it again in the same process does not run the command again; a command that fails is an error naming the key and that its command failed, which never contains the command's output.

1.5 · `storytree auth set <name>` reads the value from standard input, takes none as an argument and never prints it; `storytree auth list` prints each key's name and where it resolves from (file, command or environment) and never a value; `storytree auth remove <name>` deletes that entry from `auth.json`, leaving the others.

*Moved from storytree 0.2's library at cutover (2026-09-27), where this arc was `storytree-0-3-arc-surface-arc`. ADR numbers in this text are 0.2's decision numbers; 0.2's copy stays readable there.*

**Storytree 0.3's arc surface (ADR-0625 story 3, revised by ADR-0633 and approved as ADR-0638): per project, a read-only overlay over the forest showing what is planned, what is being worked on and by which agent, and what landed.** It shows each arc as a lane and each increment as a bar. States are derived from the library and the agent link, never typed in. ADR-0638 supersedes the original no-increments description and separate-view toggle described here before the capability review.

**Why this arc exists (2026-09-26, owner-directed).** It was split out of `trusted-circle-distribution-arc` so that more sessions can work on the 0.3 MVP at once, each driving one lane end to end. The owner asked for the split: "feels like [that arc] needs to be broken up more, like I would of assumed we could have more parrallel sessions working on this using separate arcs". A lobby session in the primary checkout (desktop title "Storytree 0.3 MVP arc breakdown") surveyed the plan and put three choices to him. Its store writes carry no branch, because the primary checkout has no ledger identity. He SELECTED these options, which that session composed: "Split as drawn (Recommended)", "Draft all 3 now, answer 1 at a time (Recommended)" and "Only what was decided for 0.3 (Recommended)". They are labels he clicked, not his words.

**Approved and built.** The owner approved the capability tree on 2026-09-27 (ADR-0638). The library's and agent link's revised trees landed, enabling the remaining work after the forest lane's part states (#35) and shared live reading (#37). The build increment `0-3-arc-surface` landed in storytree-ai/storytree PRs #101 (increment/arc states), #103 (agents), #105 (waits), #108 (briefing), and #112 (overlay and in-app proofs). Its full outcome is on that increment. Verified health is not an MVP dependency (ADR-0630); health does not appear on the overlay (ADR-0638 C0).

**Package ownership and hosting.** The story lives in `packages/arc-surface`; its `/view` subpath supplies the overlay. The app carries public reads and the desktop mounts the package view over the current forest (ADR-0649). The project switcher belongs to the app story. The overlay closes back to the same forest; there is no Forest | Arcs view toggle. The landed mount required no edit inside the desktop's forest folder.

**Cutover.** `0-3-cutover-builds-itself`, now on `storytree-0-3-cutover-arc`, waited on `0-3-arc-surface`; that build increment is now closed as landed. Its other prerequisites and dispatch remain with the cutover lane.

**Deferred work.** `0-3-floor-health-lamp-reworked` remains the existing proposal for after first users (ADR-0638 L). It is outside the completed MVP build increment; this landing neither starts nor discards it.

*Moved from storytree 0.2's library at cutover (2026-09-27), where this increment was `0-3-arc-surface`. ADR numbers in this text are 0.2's decision numbers; 0.2's copy stays readable there.*

Port the arc view from 0.2 behaviourally, without increments: in 0.3 an arc is a list of stories (ADR-0625 D8). Claims give the live who-is-on-what. The project switcher belongs to the 0.3 app story (ADR-0632 D4), whose frame hosts both the arc surface and the forest.

**Signed spec (ADR-0625, 2026-09-26).**
- Built third, after the agent link and verified health (D6).
  - *Corrected 2026-09-26 by ADR-0630: the owner dropped verified health from the MVP, so this story now follows the agent link alone.*
  - *Moved 2026-09-26 (owner-directed lane split) to its own arc, `storytree-0-3-arc-surface-arc`, whose first increment is this story's capability-tree review. In the signed diagram it reads only the library and the agent link's sessions and claims, not verified health, so the two can be built side by side.*
- Read-only. Per project it shows what is planned, what is in progress right now and by which agent, and what landed. Each story's state is derived from the records, never typed in.
- *Uses:* `projectTree`, `arcsFor`, `changesSince`, `listProjects`, and the sessions and claims from the agent link. They are kept in the agent link's own agent activity log, beside the library (decided by ADR-0626 D2).
- It gets its own capability-tree review before any code (D5).

**One 0.2 render not to port** (observed 2026-09-26). `storytree arc show` printed two lines for the same increment, which was waiting on the owner:
- "held, not work to take until that is settled";
- "⚠ `active` but NO claim holds it … Takeable".

A row waiting on the owner must never also read as takeable.

**Approved 2026-09-27 (ADR-0638); who builds what, as dispatched that day.** The owner approved the tree ("approved, please cut fresh sessions for all work on 0.3 that can now proceed"). The build may start, in two parts:
- **Now, by the forest lane** (session "Build the 0.3 forest (caps 2–6) and shared Work states", under ADR-0632 D3's shared-piece rule): this story's first landing (`stories/arc-surface.md`, `decisions/arc-surface-capability-tree.md`), capability 1 Work states at PART grain, and the live reading (part of capability 3), kept in the arc surface story's package. Do not start these a second time.
- **Later, a session of its own:** increment and arc grain of Work states, capabilities 2 (Agents on the board), 3's overlay itself, 4 (Waits) and 5 (Briefing). They need the library's and agent link's revised trees (`0-3-library-tree-for-adr-0633`, `0-3-agent-link-tree-for-adr-0633`) approved and built first.

**Built by the forest lane, 2026-09-27** (merged, not squashed; storytree-ai/storytree):
- **#35:** `stories/arc-surface.md` (the five capabilities, their shelves and 23 contracts, as ADR-0638 approved them) and `decisions/arc-surface-capability-tree.md` (ADR-0638 as the story's front cover). **Capability 1 · Work states at PART grain** (contracts 1.1–1.3) in the new package `packages/arc-surface` (`@storytree/arc-surface`): `workStates(lines)`, a pure function of the agent activity log's lines — a part is planned until claimed, in progress from its first claim until a landed line (a release or a closed window leaves it in progress, B1), landed on a landed line, in progress again on a later claim; a story follows its parts. It imports only types, so the page bundles it. `pnpm test-ratio` all: 6,342 / 5,624, 1.13.
- **#37:** **the live reading** (part of capability 3): `liveReading({ project, reads, onNews, onClock, onError, timers })` — reads everything at once, then about every 2 s asks `changesSince`/`linesSince` from where it got to (each cursor carried forward), hands on only what is new, re-reads the clock once a minute regardless, reports a failed read and retries from the same place, one ask at a time, never writes. Tested with a stand-in clock; contracts 3.4/3.5 (in-app) are proved when the overlay is drawn. `pnpm test-ratio` all: 6,466 / 5,693, 1.14.
- **Not built, left for this story's own session:** increment and arc grains of Work states (1.4–1.6), capabilities 2, 3's overlay (3.1–3.6), 4 and 5 — they wait for the library's and agent link's revised trees. The forest consumes `workStates` (its capability 2) and `liveReading` (its capability 3) from `@storytree/arc-surface`; extend them there rather than forking a copy.
