fields.title: Look at the list with every session: do unclaimed rows and several worktrees read right?
fields.answer: Q2 A - you can make the session list session expandable and then list detail on the expansion such as a list of worktrees
fields.stakes: How you tell sessions apart once every running session shows, not only claimed ones. Behaviour has landed green; only the look is open.
fields.context:
Picture (PR #227, synthetic lines on the real desktop page): https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/654e6c70a88f2922ea8dcd86dadf9ce262cd72bb/packages/forest/evidence/every-session/every-session.png

What is built (ADR-0749 D1/D2): every session that has not ended has a row, claimed or not. A claimed row is named by its claim reason (e.g. "Every session shows"). An unclaimed row is named "<harness> · <place>", where place is the branch its latest claim was taken on, else the last folder it worked in (just the folder's own name, e.g. "Codex · tidy-readme"), cut at 40 characters with "…". A session that has worked in more than one folder (a worktree is a folder) shows a muted "2 worktrees" after its name; hovering the name or that text lists the full folder paths. Idle rows are plain, now judged by your idle-after setting.

Analogy: a unclaimed row is like a name badge that says "visitor · room 4" until someone writes a real name on it. It breaks down because the "room" here is the last folder, which may change as the session moves.
fields.options:
A) Accept as built: unclaimed rows read "<harness> · <branch or folder name>"; several worktrees read as a muted count, full paths on hover. For: compact, one line per row, nothing new to learn. Against: the count hides which worktrees until you hover.
B) Name the worktrees in the row (e.g. "fix-login, tidy-readme") instead of a count. For: visible at a glance. Against: long names crowd out the task and push the bar; rows get truncated more often.
C) Something else you describe (different naming for unclaimed rows, a second line under the row, etc.).
Non-binding recommendation: A, since the row's width already has to fit the bar and total.
fields.statement: Does the running-sessions list read right with an unclaimed row named from its harness and folder, and a session in two worktrees shown as a muted '2 worktrees'?

fields.title: Look at the expandable session rows: do the worktrees and files read right?
fields.answer: A with labels and short worktree names, send it to mint
fields.stakes: How you see what a session is working on without leaving the list. Behaviour has landed green (PR #245); only the look is open.
fields.context:
Pictures (PR #245, synthetic activity on the real desktop page):
Collapsed: https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/b805ba4428b7141109f05b0420e5c5d7a4776d0d/packages/forest/evidence/row-detail/collapsed.png
Expanded: https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/b805ba4428b7141109f05b0420e5c5d7a4776d0d/packages/forest/evidence/row-detail/expanded.png

What is built (contract 7.8): every row now has one expander, a small ▸ that turns to ▾. A row with subagents or supervised lanes shows it as ▸ +1, the same single control that used to be only "+1"; clicking the row itself still selects its session, as before. Expanded, an indented block under the row lists, first, the full path of every worktree (folder) the session has worked in, oldest first, in brighter text; then the files in its window (what it has opened and still holds in its context), each once, in the order first opened. A file that a compaction dropped from the window stays in the list but muted, so you can see it was read. Its children follow below. Long paths wrap rather than cut. A session whose transcript has not reached the log says "No files: " and why. The files are read only when you expand a row, and refresh every 10 seconds while it is open.

Analogy: a folder tab you pull open to see the papers inside. It breaks down because the muted files are papers that were in the folder and have been taken out, yet their names stay listed.
fields.options:
A) Accept as built. For: one control, nothing new to learn, full paths as you asked. Against: an expanded row with many files is tall, and the list scrolls inside its panel.
B) Leave compacted-out files out entirely. For: shorter, only what is in the window now. Against: you lose sight of what the session read before compacting.
C) Show files relative to the worktree, or cap the list at the last N files with a "show all". For: shorter lines and blocks. Against: more to build, and a relative path hides which worktree a file is in.
D) Something else you describe (different order, labels such as "Worktrees" / "Files" headings, another place for the expander).
Non-binding recommendation: A; the one thing I would watch is whether the worktrees and files blocks need small headings to tell them apart at a glance.
fields.statement: Does a session row read right collapsed with a small ▸ (▸ +1 when it has subagents), and expanded to its worktrees' full paths, then its window's files with compacted-out ones muted, then its children?

fields.title: Look at the labelled session row: do Worktrees, Files and the short worktree names read right?
fields.stakes: How you read what a session is working on in the list. Your answer (labels, short worktree names) has landed green (PR #249); only the look is open.
fields.context: Picture (PR #249, synthetic activity on the real desktop page): https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/f90c9aae2c8929daa9d5bf47c9b03b0f08fe0c24/packages/forest/evidence/row-detail/expanded.png
fields.options: A) Reads right; accept. B) Adjust: say what (label size or colour, spacing, or how a worktree is named).
fields.statement: Does an expanded session row read right with small muted Worktrees and Files labels, each worktree shown by its folder's name (full path on hover)?

fields.title: Look at the sessions list with close-outs: do the header count, the reasons under "needs you" and the "N idle" fold read right?
fields.stakes: This is how you tell at a glance how many sessions are really working and which ones want you. If it reads wrong, the count goes back to being noise, the thing you asked to fix.
fields.context:
Built from ADR-0758 on your "tighten the timeout rules" / "safe to close" direction, merged as #252 and #256. Three pictures of the real desktop list, the same eight made-up sessions in each:

- Before (the list as it was): header 8, every session that had not ended, including one that had closed out safe with its work merged and three quiet for 40-55 minutes: https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/267d9b6da71559ee62813262dc2531f39fa1cdbb/packages/forest/evidence/close-out/before-list.png
- After: header 4. The session that closed out safe with its work merged is gone. "fix-login" said safe but its branch is unmerged, so it shows "needs you" with "says safe, but fix-login is unmerged" under it. One that said not safe shows "needs you" with its own reason. The three quiet ones fold into "3 idle", collapsed: https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/267d9b6da71559ee62813262dc2531f39fa1cdbb/packages/forest/evidence/close-out/after-list.png
- After, "3 idle" opened: the quiet sessions listed dimmed beneath it: https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/267d9b6da71559ee62813262dc2531f39fa1cdbb/packages/forest/evidence/close-out/after-idle-open.png

What counts in the header: working (mid-turn), waiting for you (its turn ended within your idle-after time, 30 minutes by default), or needing you. Everything else still listed is idle. A session with no unmerged work now leaves 1 hour after it goes quiet (was 12).
fields.options: A: reads right as built. B: right idea, but change how it looks (say what: e.g. the reason inline on the row instead of under it, the idle row placed or worded differently). C: the rules are wrong (e.g. waiting-for-you should last longer or shorter than idle-after, or idle sessions should not be listed at all). Recommendation, not binding: A; the reason line under the row costs one line of height per session needing you, which is the one thing I would watch.
fields.statement: Does the new sessions list read right: the header counting only sessions at work, a close-out's reason printed under its "needs you", and quiet sessions folded into one "N idle" row?

fields.title: Does the 'Holding unmerged work' mark on the sessions list look right?
fields.answer: A, as built (owner, 2026-09-30, looking at the live sessions list: five sessions at work, only the Mint session holding claude/increment-1ead578a6ef5-6321e2 marked): "this is what I see, one session with unmerged work, which looks more right. We keep getting open questions asking me if stuff looks right, if it looks wrong i will tell you we dont need an open question on it at the end of each sprint of work"
fields.stakes: Your look at a built screen; nothing waits on it, but a no becomes a small follow-up. It is the last piece of 'a session with unmerged work stays listed so you can investigate'.
fields.analogy: Like a desk with a sticky note saying 'papers still out': A puts the note on every desk, even ones in the back room; B moves any desk with papers out to the front. It breaks because a desk being worked at always has papers out, so the note also sits on busy desks.
fields.context: Landed in #268. Pictures (the real desktop page, made-up sessions, leave-after set to 3 hours): the list folded https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/70bfa8f19f0920a351e977d2bf73ad79f6e30870/packages/forest/evidence/unmerged-mark/marked-list.png and the idle row opened https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/blob/70bfa8f19f0920a351e977d2bf73ad79f6e30870/packages/forest/evidence/unmerged-mark/marked-idle-open.png. In the pictures: two sessions at work, both marked (a building session's own branch counts as unmerged too, which is true while it builds); a session quiet 3 hours with an unmerged branch sits inside '3 idle', marked; a session quiet 2 hours with nothing unmerged is still listed only because the setting is 3 hours; a finished desktop window you have not archived is counted in '3 idle'. Where a session said 'safe to close' but its branch is unmerged, the 'needs you' line and the mark both appear, so the branch is named twice.
fields.options: A. Looks right as built: the mark shows wherever the row sits, including inside the idle fold. Plus: the header keeps counting only sessions at work. Minus: an abandoned, unmerged session is hidden until you open 'N idle'.\nB. As built, but a row holding unmerged work never folds: it stays among the rows at work (not counted in the header). Plus: you see every uncleaned session without opening anything. Minus: the top of the list gets longer, and a building session is always marked.\nC. Change the look (colour, wording, or a small tag beside the name instead of a line under it); say how.
fields.statement: Rows for sessions whose branches are not merged now carry an orange line under them: 'Holding unmerged work: fix-login, tidy-readme'. Does it read right, and should such a row stay among the idle ones or be pulled up among the sessions at work?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A, and revisit B if you find yourself opening 'N idle' to hunt for uncleaned sessions.

fields.title: May the hooks record the first line of a session's first prompt, to name sessions no app keeps?
fields.answer: Neither A nor B (owner, 2026-10-01): "dont sessions write a title? the first line is unlikely to be descriptive especially if we truncate it to fit. i always imagined sessions populating this themselves could be evetually consistent." Carried by increment_b40094b350b5, rewritten: a session names itself through a tool and the command line; the hooks keep dropping prompt words.
fields.stakes: Unclaimed sessions started from a terminal or headless (Codex exec, the Mint box's CLI runs) still show as 'Claude Code · storytree03'; the fix puts a few of your own words into the shared log, which today deliberately holds none.
fields.analogy: Like a shared calendar showing a meeting's subject line, not just 'busy': more useful, more visible. It breaks down in that the full text is already in the transcript store; only its visibility on the list changes.
fields.context: The shared log is the Cloud SQL activity log both machines write. Transcripts already stream there, scrubbed of obvious secrets (keys, tokens, passwords), so full prompt text is already stored; this would copy one line of it onto the session's first prompt line, where the list can read it without a transcript reader.
fields.options: A: yes, first line of the first prompt, scrubbed, at most 120 characters. Pro: every row gets a real name. Con: your words appear in the list and the log line, not only in the transcript store. | B: no, leave terminal sessions named by harness and folder. Pro: no new words in lines. Con: those rows stay uninformative until they claim work.
fields.statement: Rows now take the desktop app's own title and status. Sessions no app keeps have neither. The only source left is what you typed: the first line of the first prompt.
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A. The transcripts already hold the text, the scrub runs, and the list is yours alone.

fields.title: How should the hooks stay current when the desktop app is not running?
fields.answer: A for 2 (owner, 2026-10-01): start the app at sign-in, in the tray, so its updater keeps the hooks it installed on each release.
fields.stakes: Twice on 2026-09-30 the sessions list showed finished sessions as still at work, because the hooks on the laptop ran an old release: fixes that had landed never reached them. Until hooks stay current by themselves, any hook fix can silently not run.
fields.analogy: Like a phone app that only updates while the phone is on its charger overnight: left off the charger, it keeps an old version. A only puts it on the charger every day; B lets the app update itself anywhere; C only shows a notice that it is out of date. Where it breaks: nothing here costs data, only freshness.
fields.context: Already landed: the sessions list and close-out ask GitHub about merges themselves (#306), and the app does too once a minute (#325), so the list no longer depends on the hooks for merges. The setup check now says at each session start when the hooks run an older release (contract 8.18). On the Mint box, which has no desktop app, hooks already follow main (contract 8.15). What remains is only how hooks on a machine with the app get newer code while the app is closed.
fields.options:
A. Start the app at sign-in, in the tray. The app already has a tray and a background mode; starting it with Windows means its updater runs all day, so the hooks it installed follow each release within minutes. For: smallest change, reuses the updater that already verifies and installs releases. Against: Windows only (the updater does not run on Linux; the Mint box keeps following main as it does now); one more thing running at sign-in; closing it from the tray brings the gap back, though the setup check now says so.

B. The hooks update themselves. Every few hours the hooks' background look asks GitHub for the latest release; if newer, it downloads only the agent tools, checks each file against the release's list of file hashes, keeps them under [home]<version>, and points the hooks at them. For: works on every machine and needs no app running. Against: the most to build (a new release asset, download, verification, clean-up); it downloads and runs release code outside the app's own updater, a second update path to keep safe.

C. Only report it (what landed now). The setup check says "hooks run v0.3.309, v0.3.333 is out: open the app" at every session start, and the agent passes it on. For: nothing more to build or run. Against: someone still has to act, and the lists can still read wrong until they do.
fields.statement: The hooks (the small programs Claude Code and Codex run after each step, which feed the sessions list) are installed by the desktop app and updated only while it runs. On the laptop the app was closed, so its hooks stayed on v0.3.309 while v0.3.333 was out. Which way should they stay current?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A. It is the smallest change, it keeps one update path, and Mint is already covered by following main. B is worth it only if machines without the app on Windows become common.

fields.title: Hosted library: local by default, Google Cloud SQL as the option, then we move onto it
fields.intent: Make where the library lives a user setting, local by default, with Google Cloud SQL as the one hosted option (ADR-0734, decision_0a16e7f63feb, owner-directed 2026-09-28), then move storytree's own development onto the cloud library so every machine (laptop and Mint box) reads and writes one board. Why now: the Mint box cannot reach the laptop's local library (127.0.0.1, trust auth, found through a local owner record), so its lanes' claims and library edits have been relayed by hand through the laptop supervisor, and the forest's sessions list cannot show them. The setting belongs with the per-user settings the agent link settings arc built (arc_748792ea3487, capability 10: settings.json in the storytree home, set from the command line); both the app and the agent link must honour it. 0.2 proved the cloud path: Cloud SQL instance [cloud-instance], Cloud SQL Node connector, keyless IAM auth from ambient ADC (read 0.2's packages/library/src/store/connection.ts in C:\code\storytree for behaviour; port behaviour, never copy code). Non-GCP hosted and self-hosted servers are out of scope for the MVP (ADR-0734 D2).
fields.endState: A user can choose in their settings between the local library (the default) and a Google Cloud SQL library; the app and every agent on a machine follow that choice. Storytree's own project lives on Cloud SQL, moved across with snapshot/restore, and a lane on the Mint box claims and writes to the same board the laptop sees, with no relaying. Local mode has had its new-user run on the old Windows test laptop.

fields.body: Author the tree, then build it test-first. Shape: a "library location" setting in the per-user settings (agent link capability 10, capability_2902dfd80083; settings.json in the storytree home, set from the command line): `local` (default) or `cloudsql` with an instance connection name and database user. Everything that finds the library today must go through one resolver that honours it: the agent link's routing (packages/agent-link/src/routing/routing.ts locateStorytree, which today reads the local owner record and returns postgres://postgres@127.0.0.1:<port>), the app's lifecycle (it starts and owns the local Postgres; in cloud mode it must NOT start one, and must say plainly when the cloud is unreachable), and the CLI's door. Cloud connection: the Cloud SQL Node connector with IAM auth from ambient ADC, as 0.2 did (C:\code\storytree packages/library/src/store/connection.ts; port behaviour). Library story capability 1 creates one database per project on the server: check the IAM user can create databases on the instance and grant it if not (an infra step; say so if it needs the owner's gcloud). Check early: the Postgres major version of the Cloud SQL instance against the embedded one, and whether any 0.3 feature needs an extension (decision_153f390ff901 keeps embedding vectors in the project's Postgres; confirm pgvector or not). Tests stay hermetic (no cloud in `pnpm test`); one opt-in live check proves a real round trip against the instance. Amend the app and agent link trees with story-author first (new contracts under settings, routing and app lifecycle); ADR-0734 is the decision, so no separate owner approval question is needed for the shape unless the tree surfaces a real fork.
fields.title: Library location setting and Google Cloud SQL support

waits.reason: the setting lives in the settings surface that increment builds

fields.objective: A user can set the library to local or a Cloud SQL instance, and the app, the agents and the command line all follow it.

fields.body:
Move storytree's own project onto Cloud SQL. Take a snapshot of the local `storytree` project (library capability 1, snapshot/restore contracts 1.6-1.8) while writes are quiet, restore it into the empty cloud project, verify record and history counts match, then switch the laptop's setting to cloud and restart the app. Keep the local data directory untouched as the fallback until the owner is happy. Then set up the Mint box: ADC credentials for the owner's Google identity or a dedicated service account (ask the owner which; launch-a-claude-session-on-the-mint-desktop memory in 0.2 has how to drive that box), set its library setting to cloud, and prove the point of the arc: a lane on the Mint box claims a capability itself and it shows on the laptop's forest as a normal row, with no supervisor relaying. Write down in the arc what relaying habits (laptop holding claims for Mint lanes, hand-applied library patches from PR evidence) can now stop, and update 0.3's guidance if it mentions them.


Learned building increment 1 (2026-09-28, PR on branch claude/increment-5e6ac23db68f-98df31), for whoever moves the library:
- Switch a machine: `storytree settings set library cloudsql [cloud-instance] <google account email>`; back with `… library local`. Everything (CLI, hooks, agent tools, desktop app) follows it; `storytree doctor` names the instance when it is on.
- The instance is Postgres 16.14 (embedded is 17); snapshots are plain rows, so restore is unaffected. No extension needed.

fields.body: Found while building increment_5e6ac23db68f (2026-09-28). With the library set to Cloud SQL the app starts no local Postgres (app lifecycle 1.9), so it writes no `<home>/pgdata.owner.json`. Everything that asks "is the app running?" reads that owner record: `storytree app status` / `app quit` (packages/app/src/lifecycle/quit.ts quitApp, `locate` default = agent link locateStorytree), the agent link's `own` shared-work line (packages/agent-link/src/tools/server.ts `shared()`, packages/cli/src/families/own.ts), and app-setup's delivery check (packages/app-setup/src/deliver/delivery.ts). In cloud mode they all read "not running" while the app runs, so `storytree app quit` would refuse to quit it and a delivery could replace a running app. Shape: the app records its own presence (pid + start) independently of Postgres, e.g. its app.json launch record gaining a live pid, and a `locateApp()` in the app story that these readers use; `locateStorytree` stays the local database's locator for routing. Contracts to author on app capability 1 (Lifecycle): "in cloud mode, app status reads running while the app runs, and app quit stops it" and on app-setup delivery the same. Not blocking increment 2 (the move): the laptop user quits from the tray.

fields.body: Seen 2026-09-29 by the Surfaces lane (arc_2ce3fdbfbf9a) in packages/app/evidence/surfaces-menu/capture.mjs: 1 of 4 runs against a throwaway local Postgres ended with body data-state=error and the text 'The forest could not be read / Connection terminated due to connection timeout'; the other runs passed. Cause in apps/desktop/src/renderer/renderer.ts: liveReading's onError (and showForest's .catch) call showMessage when data-state is not yet 'ready'; showMessage calls stopShowing(), which stops the live reading, so nothing retries. After ready, an intermittent read is already tolerated (the comment at followProjects' onError). Fix sketch: keep the reading running and show the error without tearing down, or retry the show on the next poll. Needs a red test on the pure part (for example a first-read failure followed by a success reaching ready).
fields.title: A failed first read of a project leaves the page on an error screen for good
fields.objective: When the first read of the project on show fails (a connection timeout, as a slow or cloud library can give), the page recovers on its own once the library answers, instead of staying on 'The forest could not be read' until the project is switched or the app reopened.

fields.body:
Found 2026-09-29 on the laptop, library on Cloud SQL: app.log carried 742 "storytree:wait-holds" and hundreds of "held-on-question" failures, all "timeout exceeded when trying to connect" (pg-pool: no client freed within connectionTimeoutMillis, 20 s), in bursts of 100+ per board refresh; arc-view, project-tree and changes-since failed behind them, and the forest's session list loaded slowly.

Cause: readBoard (packages/arc-surface/src/board/reads.ts) calls waitHolds for every arc and increment and heldOnQuestion for every increment, all at once. Each waitHolds reads a record and lists every arc, increment and question (WorkInFlight #snapshot); each heldOnQuestion reads a record and lists every question; each page read also lists the projects (pageReads.project). That is hundreds of concurrent queries through one 10-client pool per project; locally each is ~1 ms so it never showed, over Cloud SQL the queue outlives the 20 s bound. The live board reruns readBoard on every news item.

Breakdown: one library reading that answers every wait hold and every owner hold for the project's live work from a single snapshot (three list reads), carried page -> app -> desktop bridge as one call; readBoard uses it. The per-id waitHolds/heldOnQuestion stay the library's answers for the CLI and claims.
fields.title: The arc board reads every hold in one call, so the app keeps its connections over Cloud SQL
fields.objective: A board refresh asks the library for all wait and owner holds at once (a handful of queries), instead of several queries per arc and increment that exhaust the connection pool on Cloud SQL

fields.body:
Owner, 2026-09-29: "we should be displaying prev state while the app refreshes, this way the user at least can orient on something during the load".

Context: with the library on Cloud SQL, every read the page makes crosses the network; the arc board shows "loading" until its first read completes (watchBoard in packages/arc-surface/src/board/live-board.ts starts at status "loading" with no snapshot), and the forest's session list and tree likewise wait on their first reads. On app start, restart after an update (every merge to main), or project switch, the user sees nothing to orient on for seconds.

Shape to explore: keep each surface's last good state (board snapshot, project tree, session list) somewhere the next start can read it (the app's storytree home, owned by the app frame, served through the bridge), render it at once marked as not yet fresh, and replace it when the live read lands; on a failed refresh keep showing the previous state with the error, rather than an error screen (see increment_cac4209a4508 on the same arc, which is adjacent). Decide where the cache lives without putting story code into the frame (ADR-0649): each story package owns what it caches, the frame only persists.
fields.title: The app shows its last known state at once while it refreshes
fields.objective: On start, restart and project switch, each surface draws what it last showed, marked as refreshing, instead of an empty loading screen while its reads cross the network

fields.body:
Found 2026-09-29 on the laptop, library on Cloud SQL: `storytree adr list --load-bearing` ran past 100 s without output (twice; killed), while `arc show` answered in ~15 s.
Cause: packages/cli/src/families/adr.ts `adr list` lists every decision, then awaits `library.decision(id)` for each one in turn, so each decision costs its own round trips to the cloud library (hundreds of decisions, sequential). The session-orchestrator role makes this command every session's first read, so every session start pays it.
Breakdown: one library reading that returns every decision's view (status worked out) from a single list, used by `adr list`; the filters stay in the CLI. Pin it with the decision story's contract for listing; measure the command against Cloud SQL before and after.

Found on 2026-10-02 while checking the README's claims against the code (increment_156a4fa2606b, arc_cfc7db517fae). The README's section "This repo's own library" names two scripts that do not do what it says, now that storytree's own project lives on Cloud SQL (since 2026-09-28; `pnpm storytree settings show` reads `library: cloudsql [cloud-instance]`).

1. **`pnpm library:export` reads only the app's local library.** packages/dev-loop/src/export-library.mjs opens `[home] (it prints "the app's library: <pgdata>") through library-server.mjs and never reads the `library` setting. From a machine that follows the setting, it cannot export the real `storytree` project. `pnpm check:own-health` already follows the setting (packages/dev-loop/src/own-health.mjs, `recordingTarget`), so there is a model to follow.
2. **`pnpm library:restore` does not exist.** The README says "`pnpm library:restore <snapshot>` puts one back, only into an empty project", and library-server.mjs's header names `library:restore`, but the root package.json has no such script (it has `library:export` and `check:own-health`). **Done when.** Both scripts reach the library the `library` setting names (local, Cloud SQL or a Postgres address, ADR-0734 and ADR-0846), and `pnpm library:restore <snapshot>` runs; or, where one is deliberately local-only, it says so when run and the README says so too. Test-first in packages/dev-loop, the owning package (ADR-0623, ADR-0649). When it lands, correct the README's lines about these two scripts in the same pull request.

fields.title: Which Google identity should the Mint box sign in to the cloud library as?
fields.answer: Owner, 2026-09-28: "service account for the Mint box, go ahead and set it up"
fields.stakes: Until this is answered the Mint box cannot sign in to the cloud library, so its lanes stay invisible on the laptop's board and their claims and library edits keep being relayed by hand through the laptop. Nothing else in the move is blocked: the laptop can switch to the cloud library without it.
fields.analogy: Option A is lending the Mint box your own office keycard; option B is issuing it a visitor card that opens only the library room. The analogy breaks on revocation: a lost visitor card is cancelled without touching yours, but cancelling a lent keycard here means revoking one specific login token, not your whole account.
fields.context:
The cloud library is the Cloud SQL database 0.2 used (instance [cloud-instance]). Storytree signs in "keylessly": each machine uses whatever Google login it already holds (Application Default Credentials, set with `gcloud auth application-default login` or a service-account key), and the database lets that identity in as a user. No database password is stored.

Your account (hua.mick@gmail.com) is already set up on the database, including permission to create a new database per project (through a role called storytree_creator). The laptop will use it. The Mint box currently has no Google login for this.

Every write a machine makes is recorded with the session that made it, not the Google identity, so the board attributes work the same either way. What differs is who can act as whom, how revocable it is, and how much setup it takes.
fields.options:
A. Your own Google account on the Mint box. Run `gcloud auth application-default login` there once, in a browser, as hua.mick@gmail.com. Pros: no new identity, nothing to grant, works today. Cons: the Mint box then holds a refresh token that can act as you across all your Google Cloud projects (whatever your account can do), until revoked; revoking it logs out every machine that uses the same grant flow only if you revoke that specific token.

B. A service account just for the Mint box (for example storytree-mint@[cloud-project]). You (or I, with your go-ahead, using your gcloud on the laptop) create it, give it only Cloud SQL Client + Instance User on this project, add it as a database user, grant it storytree_creator, and put its key file on the Mint box. Pros: least privilege (it can reach this database and nothing else), revocable on its own, clearly one machine. Cons: a key file lives on the Mint box (a long-lived secret to guard), and about ten minutes of setup that changes IAM on your project, which is why I am asking rather than doing it.
fields.statement: Which Google identity should the Mint box sign in to the cloud library as: your own Google account, or a dedicated service account for that machine?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: B. The Mint box runs agents unattended; a credential that can only reach this one database limits what a misbehaving lane could touch. If you want the Mint box on the board today and will tighten later, A works immediately.

fields.title: May the Mint box get storytree's agent hooks, so its lanes show on the board themselves?
fields.answer: Owner, 2026-09-29: "yes you can install hooks on the mintbox"
fields.stakes: Until this is answered, Mint lanes still cannot appear on the board by themselves: they reach the cloud library now, but nothing on the Mint box records their sessions or claims, so the laptop supervisor keeps relaying them by hand. That relaying is the thing this arc exists to end.
fields.analogy: The Mint box now has a key to the shared office (the cloud library), but no badge reader on its door, so nobody sees when its staff come and go; the hooks are the badge reader. Where it breaks: a badge reader is visible to the staff; hooks are invisible to the agents, and a broken one fails silently instead of locking anyone out.
fields.context:
Done overnight (2026-09-28): the laptop's library moved to Cloud SQL (verified count for count), the desktop app reopened on it, and the Mint box reads and writes the same database as its own service account (storytree-mint), with [home] updated to main. Its two running lanes (winhooks, winupdate) can reach the board from their folders.

What is missing: the "hooks", small commands Claude Code and Codex run on every session start, prompt, edit and command, which is how a session shows on the board and in the forest's sessions list. On the laptop they are registered in [home] and [home], pointing at a built copy of the agent link. The Mint box has none. Installing them means building the agent link on the Mint box and running its setup, which adds storytree's entries to the Mint box's Claude Code and Codex settings (nothing else is touched; `storytree setup remove` takes them out again). I did not do it unasked because it changes persistent settings on another machine while two unattended lanes run there.
fields.options:
A. Install now (the next session does it at once): build the agent link in [home] on the Mint box and run its setup. Running lanes pick the hooks up on their next event, so their sessions appear on the board mid-run. Risk: a hook failing on the Mint box is silent by design (hooks never break the agent), so the worst case is lanes that still don't show.

B. Install between lanes: same steps, but only once no lane is running, so no running session changes behaviour mid-run. Costs a wait until the current lanes finish.

C. Don't install: keep relaying Mint lanes through the laptop. Nothing changes, and the arc's end state (Mint lanes on the board with no relaying) is not reached.
fields.statement: May I install storytree's agent hooks on the Mint box, so its Claude Code and Codex lanes write their own sessions and claims to the cloud board?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A. Hooks only record; a failing hook is silent, so the running lanes are not at risk, and waiting for B costs a day of relaying.

fields.title: May a lane run the two live Cloud SQL checks, and against which instance?
fields.stakes: Two parts of the hosted library show as untested on the health board and will stay so until someone runs their live checks; running them writes test data to a real Cloud SQL instance and may cost a little.
fields.analogy: Like test-driving a car on the public road in a marked lane (A) or hiring a track for an hour (B); the analogy breaks in that A's 'lane' is a separate project, so nothing in the real plan is changed.
fields.context: They are opt-in: the normal test run skips them. 'Untested' on the health board means no run has reported them. The only instance today is storytree's own shared library (storytree-pg), which holds the real plan; the Mint box signs in as its service account. A throwaway second instance would keep test writes away from the real plan but costs money while it exists.
fields.options: A) Run both against the shared instance in a scratch project the run creates and removes. Cheap and quick; test writes touch the real instance (in their own project). B) Create a throwaway instance for the run, then delete it. Keeps the real library untouched; costs a few dollars and needs your go-ahead on spend. C) Not now: leave both untested and parked.
fields.statement: Two checks only run against a real Google Cloud SQL library: (1) the library's whole behaviour suite, run unchanged over Google sign-in; (2) the agent activity log, written from two machines and read back from either. Should a lane on the Mint box run them, and against which instance?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A, if the run's scratch project is removed afterwards.

fields.title: 0.3's own sessions reach both front doors, and we see which they choose
fields.intent: Carry out ADR-0793: register the agent link's tool server for 0.3's own sessions (Claude Code and Codex, every worktree), rewrite the guidance so each step offers the tools and the command line as equal options for the agent to choose, then measure what agents actually pick. Opened 2026-09-30 from the owner's answer to question_90e0c957cc4d.
fields.endState: The three increments on this arc are landed or closed with a reason, and the usage reading has gone to the owner. Nothing else is added (ADR-0792 D2).

fields.body:
ADR-0793 D2. Today no .mcp.json exists, so 0.3's own sessions cannot reach the tools at all (the reason 85 transcripts made zero tool calls). Register the server so it works from every worktree provisioned by scripts/provision-worktree.mjs and for Codex lanes on the Mint box. Decide whether the registered server is the installed app's or one run from the checkout's source, and record why. Test that goes red: a fresh worktree's session config names the storytree server and a tool call (e.g. search_notes) answers against the storytree project. Tools a branch is still building go through the command line until they ship.

**Built (2026-09-30, Mint lane mcpreg).** `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) and `.codex/config.toml` `[mcp_servers.storytree]` (Codex) both start `node scripts/provision-worktree.mjs --serve`. That launcher waits for the session-start install (the same script's `--hook`, which both harnesses already run), then runs `packages/agent-link/src/bins/storytree-mcp.ts` under tsx from that worktree, with the worktree as its folder, so `.storytree.json` routes it to project `storytree` and the `library` setting (Cloud SQL) is honoured. `.claude/settings.json` lists the server in `enabledMcpjsonServers`; Codex's entry sets `default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"`, because Codex lanes run with `approval_policy = "never"`, which refused every tool call until then (measured: "MCP tool call requires approval, but approval policy is never").

**Decision: the checkout's source, not the installed app.** (1) A checked-in file can name a source path relative to the worktree, which is the same on Windows and Linux; the installed app lives at a different place on each machine, and this Mint box has no installed app (its `storytree` command points at a hand-built dist in a stray worktree). (2) Run from source, no built `storytree-hook.mjs` sits beside the server, so its setup check registers no hooks and puts no command on the path: it cannot rewrite the user's `[home] or `[home] hooks, which the installed app's server would repoint at itself. (3) Each worktree serves the code on its own branch, which tracks main as it lands, so 0.3 sessions use the tools 0.3 ships. Cost: the server needs the worktree installed (hence `--serve` waits) and starts through tsx (about a second).

**Evidence.** Before: `claude mcp list` in a worktree named no storytree server. After, from the worktree: `claude -p` listed 47 `mcp__storytree__*` tools and `search_notes "merge ceremony"` returned "Merge ceremony" (process_0967b1a1d3cb); `codex exec` did the same. A fresh `git worktree add` with no node_modules: before `--serve`, the session had 0 storytree tools (the server died before the install); after, Codex answered with process_0967b1a1d3cb and Claude Code had the tool (that one call was refused by Cloud SQL, out of connection slots under other lanes' load, filed as friction). `[home] was untouched throughout. Red→green test: scripts/provision-worktree.test.mjs "the tool server starts in a fresh worktree once the session-start install has finished".

**Known limits.** On a machine where the 0.3 checkout was never accepted in Claude Code's trust prompt (this box's unattended checkout), interactive `claude mcp list` shows the server as pending approval; headless (`-p`) sessions get it anyway, and a trusted checkout's worktrees (nested under it) inherit the project approval. Codex trusts worktrees under the trusted checkout (verified here); a worktree created elsewhere needs its own trust entry. Not verified on Windows by hand: the commands are `node` with forward-slash relative paths, which Node accepts there, and CI runs the launcher's test on Windows.
fields.title: Register the agent link's tool server for 0.3's own sessions

outcome.note: 0.3's Claude Code and Codex sessions, from the checkout and every worktree, now start storytree's tool server from their own source (.mcp.json, .codex/config.toml via provision-worktree.mjs --serve) and can call its tools against 0.3's library.

fields.objective: A Claude Code or Codex session started in this checkout or any of its worktrees lists storytree's tools and can call them against 0.3's library

fields.body: ADR-0793 D1, in the owner's words: 'give agents both options and see if not determinism leads them to use both.' Edit the roles in the library (library edit ceremony), the hand-written CLAUDE.md header, and the Mint lane brief; then pnpm build:guidance and pnpm gate -- --guidance. Where a step names a verb, name both forms, e.g. the claim tool or storytree workspace <increment> --reason. No wording that prefers one door. fields.intent:

The site's forest (ADR-0798 D4) draws a saved snapshot of 0.3's own library with the app's own engine, `@storytree/forest-world`, consumed from the workspace with no vendored copy. It mounts in the slot the home-page increment leaves. Where WebGL is missing, the page shows a still of the same scene.

The snapshot is a committed file that a session refreshes from the library with one command. CI cannot read the library.

Keep the page fast and usable on a phone: load the 3D lazily, after the text. Stay inside forest-world's public exports. If the site needs something forest-world does not export, add the export there, in its own small PR, rather than reaching into its internals. Never copy code out of the desktop app's `packages/forest` (that is the forest story's package).

It is a visual unit: its look lands with its pictures (ADR-0794).

### Site-b residue — 2026-09-30

HELD at a cross-lane dependency boundary, before code edits. The required five-minute poll first found both prerequisites at 12:23 UTC: the planning increment closed as landed in PR #326, and freshly fetched origin/main contained packages/website. Site-b created a clean worktree at 7eb27c62aca3e591d556faedfd362ca7af6f284b and claimed this increment plus Saved snapshot (capability_88dfe8ee2706).

The scaffold reserves src/forest.ts and #website-forest, but its manifest declares only @storytree/forest-world as a runtime dependency. From that package's resolution context, react, react-dom/client, @react-three/fiber, @storytree/forest and @storytree/arc-surface all return MODULE_NOT_FOUND. The existing PlanetWorldCanvas public export is sufficient for the basic scene; no shared-engine implementation change has been justified. Public @storytree/forest functions (forestScene, storyNodes, placeOnPackedGlobe, PLANET_RADIUS) can derive the desktop-equivalent snapshot without copying desktop code. The refresh command can use locateLibrary, connect, projectTree, changesSince and workStates through public story-package functions, publishing derived drawing fields only.

The needed package dependencies also require root pnpm-lock.yaml changes. Site-b's explicit file fence covers forest files and the mount within packages/website, and public exports in packages/forest-world; it excludes that shared lockfile. The common brief directs this lane to leave a real cross-lane edge as residue. Do not bypass dependency declarations or copy desktop code to avoid the seam.

Concrete handoff for site-a: /tmp/site-b-dependencies.patch contains only packages/website/package.json plus the website importer in pnpm-lock.yaml. Runtime additions: react ^19.1.1, react-dom ^19.1.1, @react-three/fiber ^9.6.1. Development additions: @types/react-dom ^19.1.6, and workspace @storytree/forest, @storytree/arc-surface, @storytree/agent-link, @storytree/library. The patch was generated in /tmp from the existing manifests and lockfile using pnpm install --lockfile-only --offline --ignore-scripts; it introduces no new package versions and was not applied to a repository checkout. Merge these shared prerequisite declarations in site-a's permitted lane, or explicitly extend site-b's fence to the manifest and generated root lockfile, before rerunning site-b.

No product code, tests, captures, bundle measurements or first-render measurements landed. No pull request was opened and there is no red branch to recover. The read-only API scout completed. The prerequisite poll exited normally. This lane releases its claims and removes its unused worktree. No owner design question is needed: this is lane coordination, not an unresolved product choice. Resume from freshly fetched main, reclaim this increment and its two capabilities, and implement snapshot export and lazy rendering test-first under the recorded website contracts. Keep the still and both comparison captures on exactly the same saved scene, with a 390 px phone capture and measured bundle/first-render timing.

### Dependency handoff resolved — 2026-09-30

PR #331 merged at b0c9e4ffdfe63f4e303c827cfc57b12e212f460c and landed the website manifest and lockfile dependencies needed above. Site-b can resume from freshly fetched main and reclaim the forest work. The home page now links forest.js; replace the reserved src/forest.ts stub with the lazy forest bootstrap. The temporary eager renderer bundle (1.43 MB) still needs to be removed from the initial load as part of this forest increment. The saved snapshot, live scene, same-scene still fallback, mobile captures and performance verification remain open; this note resolves only the dependency handoff.

### Shared-renderer handoff — 2026-09-30

Resume from freshly fetched main after PR #333 (cf1430419f4251c50178b89addf1c0913c83b1c5): owner-directed ADR-0804 D1 removes pines and plants, and PlanetWorldCanvas now draws flat story islands. Its kitBytes prop is removed. Use the current public renderer and capture that flat scene plus its matching still; never restore pines on the website or copy the app's territory/file-circle implementation. ADR-0798 D4 and ADR-0801 retain the same-engine boundary. Snapshot export, lazy activation, fallback and measured phone behavior remain open.

The home-copy follow-up (increment_64fd633459e6) places a truthful future-tense placeholder inside #website-forest. Site-b replaces that mount content when it mounts the scene or still, so the pending-state copy vanishes. Do not leave a stale promise around the finished scene.

PR #337 (334d7df56239d27877684878ae994254297cad48) subsequently landed capability territories and file circles in the app. At that merge PlanetWorldCanvas draws the island surface and passes the coast through plateChildren; the app's PlanetView supplies the territory/file-circle overlay. Importing PlanetWorldCanvas alone therefore does not establish that the website draws those marks. Inspect the current public interface when resuming, preserve the no-copy boundary, and claim only what the website's saved snapshot and renderer actually display.


### Site-b partial landing and claim refusal — 2026-10-01 AEST

The resumed lane started from fresh main and implemented the independently claimed Saved snapshot capability. Commit a2bc507 adds packages/website/src/refresh-forest.ts, forest-snapshot.ts, forest-data.ts, the committed JSON, two behavior tests and FOREST.md. One command reads the public library and activity functions, derives the public drawing through forestScene/storyNodes/placeOnPackedGlobe, and atomically replaces the JSON. It exports no raw records, descriptions, activity lines, session identities, credentials or source paths. A failed read leaves the previous file intact. The captured drawing at 2026-09-30T14:01:15.066Z is 30,362 bytes: 14 stories, 90 capabilities and 131 dependency links. The snapshot contains the base islands/pathways, not a source survey or the app's territory/file-circle overlays. The library, history and activity reads are separate, not an atomic database backup.

HELD for a binding claim refusal: the forest-on-site capability (capability_18562ff0841c) was held by live site-a Codex session 01a0f227-987d-74e1-a9f6-7ac421f4d608, reason “Align map plan with shared engine”. Site-b did not edit its renderer or mount and did not queue for the claim. Only the green saved-snapshot work is being landed; the increment remains open and all site-b claims will be released after that landing. This is lane coordination, not an owner question.

Remaining: replace the eager 1.43 MB renderer stub with a lazy bootstrap after the page text; mount the shared engine against the committed drawing; capture a same-scene still; prove absent WebGL and failed initialization preserve a usable page; capture the site and desktop-equivalent engine on that same JSON at desktop and 390 px phone widths; measure bundle bytes and first render. No visual unit, screenshot or renderer performance result is claimed by this partial landing.

Local checks: new tests observed red before implementation; pnpm gate passed all typechecks, 25 website tests and 7 boundary tests (scope: packages/website). The static build and a real refresh passed. Guidance NOT RUN because no roles or guidance notes changed. Test-ratio report read: website 0.56, whole repository 1.03. Curation residue: ADR-0798 D2 and stories/website.md:36 falsely say the old site never rendered the vendored engine. This was introduced by storytree-web commit 2325978d7a240ba5b112c6c1a52b9e3928be1e31 on 2026-09-24; cad6baf subsequently removed the prior flat picture. PR #341 merged by CI at d779c96814e4081a22b7de51ad2f589f237501bb. fields.title: Which web address should the 0.3 site live at?
fields.answer: keep the here.now address for now.
fields.stakes: This is the address first users and anyone they tell will type or share. Changing it after people have shared it breaks their links. It holds only the publish step. Planning and building the site go ahead without it.
fields.context: The 0.2 site is published to here.now under the slug crisp-globe-bf6v. A slug is here.now's name for a site, and it forms the site's address. The survey found no custom domain configured. ADR-0798 keeps here.now as the host, publishing on every merge. here.now can serve a site at a domain you own, but that needs a DNS record (the setting at your domain registrar that points the name at the host), which only you can add. First users don't wait on the site (ADR-0798 D7), so there is no deadline.
fields.options:
A: Keep the here.now address. There is nothing to buy or configure and it is live today, but the address is a random-looking name that doesn't say "storytree" and is hard to remember or say aloud.
B: Use a domain you already own. It looks like a product and is shareable, but you add one DNS record and give its name here.
C: Buy a new domain (for example a storytree-something name). Same benefits as B, but it costs a yearly fee, and the purchase and DNS are yours to do.
Analogy: a here.now address is like a phone number the carrier assigned, while a domain is a number you chose. People can still reach you either way, but only one is worth printing on a card. Where it breaks: a domain costs money every year and can lapse.
fields.statement: Should storytree's website stay at its here.now address, or move to a domain you own (one you have already, or a new one to buy)?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: B if you already own a fitting domain, otherwise A for now. Nothing gates first users on the site, and the domain can be pointed at here.now later without rebuilding anything.

fields.title: here.now cannot show the site's own not-found page: which way?
fields.stakes: What a visitor sees on a mistyped or stale link to the public website. Today it is a blank white page with the two words "Not found" (plain text, status 404), not the site's own styled "This path hasn't grown yet" page with a way home. Low traffic stakes; it is about how finished the public face looks, weighed against moving the site or bending how it answers.
fields.context: Checked 2026-10-02 against here.now's documentation (here.now/docs, llms-full.txt) and its full API description (openapi.json): there is no not-found, error-page or 404 option anywhere, and no site manifest for one (the only site manifests are for proxy routes and data). The one related switch is "SPA mode" (single-page application mode, for sites whose pages are drawn by JavaScript in the browser): with it on, any address that matches no file gets the home page instead of a 404. A live probe of a missing address today returns status 404, text/plain, body "Not found". Our build already makes a styled 404.html (website contract 1.4), and the publisher uploads it, but here.now never serves it for a missing address; it only answers at /404.html itself. Terms: a "404 status" is the code that tells browsers and search engines a page does not exist; a "soft 404" is a page that looks like a not-found page but answers "200 OK", which search engines treat as a mistake. The address question you settled earlier (keep the here.now address, no custom domain) is why option C is a real cost, not a free switch. Analogy: here.now is a landlord whose building has one fixed "no such room" sign on every wrong door; option B is putting our own sign on the lobby and sending every wrong door there, which works for people but tells the post office the room exists. Where it breaks: unlike a post office, search engines usually spot and discount soft 404s rather than being fooled for long.
fields.options:
A. Accept the host's bare "Not found". Cost: none; nothing to build; the increment closes as not doing it. Downside: a mistyped link shows a blank page with no way home and none of the site's look.
B. Turn on here.now's single-page mode and have the home page, when loaded at an address it does not know, show the not-found content with a link home (and a noindex tag). Cost: a small change in the publisher (send spaMode) and in the home page's script, about one increment, staying on the here.now address. Downside: missing addresses answer "200 OK" with the home page's HTML first (a soft 404); search engines and link checkers see a real page; without JavaScript the visitor sees the home page, not a not-found page; and every future page we add must be known to that script.
C. Move the site to a host that serves 404.html with a real 404 status (for example GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages, both free for this). Cost: a new publish path and its credentials (a couple of increments), and a new address, which reopens the address you settled (keep here.now, no custom domain) and every link already given out. Upside: the site's own not-found page with a true 404, and no reliance on here.now's feature set.
fields.statement: The host the website lives on (here.now, at crisp-globe-bf6v.here.now, the address you chose to keep) has no setting for a custom not-found page, so the site's own 404 page cannot be wired in as asked. Which do you want: keep the host's bare "Not found", turn on the host's single-page mode and have the home page draw the not-found page itself, or move the site to a host that serves 404.html?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A for now. The site has one page and few visitors, B trades a correct 404 for a soft one, and C reopens the address decision for a cosmetic gain; revisit with C if a custom domain or more pages ever come.

fields.title: Storytree 0.3 on macOS: a signed Apple Silicon app, a curl one-liner, and agents connected
fields.intent:
**A vibecoder on an Apple Silicon Mac can install storytree 0.3 with one command and get the same smooth first build a Windows user gets.** Opened 2026-09-30 from the owner's "what we can do for mac support since i dont own a mac". It is governed by decision_dfb6e40aa9f7: Windows first users go first, the app is Developer ID signed and notarised ($99/yr Apple Developer Program), and only Apple Silicon is supported.

Where it starts (explorer sweep, 2026-09-30):
- The runtime is mostly cross-platform, and CI runs typecheck and tests on macOS for every pull request.
- Missing (1), packaging: `apps/desktop` electron-builder has only a `win` target. `extraResources` hardcodes `@embedded-postgres/windows-x64`. `tools.mjs` stages Node and tools for win32 only.
- Missing (2), the release: `release.yml`'s publish job runs only on `windows-latest`.
- Missing (3), delivery: `install.ps1` only, and `packages/app-setup` `delivery.ts:93` refuses anything other than win32.
- Missing (4), updates: `packages/app` uses `NsisUpdater`, and `apps/desktop/src/main/releases.ts` turns updates off unless the platform is win32.
- Unknown: the Codex desktop CLI's location on macOS.
- Already present: POSIX hook quoting, the shell launcher, darwin app-data paths and darwin process observation.

Proving without owning a Mac is an open question on this arc. The options are GitHub macOS runners, a rented cloud Mac, or a trusted-circle Mac user.
fields.endState: Closed when an Apple Silicon Mac that has never seen storytree runs one `curl … | sh` command, gets a Developer ID signed and notarised storytree 0.3 app that opens with no Gatekeeper warning, has Claude Code and Codex connected with hooks firing, grows a project in a real signed-in session, and later takes an ordinary release update by itself. This is proven by the method the owner chooses on this arc's proof question, and every 0.3.<n> release then publishes the Mac build next to the Windows one.
fields.description: Brings 0.3's app setup to Macs. The code already passes CI on macOS; this arc adds the packaging, installer, updater, signing and the proof. Parked by the owner on 2026-09-30: Windows first users go first.

fields.body:
This is owner action (spend and identity), per decision_dfb6e40aa9f7 D2. Start it early, because Apple's enrolment checks take days to weeks.
- The owner enrols at developer.apple.com ($99/yr). Individual enrolment shows his personal name as the developer. An organisation shows the company name but needs a D-U-N-S number. This is his call when he enrols.
- A session guides the export of the Developer ID Application certificate (.p12 plus password) and an App Store Connect API key (key id, issuer id, .p8). They go into repo secrets: CSC_LINK, CSC_KEY_PASSWORD, APPLE_API_KEY, APPLE_API_KEY_ID, APPLE_API_ISSUER. The agent never handles the secret values. The owner pastes them into GitHub himself.
- Done when a CI dry-run step on macos-latest imports the certificate into a temporary keychain and `security find-identity` lists it.

fields.body:
This is the Mac twin of increment_44bd7a583f32. It is held by this arc's question on how to prove the Mac path without owning a Mac.
- Whatever the choice, the automated floor is a macos-latest runner job on each release. It runs `curl | sh` against the published release, opens the app and takes a screenshot, checks that local Postgres started, runs the setup check, checks that hooks were written, and runs `spctl --assess`.
- The human-level proof (a signed-in Claude Code and Codex subscription session, what first open looks like, folder-permission prompts) comes from the chosen method. Evidence goes to `packages/app-setup/evidence/mac-acceptance/`.


TO RAISE WHEN THIS ARC IS UNPARKED (2026-10-01): question_6ce31121b7f6 "How do we prove the Mac path without owning a Mac?" was retired because a parked arc raises no questions (ADR-0835). Its options, to re-raise: A GitHub macOS runners only (free; proves install, launch, Postgres, setup check, hooks, spctl, an API-key Claude Code run; not subscription sign-in, Codex login, Gatekeeper's first open or permission prompts); B runners plus a rented cloud Mac per acceptance (AWS EC2 Mac ~$25-30/day, 24 h minimum; Scaleway cheaper); C runners plus a trusted-circle Mac user as tester (free, but they meet our bugs first); D B then C. The earlier session's non-binding recommendation was D.

fields.body:
Found by the first-build round on the reset laptop (increment_44bd7a583f32, evidence packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build, shot p3-island-todo-claude.png).

**What a first user sees.** Claude Code built TodoMVC in project todo-claude: 1 story, 5 capabilities, 14 contracts, 14 browser tests named by the contract titles, each reported red then green. The official TodoMVC suite passes 24 of 29 on it (the ceiling: the other 5 are the suite's own bugs on Cypress 15). Yet every capability card in the story panel reads UNTESTED, with only a tiny "the agent reports: passing", and the panel says "Why not green: no test names Main and footer hidden when there are no todos, … The agent moves this one." `storytree tree` says the same: "agent says passing · storytree verified not checked; untested — no test names it, the agent's to move". Codex's project reads the same way.

**Why.** Nothing writes the verified column for a user's project in the MVP (ADR-0630, decision_6be3b0bfb19e: "Nothing writes it for users' projects in the MVP"); the only writer is storytree's own CI (packages/dev-loop/src/own-health.mjs). capabilityWhy hard-codes mover "agent" and reason "no test names it" for any contract with no verified record (packages/library/src/health/health-record.ts:357). In a user's project the agent cannot move it: no test title, runner or tool reaches that column, and the agent is never told how a test "names" a contract.

**The gap.** The words are false for a user's project, and they discourage: a first user is told the work is untested and the agent's to fix, when the agent tested it and nothing it can do changes the label. ADR-0630 already says a user's project shows the agent's report, labelled as such; the label and the reason should say that truly.

**Done when.** In a project whose health nothing verifies (any user's project in the MVP), the story panel, its cards and `storytree tree` lead with what the agent reported, labelled as the agent's, and say plainly that storytree does not check this project's tests yet, without "untested", "no test names it" or "the agent moves this one". storytree's own project keeps today's verified health. Test-first in the package that owns the wording (library health reason, forest story panel). If making the user's-project case distinct needs a product choice beyond ADR-0630 (for example, whether storytree should start verifying users' tests), raise it as a question on this arc rather than deciding it.

fields.body:
Follow-up from increment_868eaff67b23 (PR 462). forest-world's five CI hangs were one shape: a test file's tests all pass, then its process never exits, and nothing notices until the unit's 180 s deadline kills the whole unit (and, in the merge queue, evicts a pull request). Reproduced once on the Mint box under CPU contention (about 1 in 2,500 runs of the underlay file): the file's process sat in futex wait in Node's exit teardown, with 2 of 4 V8 worker threads already joined and its esbuild child already a zombie. That is a Node/V8 exit deadlock, not test code. PR 462 removed the trigger it correlated with (the only test loading React/fiber/drei/three), but any file can still hit the same deadlock.
- In packages/dev-loop (unit-run.mjs, test-running-reporter.mjs): when every test a file started has ended and its file-level entry has stayed open for a short grace (seconds, not minutes), kill that file's process (or fail the unit) at once and name it as "tests ended, process did not exit", so the run fails fast instead of waiting out the unit deadline.
- Evidence: CI jobs 110048534910, 110147466069, 110192547070, 110425271794 (Linux), 110292772210 (Windows): each log shows the file's 9 tests passing about 2 s into the unit, then silence until the 180 s kill; the harness names it as "<file> › <file>" (the file-level entry, whose name is a path, not a basename, so it is not shown as "outside any test").
- Not: raising the unit limit.
fields.title: A test file whose tests have ended but whose process does not exit fails fast, not at the unit deadline

Found by the devloop lane on 2026-10-02 (increment_67a3090c077c, PR 470). On the Mint box, packages/forest/src/view/browser-build.test.ts hung at exit after its one test passed, on two full gates in a row. Neither branch touched forest.

fields.body:
**What a first user reads.** README.md's opening "Storytree 0.3." paragraph ends: "Health shows what the agent *reported* separately from what storytree *verified* for itself." For a user's project that overstates the product. Nothing writes the verified column there (ADR-0630, decision_6be3b0bfb19e: "Nothing writes it for users' projects in the MVP"; ADR-0744, decision_a18c5e1d110b, D5: a user's project keeps proposed / untested until storytree can read that project's CI, which is later work). So the panel's "storytree saw" mark never appears (packages/forest/src/drill-down/drill-down.ts, contractLine shows it only once the column is written), and capability cards stay proposed or untested (packages/library/src/health/health-record.ts, capabilityStatus). Only storytree's own project gets checked health, from its CI on main (.github/workflows/own-health.yml) and its acceptance runs. ADR-0798 (decision_67b283aa164b) D3 requires the public claims to match 0.3 as it is, and D7 makes the README the page first users are sent to.

**Breakdown.**
1. Reword that sentence so it is true for a user's project: health is what the agent reported, labelled as the agent's report; storytree does not yet check your project's tests itself; so far it checks only its own, shown separately. Keep what is shipped (the agent's report, labelled; storytree's own check, kept apart from it). Name no card word ("untested", "proposed"): increment_ef066f718a63 is changing those words for a user's project, and the README must stay true when it lands.
2. Check apps/desktop/README.md and the first-run guide (packages/app-setup/src/view/guide.ts) for the same overstatement. Read on parking: neither carries it. The desktop README's "verified installation" is the installer's checksum; the guide says only "a story and its capabilities appear as the agent plans them, with activity and health as work proceeds".
3. Prose only: no test pins its wording (ADR-0623). `pnpm gate`, then a non-draft pull request.

**Done when.** The README's opening paragraph makes no claim that storytree checks a user's project: it says health is the agent's report, labelled as such, and that storytree's own check is not yet available for a user's project.

outcome.note: The README opening now says health is what your agent reported, labelled as the agent's report, and that storytree does not yet check your project's tests itself: so far it checks only its own, shown separately. The desktop README and the first-run guide carried no such claim and are unchanged. Gate: typecheck, full tests (16 units) and plan edges PASS.
