fields.title: Adopt the health maintenance proposal, and bring back model user acceptance?
fields.answer: for everything except D3, add increments or arcs and send it to the mintbox. For D3 mock it for me, or draw a diagram, the fact that you suggest blight makes me think your not grounded on the latest look, we no longer do forest.
fields.stakes: Whether the forest's colours can be trusted without you chasing them, and whether a model playing a user counts as proof. Accepting starts four increments; the quick fixes go ahead either way.
fields.analogy: Like a building inspection. D1-D4 make sure every room either has a current certificate or a note on the door saying why not and who is fixing it. D5 decides whether a trained walk-through, someone actually using the lift and the doors, counts toward the certificate. Where it breaks: the walk-through here is a model, which is fast and repeatable but has no taste, so taste stays with you (ADR-0794).
fields.context:
Today 46 of 90 capabilities are healthy, 24 untested, 19 proposed and 1 unhealthy. The one red card is a stale hand run from 27 Sep that CI can never overwrite, because CI skips that test and writes nothing for a skip. The forest's ground is coloured by the agent's own report, not by what storytree verified. Nothing turns a grey or red card into work, and nothing shows which ones wait on you.

ADR-0825 proposes:
- D1: every card that is not green says why, and whether an agent or you moves it.
- D2: a skipped test marks the old verdict "not re-run" instead of leaving it standing.
- D3: territories are coloured by the verified word, with a signpost where you are needed.
- D4: every landing drains the three oldest non-green cards into work, as friction is drained today.
- D5: model user acceptance.

"Model user acceptance" (UAT): an agent session drives the real app on the Windows test laptop as a new user would (claude -p or codex exec), and the harness records what happened. 0.2 ran this from August to its freeze (ADR-0295; 76 UAT commits in September alone). 0.2's other variant, a model grading screenshots against a rubric, died: 0 of 256 checks ever used it. 0.3 already does the driving part for the new-user experience (the Windows first-run acceptance, the first-build increment), but its results stay as reports and never colour a card.
fields.options:
A) Accept all of ADR-0825, D5 included. Journey contracts (first run, first build, website) get a real verified result from acceptance runs, so those territories can turn green or red. For: the new-user experience you care most about becomes visible in the forest. Against: a model-driven run can pass something a person would find clumsy (0.2 accepted that cost, ADR-0295 D3), and it needs the Windows lane running regularly.
B) Accept D1-D4, and keep acceptance as it is today: reports and parked increments, not health. For: simpler, and no new identity allowed to write health. Against: the journey contracts stay grey for good, and would show as "needs owner" or "out of CI's reach".
C) Accept D1-D4, and drop model acceptance. For: least machinery. Against: nothing proves the first-run experience beyond unit tests.
fields.statement: Accept ADR-0825 (health you can maintain)? In particular D5: should a model driving the product as a user, with the test harness (not the model) deciding pass or fail, write the verified health of user-journey contracts?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A. It matches your gut feel, reuses the harness the Windows acceptance already built, and keeps the one lesson 0.2 paid for: the harness decides pass or fail, never the model.

fields.title: How is code that only runs in a browser window allocated?
fields.stakes: About 1,700 lines of code can't be given to any capability by a test today, because that code only runs inside a browser window (the app's screens, the arc bar, the setup guide, the forest's globe view, the website's forest). Until you choose how that code is allocated, the "no unallocated code lands" guardrail can't be switched on, because it only switches on at zero.
fields.analogy: Like a theatre: Node tests rehearse the actors (the functions) on a bare stage; mount code is the set and lighting, which only exist in the real theatre (a browser). A gives the rehearsal room a cardboard set; B films the real performance and counts who was on stage; C credits the set to the play it was built for without filming it. Where it breaks: a mount does have behaviour (clicks), unlike a set.
fields.context:
Every other kind of code now has a route: tests that import it (tracing), tests that run it in a process they start (coverage), types reached by imports, and new contracts with their tests, which this lane is adding story by story. What is left is "mount" code: the files that build a screen's elements and wire its clicks (packages/app/src/view, arc-surface view/mount.ts, app-setup view/mount.ts, the forest's view/*.tsx, the website's forest.ts and forest-scene.tsx, the planet canvas). Their logic is already tested where it was pulled out into plain functions; the mount itself needs a page.

Our numbered tests run in Node, which has no page. The pictures in each story's evidence folders are taken by capture scripts that drive the real app or a real browser, but those scripts are not numbered tests and are not run by pnpm test or CI.

Some of these files sit inside other sessions' open increments (the forest's story-node render contracts, the app menu, settings 10.9), so they would be allocated by whichever route you choose, through that work.
fields.options:
A. A page-in-Node test kit (happy-dom or jsdom, one dev dependency): numbered tests mount a screen and click it, run by pnpm test and CI on all three systems. Gains: the guardrail holds in CI; real clicks are tested. Costs: new test infrastructure (ADR-0623 asks for a named behaviour, which each mount's contracts give); WebGL canvases still can't run, so the globe and planet canvases would need option B or C anyway.
B. The capture scripts record coverage too: a capture named by its contract numbers (say "3.4 click a territory") writes the files it ran into the same coverage map. Gains: no new kit; the pictures we already take become the proof, WebGL included. Costs: captures need Electron or a browser, so they run on the Mint box when the map is regenerated, not in CI; the map can go stale between runs.
C. Thin mounts belong to what they mount: pull every bit of logic out of a mount into tested functions, and give the remaining mount file to the capability whose code it imports most. Gains: no kit, no browser, cheapest. Costs: it is an allocation by inference, not by a test reaching the file, which is close to the catch-all you ruled out.
fields.statement: How should code that only runs in a browser window be allocated to a capability?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A for the screens (cheap, in CI, and it tests clicks), plus B only for the WebGL canvases (globe, planet, world canvas), which no page kit can run.

fields.title: The app's copied lifecycle promises and its outdated empty-page promise: retire, reword or keep?
fields.stakes: The app's card for Lifecycle stays "untested" for as long as five of its promises are copies of promises two other parts already keep and test; and one Projects promise (2.5) describes an empty page the app no longer shows. Nothing is broken for a user; this is about what the health board says and what the app's plan promises.
fields.analogy: A filing cabinet with the same letter photocopied into two folders: the copy in the app's folder never gets the stamp the original got. Where it breaks: here the copies have already drifted a little, so they are no longer quite the same letter.
fields.context:
Terms: a "contract" is one testable promise on the plan; the health reader counts it tested only when a test names its number; "retire" removes a promise from the plan with a reason. Agents never retire one: that is your call.

The copies, side by side (the app's promise | the promise it copies, which is already tested where it lives):

- App 1.1 "Starting runs the database on the app's data folder, it answers at the address handed back, and stopping stops it." | Local database 2.2 "A started server answers SELECT 1 at the url handed back; stop stops it, a second stop is harmless, and it can be started again, on a port asked for."
- App 1.2 "A second start on a data folder that a live process holds is refused, naming that process, and its database is left running." | Local database 2.3 "A start on a data directory a live process holds is refused with a DataDirInUseError naming that process and its owner, and the holder's server is left running."
- App 1.3 "A database left running by a process that died is stopped and replaced, and a dead owner's record alone is cleared." | Local database 2.4 "A server left running by a process that died is stopped and replaced, and a dead owner's record alone is cleared, so the start goes ahead."
- App 1.4 "With the app's database stopped, an agent's session asking where to send its activity is told "storytree isn't running" in well under a second." | Agent link 1.4 "With the app's database stopped, asking where to send activity answers "storytree isn't running" in well under a second."
- App 1.5 "A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: the answer comes in well under a second and never hangs." | Agent link 1.5 "A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: it answers in well under a second and never hangs."

The app never starts the database itself: the desktop frame calls the local database's start (apps/desktop/src/main/main.ts, openAppLibrary), and the "is storytree running" answer is the agent link's. The app's only own part here is the wording of the in-use refusal it shows.

Projects 2.5 says: "With no projects, the app tells the user to start Claude Code or Codex in a folder and say yes when asked to set it up." The empty page today says: "Add a folder as a project from the gear menu: Projects → Add project…, or run storytree doctor --set-up <name> in the folder." (apps/desktop/src/view/view.ts, renderNoProjects).

Already landed on this increment: Projects 2.1's remaining clauses (choosing switches and closes the overlay; a failed choice shows its reason and the list stays free to retry) are now tested.
fields.options:
A. Retire app 1.1 to 1.5 as copies, each with the reason "kept and tested as local database 2.2 to 2.4 / agent link 1.4 and 1.5". For: one promise lives in one place; the app's card turns healthy once its other contracts are. Against: the app's plan no longer says, in its own words, that the app's database starts and stops safely; you read that on the other two stories.
B. Reword them to the app's own part (for example "the app shows the in-use refusal naming the holder, and opens no second window"), then a test in the app names each. For: the app keeps promises that are really its own. Against: new tests and some code to reach (the refusal's wording lives in the desktop frame today), for behaviour users rarely meet.
C. Keep them word for word and let the other parts' tests also name them, by the rule landed today (a test titled "app 1.2: …" in another package counts for the app's 1.2). For: no plan change. Against: each of those tests would then carry two numbers for one promise, and the copies drift apart over time, as 2.3 and app 1.2 already have.
For 2.5: (i) reword 2.5 to the Add project path the page shows now, after which a test of the empty page names it; or (ii) change the page back to "start Claude Code or Codex and say yes". The page also sits in the desktop frame, not the app's package, so either way moving it into packages/app comes with the test.
fields.statement: Should the app's five copied promises (Lifecycle 1.1 to 1.5) be retired from the app, reworded to the app's own part, or kept and proven by naming the other parts' tests after the app; and should Projects 2.5 be reworded to the page the app shows today, or the page changed back to what 2.5 says?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A for 1.1 to 1.5, and (i) for 2.5. The copies add no promise of the app's own, and the page as it is now matches how a user really adds a project.

fields.title: Who decides what: the owner's responsibility framework in 0.3
fields.intent: Who decides what, in 0.3: the owner's split between what models are responsible for and what needs his call. 0.2 wrote it down as decisions (0.2's ADR-0409, ADR-0348, ADR-0410, ADR-0110); 0.3 carried the rules over as three notes on the session-orchestrator role (Machine in the loop is the default; The owner-fork bar; The owner owns the outer loop) but not the decisions they stand on, and no register of what he has already delegated, which each note tells a session to check first. Owner, 2026-10-01: "bring the the ADRs across as per your recommendation, them tell me if you think this should be a configurable surface for our users".
fields.endState: 0.3's decision log carries the framework's decisions with the owner's own words, the three notes link to them, a register of standing delegations exists that a session can check before escalating, and whether users of storytree get to configure their own version of this split is either decided by the owner or waiting on him as a written question.

fields.body:
Bring four 0.2 decisions into 0.3's log, each with a new 0.3 number, "0.2's ADR-NNNN" in its title, a "Full record" pointer and an owner-directed stamp quoting the owner's words as 0.2's record kept them (all four kept verbatim quotes, so ADR-0791 does not block them):
- 0.2's ADR-0409: machine in the loop is the default; a human only for taste or a capability models lack (standing, accepted).
- 0.2's ADR-0348: the human witness narrows to taste; live spend and outward-facing commitments are not bases (accepted; its UAT-label machinery has no 0.3 counterpart, so it is recorded for its rule).

fields.title: Should users configure who decides what?
fields.answer: 2026-10-02: Go with A for now, think this really should just be more of a exposure surface, your right that the agents.md should override this anyways or can pull against this. I just noticed this is something i wanted to look at from time to time without having to ask an agent. making it configurable might be on overreach at this stage
fields.stakes: Every storytree user's agents either ask them too much (the user becomes the queue their work waits on) or decide things the user wanted to call. Today users' agents are told only "when only the owner can decide, raise a question", with no definition of what that covers, so each agent guesses. Whatever we choose here is what users see on first use, so it is outward-facing.
fields.context:
Terms. "Decision rights": which kinds of decision the agent makes itself and which it raises as a question for the project's owner. "Standing delegation": a kind of decision the owner has handed to agents for good (for storytree itself, the definition "Standing delegation" now lists eight, from both libraries). "Habits card": the short text (under 60 lines) the agent link hands every user's agent at the start of each session.

What exists. Storytree's own split is now in 0.3's log: ADR-0826 (0.2's ADR-0409: a human only for taste or what models cannot yet do; no model signs off its own output), the owner-fork bar (ask only when irreversible, outward-facing, or value-laden and unsettled) and the guardrail "The owner owns the outer loop". None of it reaches users: packages/agent-link/src/instructions/habits.ts line 18 is the only line about it.

Why part of it should vary by user. The owner-fork bar's own test includes risk appetite and value calls, which are each owner's by definition: a solo hobbyist may happily let an agent publish a release, while a team with paying users will not. Why part must not vary: an agent never signs off its own output, tests are never skipped, and a question is written, not only asked in chat. Those are storytree's honesty promises, not preferences, and they would stay off the list.

Proposal (option B), sketched:
Kind of decision | default
- Reversible engineering choices | decide and record
- Whether a built look reads right | decide, show the pictures
- Choosing between designs before building | ask me first
- Outward-facing changes (releases, public interfaces, messages to others) | ask me first
- Irreversible or wide-reaching (deleting or migrating data, rewriting history) | ask me first
- Spending money or adding a paid service | ask me first
- Dropping or reshaping the work asked for | ask me first
Each can be set to "decide and record", "decide and tell me in the debrief" or "ask me first". Below it, the user's own delegations in their words ("bump dependencies without asking"); settling a question with "don't ask me this again" offers to add one. It is kept with the project in its library, so every session, machine and collaborator sees the same rules, and it is edited in the settings panel behind the gear or from the command line. Every session's habits card carries it.

Analogy: a company's delegation-of-authority chart (what staff may sign without the boss). Where it breaks: agents are not accountable the way staff are, which is why the honesty promises are not on the chart; and the chart does not enforce anything. The agent CLI's own permission prompts still govern what runs. This setting governs only when the agent asks.
fields.options:
A. Fix the definition only: add storytree's fixed split to the habits card (a few lines, one increment), with no setting. Cheap and fixes today's gap; but users with a different appetite for risk cannot change it, so they get over- or under-asked.
B. A plus the configurable decision rights above (a new capability: the list, its storage, the panel, the card rendering, the "don't ask again" path). Fits each user; but it is several increments, adds a setting users must understand, and badly chosen settings could let an agent decide what the user wanted to call (softened by conservative defaults).
C. Neither for now: keep the split internal to storytree's own development. No cost; users stay with an undefined line.
Staging: A then B is possible, because A's text is B's default, so A is B's first step, not throwaway.
fields.statement: Should storytree give its users a setting for which decisions their agents make and which they are asked about, and if so, now or after we fix the missing definition?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: A now, then B. A closes a real gap in a few lines this week; B follows as the next increments on this arc, with its shape approved by your answer here and authored as a capability before it is built.

fields.intent: The owner regularly asks a session to drip-feed him the open questions arc by arc, re-onboarding him with diagrams and analogies, then to record his answers and feed the unblocked work to the Mint box. 22 such sessions ran 2026-08-22 to 2026-10-01 (18 in 0.2, 4 in 0.3), and the same corrections recur: a stale premise (13), too little re-onboarding (12), not his call (10), options missing the obvious one (8), the list not refreshed mid-round (7), plus 'does it look right' questions and questions on parked arcs. Owner, 2026-10-01: 'feels like we should setup a reusable skill for sessions like this, then you can put the guidance in that skill on writing up proposed adrs.' A skill carries the procedure so each round starts right.

Today it reads only library notes of kind agent (packages/dev-loop/src/build-guidance.mjs, rules in guidance.mjs): the orchestrator role becomes CLAUDE.md's generated part and AGENTS.md, every other role .claude/agents/<name>.md and .codex/agents/<name>.toml. The library has no skill kind (packages/library/src/knowledge/knowledge.ts:99: principle, guardrail, pattern, process, agent, friction, resteer, techstack). There is no .claude/skills folder yet.
Build: a process note marked as a skill (a field or tag the build reads; choose the smallest shape, and record the choice) is written by build:guidance to .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (frontmatter name + description from the note, body from its text), and check:guidance reports drift for those files the way it does for roles. Red first on the build writing one skill note to its file, and on check:guidance flagging a hand edit.
Why not a hand-written SKILL.md: it would work today, but it breaks the guardrail "The library is the edit surface" and nothing would drift-check it. Why not a subagent role: the procedure runs in the conversation with the owner, and subagents cannot talk to him.

Name: the owner picks; candidates from the trace farm: question-round (the draft's pick: names the unit of work, matches his "next Q"), drip-feed-questions (his own words), owner-questions, reonboard-and-ask, decision-round (too broad), catch-me-up (reads as a status report). The description carries his trigger phrases, so the name matters less.
Unsure (from the trace farm): on 2026-09-06 he said exploratory work "should just stay in the arc", while on 2026-10-01 he asked for proposed decisions recording his collaboration model; the draft follows the later wish and ADR-0829. The Mint box lane launcher ([home]) is not documented in the library, so the draft describes dispatch generically; consider a process note for it. Things this session (878065a1) learned that the draft should keep: verify every question is still live before presenting it (a settled sibling question, a closed increment that already measured it, a landed PR, another session already handling it); give credential steps complete the first time (the merge-queue token needed Contents, Pull requests AND Merge queues write, org-owned, and five round trips to find that); check what another dispatcher already sent to the Mint box before launching lanes (friction_f1d70ab6f779); a retired-question hold must be cleared first.
Evidence digest (sessions, counts, quotes): see the second half of this body.

===== DRAFT SKILL.md (from the trace farm, 2026-10-01) =====
---
name: question-round
description: >-
  Walk the owner through storytree's open questions one at a time, arc by arc, re-onboarding him on
  each with a diagram and an analogy so he can answer, then record every answer and send the work it
  unblocks to the Mint box. Use when he says "drip feed me the open questions", "arc by arc",
  "reonboard me", "re-onboard me so I can answer", "walk me through the open questions", "talk me
  through the questions waiting on me", "any open questions I need to answer", "next Q", or asks
  for diagrams and analogies to help him decide. Also use for a single named question ("walk me
  through oq-…", "reonboard me on this question").
---

# Question round

The owner answers storytree's open questions in bursts, often after time away, jumping between
sessions. Your job is to make each answer cheap: check the question still deserves him, re-onboard
him just enough, give him a clean choice, record what he says exactly, and turn it into moving work
before you show him the next one. He sets the pace.

Stands on (search the library by title; do not restate them to him): **Register follows audience** ·
**Plain language first** · **The owner-fork bar: escalate ownership, not uncertainty** · the
definition **Standing delegation** · **Escalate inline, or on a named signal** · **A human's words
are stored verbatim, or not at all** · ADR-0794 (a built look lands with its pictures) · ADR-0829
(directed decisions are born accepted) · ADR-0835 (a parked arc raises no questions) · pattern
**Parallel build-lane fan-out**.

Both front doors work (ADR-0793): the agent link's tools (`show_plan`, `settle_question`,
`retire_question`, `correct_question`, `edit_plan`, `record_resteer`, `raise_question`) or the
command line (`pnpm -s storytree …`). Commands below use the command line for brevity.

## 1. Before the first question: build a list that deserves him

1. Read `storytree adr list --load-bearing` (once per session), then `storytree question list`.
2. **Verify every question is still live** before it reaches him. Stale premises were the most
   common correction (13 times). For each one check, with a subagent if there are many:
   - the arc is **not parked** (ADR-0835). If it is, retire the question and move its substance into
     the arc's increment body; do not show it, or list it as "parked, skipped".
   - it was **not already answered**: settled questions and resteers on the same arc, decisions since
     it was raised, and anything he said in another session that day.
   - it was **not overtaken**: the held increment is still open, no merged PR or measurement already
     answers it (`gh pr list --state merged --search …`, the increment bodies, recent friction).
     If a measurement changes the question, lead with that fact.
   - it is **above the owner-fork bar** and **not a standing delegation**. A reversible engineering
     call, a "can a session do this itself?", or a premature "decide later" item is decided and
     recorded by you, not asked.
   - it is **not "does it look right?"** (ADR-0794). Built looks land with pictures; he raises what
     looks wrong. Propose retiring these.
3. **Open with an overview table**, answer first: "N questions across M arcs, each checked live."
   Columns: # · Kind (design call / credential only you can create / spend / probably shouldn't
   exist) · Arc · Question in plain words. Put the ones you would retire in the table with the
   reason, so he can clear them with one "yes, retire". Say which questions are coupled and will be
   taken together. Then go straight into question 1 in the same message.

## 2. Each question: one message he can answer in one line

Use this shape. Skip a part only when it truly adds nothing.

- **Heading:** `Question n of N: <the decision in plain words>`.
- **Arc re-orientation, only when the arc changes:** "Where it stands" in 3 to 6 bullets: what has
  landed, what is parked, what this answer unblocks. Same arc: say "same arc, no re-orientation".
- **The problem, stakes first:** what broke or is blocked, with the date or incident that raised it.
  Then what is already true or already fixed, so he decides only what is left.
- **Terms:** gloss only the machine vocabulary he lacks (tool names, lifecycle states, decision
  numbers), naming each thing by what it does, id in parentheses at most. He set the project: never
  re-explain it to him.
- **Diagram** when the subject is a structure, flow or before/after: a small ASCII block in a code
  fence. Offer it unasked; being asked for one is the failure signal. Reserve an HTML mock or
  artifact for the most complex cases.
- **Analogy**, one line, then **"Where it breaks:"** one line.
- **Options**, lettered (or coded per question, `N1`/`N2`, when questions share a message):
  what happens, *For*, *Against*. Use a table when there are three or more, or when the question has
  been reframed. Before sending, challenge your own framing (8 corrections came from here):
  - Is there an obvious option missing, such as "the system already does this", "a session does it
    itself", "both, not one or the other", or "the simplest version first"?
  - Are the options really exclusive? Say when they combine.
  - Is any option overbuilt for what he asked? Say so yourself.
  - "Leave it as is" is a valid answer; say it will be recorded as decided.
- **My recommendation (non-binding):** the pick, one sentence why, and what would flip it.
- **The ask, last line, bold:** "**A, B or C?**" Coded options let him answer "A for 2, NO for 4".

Keep every option's description in the same message as the ask. If a question is reframed, split
by a digression, or followed by status updates, **re-post all its options in one place** before
asking again (he once could not find them).

**The picker** (AskUserQuestion) is fine for a quick pick *after* the full text is shown, never as
the only place the options live. Free text always wins: if he answers outside the picker or
dismisses it, read his words and record nothing he did not say.

## 3. Pace

- One question per message; a coupled pair together when it is one problem (say so).
- Arc by arc, but take an order that lets one answer settle others.
- He drives: "next", "next arc", "next Q". After each answer, do the writes (section 4), give a
  2 to 4 line receipt (what was recorded, what started), then the next question in the same message.
- When he asks back ("still not following", "what do you mean by…", "why is this a question?"),
  answer that first with a new angle: a concrete example, a different analogy, a diagram. If his
  "why is this a question?" is right, say so, decide or retire it, and move on.
- When he proposes his own direction, check it honestly against the facts (measurements, landed
  work) before agreeing; if it is exploratory, confirm with one line ("Go ahead, or anything to
  change first?"). If he directed it, record it without asking again.
- Interruptions (status checks, lane crashes, credentials) get short answers, a table for lane
  status, and every such message ends with **"Still with you: Qn, A/B/C?"**
- Re-run `storytree question list` at each arc boundary and before you say "that's all":
  sessions file new questions during the round (7 corrections came from a stale list).

## 4. After each answer

Do these before showing the next question. Library edits need no worktree.

1. **Settle with his exact words:**
   `storytree question settle <q> --answer @answer.txt [--decision <decision>]`. Quote him
   verbatim, with the date; your interpretation goes in the increment body, not the answer field.
   A question he answers "skip" on a parked arc is retired, not settled.
2. **Rewrite the held increment's body** (`storytree arc increment edit <inc> --body @body.md`):
   lead with `OWNER'S ANSWER <date> (<question id>): "<his words>"`, then what it means for the
   build, so the lane that picks it up needs nothing from this chat. Clear `--held-on` if it still
   points at the question. Close increments his answer made moot
   (`arc increment close <inc> --disposition withdrawn --note …`), and park new ones it creates.
3. **Write the decision** when the answer sets a rule future sessions must follow or narrows a
   standing one (section 5). Leave an in-place note in any decision it narrows, in the same pass.
4. **Record a re-steer** (`storytree resteer new … --evidence "<his words>" --disposition
   defect|taste --judged-by owner`) when he picked neither option, reframed the question, or said it
   should not have reached him. Your own account goes in `--self-report`.
5. **Retire what should not exist** (`storytree question retire <q> --reason …`), keeping any
   substance on the arc. Never retire an answered question: settle it.
6. **Dispatch** (section 6), then message any session that was blocked on what he just fixed,
   only once the fix is proven to work.

## 5. Writing up decisions: accepted vs proposed

- **Accepted** when he decided: he picked an option on a fork, said "record it that way", "go with
  your recommendation", or stated a rule. Write it born accepted (ADR-0829):
  `storytree adr new --title … --text @adr.md --status accepted --basis owner-directed
  --owner-said @said.txt`. Never ask him to ratify what he already decided.
- **Proposed** when he is thinking aloud about a direction: "I imagine…", "in the future we would…",
  "not sure yet", a model of how something should work that no increment builds yet (for example
  his collaboration model, ADR-0830). Write `--status proposed`, say in the text that it is his
  current thinking recorded while he explores and not a build commitment, list the open points, and
  link the arc where it would be shaped. Do this unprompted: he expects his thinking stored for
  future sessions.
- Not every answer needs a decision. A pick among options inside a standing decision lives on the
  settled question and the increment body.
- His words go verbatim in `ownerSaid`, the answer and resteer evidence; a paraphrase there is a
  defect. Keep accepted text free of meeting minutes: the decision, its reasons, what it narrows.
- Read the "why" of any decision an answer collides with. Decisions are not law; if his answer
  overturns one, write a new decision that supersedes it, not a workaround.

## 6. Dispatch: keep the Mint box busy

He asks for this in most rounds: send **everything safe and ready**, not only what his answer just
unblocked.

1. After each answer, or each arc, have a subagent list ready increments: open, unclaimed, not
   waiting, not needing the laptop or the owner (`storytree arc list`, `arc show`, `noticeboard`).
2. Check what is already running on the Mint box (`ssh mint`, its lane list) and which claims
   other sessions hold, so two dispatchers never feed it the same increment.
3. Launch each lane with a self-contained brief and a file fence that keeps it out of running lanes'
   files, through the Mint lane launcher. Queue lanes that overlap behind the one they collide with.
4. Confirm each lane claimed its increment, then tell him in a short table: lane, work, state.
   Laptop-only work (Windows app checks, his live attestations) is listed as his, not dispatched.

## 7. Owner-only actions (credentials, applies, spend)

Before asking him to act, find every requirement first (org policy, every permission, the resource
owner, expiry limits) and give the complete steps once, with the exact command. Test what he
provides before storing it, never print a secret, and switch anything you enabled back off if it
fails, so no lane is left stuck. Each extra round trip costs his attention.

## 8. Ending the round

Re-check the question list. Then a short summary: each question, his answer, and what it became
(settled, decision number, increment, lane), what is still waiting on him, and what is running.
Close out per the session role: friction for what fought you, claims released, `storytree
processes` clean, `storytree session close-out --safe yes|no --why …`.

# Evidence digest: the owner's "drip feed me the open questions" sessions

Source: every top-level transcript under `[home] (424 folders, 4,163 session files), with the owner's prompts pulled out by script (`extract.mjs`, `prompts.jsonl` in this folder), then each core session read prompt by prompt, and the assistant side read for the best and worst rounds. Quotes are the owner's words, cut short. Timestamps are UTC.

Resumed sessions appear as several files with the same prompts (13d5a9d7/f79c1bcc; 1492d226/ea4130aa; 3cc59e3b/d0b103a1/e5df80ad); each is counted once, under the largest file. The desktop session "Arc-by-arc relearning with analogies" is CLI file `e7913ed5-a9ab-427b-a654-c864871c9b18` (the desktop id 53fa514d does not exist as a transcript file).

## 2. What a good round looks like (assistant side)

- **Overview first, with a verdict column.** 878065a1 09-30T21:20: "I've read all nine open questions and checked that each one is still live", then a table # / Kind (credential, design call, spend + "arc is parked", "⚠ Probably shouldn't exist") / Arc / Question, and "Questions 2, 3 and 4 are linked, so I'll take them back to back."
- **Arc map + "Where it stands".** e7913ed5 09-30T02:41: an ASCII list of four arcs with question counts and "← starting here", then a 5–7 bullet "Where it stands" per arc; "Same arc, so no re-orientation needed" for the second question on it.
- **Per question:** "Question n of N: <plain title>" → **The problem** (dated incident, what is blocked) → what is already fixed/true → ASCII diagram → **Analogy** + "Where it breaks" → lettered **Options** with *For* / *Against* → **My recommendation (non-binding)** with the condition that would flip it → a one-line ask ("**A or B?**"). (878065a1 Q1, Q3, Q6; e7913ed5 Arc 1 Q1.)
- **Coded options for one-line answers.** f79c1bcc 09-26: "A one-line answer like 'approve, N1 P1 C1 R1' is enough"; he answered "N1, P ... C2, R1". 878065a1 22:15 "A for 2, NO for 4". 177651f0 07:19 "Q1 A, Q2 A".
- **"Leave it" is an answer.** eecc30ab 08-22: "If your answer is 'leave it as-is', that's a complete answer and I'll record it as decided".
- **Receipt then next question in one message.** 878065a1 22:39: token result, "Q3, your direction: you're right, and the question should have offered this", what gets built, "I've recorded your correction as a re-steer", then `## Question 5 of 9`.
- **Pin the open ask under every interruption.** 878065a1 22:25, 23:51, 01:49, 01:57 each end "Still with you: question 5 ... 5a: i/ii/iii/iv; 5b: A/B/C/D".
- **The picker.** AskUserQuestion was used for quick picks (7f8eec04 x8, 26f87539 x7, a60c829c x2) and usually answered with the recommended option; he overrides it with free text when the framing is off (26f87539 08:47, 7f8eec04 03:26) and once dismissed it (e7913ed5 02:51: "You closed the answer picker without choosing, so I've stopped there and recorded nothing").

- **Dispatch unblocked AND other safe ready work (13 sessions).** 885770f1 06:24 "for anything we unblocked can you cut self perpetuating sessions"; 83e53689 11:55 "cut a fresh session to drive the arc, then in this session move to the next arc"; 6509c0f0 08:23 "everything that is safe to run and no other session has claimed"; e5df80ad 02:52 "cut fresh sessions each time for any work that can proceed"; 7f8eec04 13:09; 26f87539 05:47; ec0d2b9e 12:53 "if my answer unblocks work send it to the mintbox"; e7913ed5 03:09, 09:07, 09:58 "I'm seeing 11 arcs unclaimed and ready ... why havn't we sent this work to mint"; 878065a1 22:15 "feed any unblocked work to the mintbox (everything that is safe to do not just what i have unblocked with an answer)"; 33c91533 21:33; 7e0b4917 09:29. In 0.2 the target was fresh local sessions; from 09-27 it is the Mint box lanes.
- **Message sessions blocked by what his answer fixed.** 878065a1 23:22 "if this works you need to msg the other sessions that were complaining they were blocked by this" (the session waited until the fix was proven before messaging: 23:50).
- **Decisions, proposed vs accepted.** 878065a1 03:18 "With my colloboration notes did you write up ADRs in a proposed state so as to store these for future sessions" → ADR-0830 proposed, ADR-0831..0835 accepted with `--basis owner-directed`. 885770f1 10:48 "while an ADR is proposed it can be a working scratchpad ... when it moves to accpeted ... reduced down to durable decisions". 885770f1 10:37 "an accepted ADR shouldnt have such noise". Earlier counterpoint: 96fc0a57 09-06T05:41 "If something is still in the exploration or plannng phase then it should just stay in the arc".
- **In-place notes on narrowed decisions.** e7913ed5 02:56, 03:04 (ADR-0789 noted for ADR-0792 and ADR-0793).
- **Re-steers when he picks neither option or reframes.** 878065a1 22:39 ("Sessions name themselves rather than borrowing prompt text"); e7913ed5 03:01 (both front doors).
- **Settle with his words; rewrite the held increment.** 878065a1: six `question settle <q> --answer` with his quoted words; `arc increment edit <inc> --body @file` beginning "OWNER'S ANSWER 2026-10-01 (question_…)"; increments his answer made moot closed `--disposition withdrawn` with the reason (22:23).
- **Retire, keep the substance.** 878065a1 03:21: Mac question retired under ADR-0835, its options appended to the arc's acceptance increment body and `--held-on ""` cleared.
- **Avoid double dispatch.** 878065a1 01:48: two laptop sessions re-fed the Mint box with the same increments → friction f1d70ab6f779.

## 5. Other recurring things

- He drives the pace ("next", "next arc please", "next Q"), and often answers two questions in one line.
- He asks for status mid-round (e7913ed5 09:07 "give me a table of the lanes"); a table answers it.
- Live verification beats guessing: 878065a1 23:13 "you can spawn a codex session on mint if you want and ask it".
- Owner-only steps (credentials, Terraform applies) recur; he prefers the session do what it can (75a5fcf5 12:48 "I'd prefer you just did it with my explicit permission").
- When he reframes, he wants an honest check, not agreement: 878065a1 03:02 opened with the measured fact that changed 5a before agreeing on 5b.

## 6. Library rules the skill stands on (read 2026-10-01)

- principle "Register follows audience" (principle_653f7dd8ad04): decision format for the owner; "Offer the analogy or diagram unasked — being asked for one is the failure signal."
- principle "Plain language first" (principle_bd1191c7312a): stake in sentence one; for the owner translate machine vocabulary, never re-explain the project.
- principle "The owner-fork bar: escalate ownership, not uncertainty" (principle_5a995978191e) and definition "Standing delegation" (definition_d42095d5c9e8, four delegated kinds).
- principle "Escalate inline, or on a named signal" (principle_94a7609d8047).
- principle "A human's words are stored verbatim, or not at all" (principle_8048cf08cfde).
- ADR-0794 (a built look lands with its pictures), ADR-0829 (born accepted when directed; proposed while exploring), ADR-0835 (a parked arc raises no questions; friction_333dddab341a says tooling does not enforce it yet).
- `storytree question check <q>` / `renew` exist (a lease on whether a question still holds).

fields.title: The app keeps up: no noticeable lag, stale before slow
fields.intent: Make the 0.3 desktop app respond at once to every click and hover while agents are busy, by making live updates cost only what changed and letting reads be stale rather than slow (ADR-0836).
fields.endState: With agent sessions active on the Cloud SQL library, the desktop page is blocked less than 10% of the time at idle and on interaction, no live update produces a frame over 200 ms, background reads are batched (no per-arc or per-session fan-out on every change), the code survey re-reads only what changed, the app is ready from its kept reading within 3 s of opening, and each of these is re-measured with the harness on the laptop after landing.
fields.description: Owner-directed 2026-10-01 after he noticed delay clicking around the app. Measured that day on main daf9ece (Cloud SQL library, agents active): the page was blocked 45-70% of the time in frames up to 1.5 s; root causes are the globe rebuilding everything on every live poll, a per-arc read storm on the main process, a whole-checkout code survey on every change, and each live reader pulling the whole history at start. Measurement harness: an instrumented second app instance (isolated STORYTREE_HOME, same library) timing IPC handlers, main event-loop lag, Event Timing, Long Animation Frames and a CPU profile.

fields.body:
**Measured (2026-10-01, main daf9ece, CPU profile of 64 s of page time):** the 3D loop took 29 s, of which three.js `setProgram`/`getProgram`/`getParameters` about 18 s (fresh materials each needing a shader-program lookup); the forest's `Territories` memo (packages/forest/src/view/planet-view.tsx) 18.5 s re-cutting territories and file circles (`territories`, `fileCircles`, `territoryAt`); A* pathway search (`buildGrid`, `runAstar`) about 3 s. Long animation frames of about 1.4 s arrived every ~2 s, at idle too: page blocked 47% at idle, 43-70% while interacting.

**Chain.** Every live poll with news (nearly every 2 s while agents log lines) runs `onTree` in apps/desktop/src/renderer/renderer.ts, which calls `view.show(forestScene(...), new Map(...))`. `ForestView.show` (packages/forest/src/view/forest-view.tsx) reuses islands by key but always builds a new scene object and passes a new `places` Map, so `planetLayout` (useMemo on [scene, places]) recomputes, `PlanetWorldCanvas`'s `planetPathwayDrawing` (packages/forest-world/src/planet/PlanetWorldCanvas.tsx) recomputes, every plate gets a new coast, and every `Territories` memo re-cuts and builds new meshes and materials. Separately the sessions list's refresh calls `onWisps` with a new array each time even when unchanged, so `claimTints(wisps)` gets a new identity and every territory re-cuts again. forest-view.tsx's own header promises "Unchanged islands retain their objects so only changed plates are recomputed": that promise does not hold.

**Breakdown.**
1. `show()` with content equal to what is on show (same island keys in the same order, equal places) does not re-render. Red test first: render count or a recompute counter on an identical second `show`.
2. `showWisps()` with wisps equal to those on show does not re-render; claim tints keep identity when equal.
3. When one island changes, only that island's plate re-derives: layout/pathways keyed by content (story ids, places, reaches), not object identity; `Territories` and coasts stable for unchanged plates; materials shared or cached rather than new per rebuild where three.js allows.
4. Pointer hover picking (`pickGlobe` plus `pointedFile` on every pointermove in `Navigation`) throttled to one pick per animation frame.

**Write fence.** packages/forest/src/view/{forest-view.tsx, planet-view.tsx, territory-land.ts, file-circles.ts, session-tints.ts, planet-navigation.ts} and packages/forest-world/src/planet/. Not sessions-list.tsx (lane "Background reads are batched"), not the code survey, and not apps/desktop/src/renderer/renderer.ts unless one line is unavoidable.

**Done when** a test pins items 1-3, the forest's existing contracts stay green, and the PR states before/after numbers: page time blocked at idle with agents active, and the longest frame on a live update (target below 10% and below 200 ms).

fields.body:
**Measured (2026-10-01, main daf9ece, Cloud SQL, IPC handlers timed in the main process over 95 s):** 630 `storytree:arc-view` calls, p50 2.15 s, p90 3.0 s, max 4.0 s. Root: the sessions list's live reading (packages/forest/src/view/sessions-list.tsx, `onNews`) runs `Promise.all(nextTree.arcs.map(id => reads.arcView(project, id)))` on every change, so about 20-plus parallel arc reads (each several sequential queries in `WorkInFlight.arcView`) hit the Cloud SQL pool together every few seconds. The same pool then serves the user's reads late: `window-reading` (210 calls, one per session every 10 s from `askFiles`) p50 0.5 s, p90 2.3 s, max 3.4 s; `context-readings` max 4.1 s; `window-readings` up to 3.8 s.

**Breakdown.**
1. One read for every arc the sessions list needs: a library call that returns all arc views of a project in one go (few queries, not per arc), carried by @storytree/app's page reads and the bridge. Red test first on the library call (same answer as N single calls; bounded query count) and on the sessions list asking once per change.
2. Only re-read arcs when the change touches work records (increments, arcs, claims), not on every change.
3. The sessions list asks session windows with the existing batched `windowReadings` instead of one `windowReading` per session.
4. Background reads may be stale (ADR-0836 D2): coalesce overlapping asks, never more than one in flight per kind.

**Write fence.** packages/forest/src/view/sessions-list.tsx; packages/library (the new batched arc read); packages/app/src/surfaces/reads.ts and the bridge/preload/main channel lines it needs; packages/knowledge-core only if its window polling needs the same batching. Not the globe files (lane "The globe redraws only what changed"), not the code survey.

fields.title: Background reads are batched: no per-arc or per-session fan-out

outcome.note: Landed in #391. The library answers every arc's view from three lists (arcViews, contract 7.8); the sessions list asks it once per reading and only when a change touches an arc, increment or question, and asks expanded rows' windows in one batched windowReadings ask, one in flight. Measured on the Mint box via the app's page reads over a throwaway Postgres (25 arcs, 200 increments, 20 ms added per query, median of 5): 111 queries / 212 ms per change before, 15 queries / 62 ms after; a click's read made during it 124 ms before, 57 ms after; arc IPC calls per change 25 -> 1 (0 for non-work changes); window reads every 10 s one per expanded session -> 1. fields.body:
**Measured (2026-10-01, main daf9ece):** `storytree:code-survey` ran 14 times in 95 s (every tree read after a change), each 1.9-4.2 s (p50 2.7 s), returning the same 95 KB each time. One main-process event-loop stall of 4.7 s was seen in the same window (others 100-330 ms). Root: apps/desktop/src/main/main.ts's code-survey handler calls `projectTree` again and then `readCodeSurvey` (packages/forest/src/code-survey/read-survey.ts), which runs a synchronous `git rev-parse` (`execFileSync`), reads every source file of every story's package, and runs `surveyStory` over all of them, on every call. The page asks again on every tree re-read (packages/forest/src/render/forest-reading.ts).

**Breakdown.**
1. Cache per file by path plus mtime and size: an unchanged file is neither read nor re-surveyed; a story whose files are unchanged returns the same survey object. Red test first: a second survey with no file changes reads no file contents.
2. No synchronous child process on the main process's path: resolve the main checkout once per folder (async, cached).
3. Coalesce: one survey in flight per project; the page keeps the last survey while a newer one runs (ADR-0836 D2), and the forest reading asks for a survey at most every N seconds rather than on every tree read.
4. The handler reuses the tree it already has rather than reading `projectTree` a second time.

**Write fence.** packages/forest/src/code-survey/, packages/forest/src/render/forest-reading.ts, and the code-survey handler in apps/desktop/src/main/main.ts. Not the globe view files, not sessions-list.tsx.

**Done when** tests pin 1 and 3, and the PR states before/after code-survey time and main-process stall maximum with agents active.
fields.title: The code survey re-reads only what changed

outcome.note: Landed in PR #390. The code survey keeps each file by size and modified time and reads only changed files (a story with nothing changed keeps its survey); the checkout is found by an async git call, once per folder, so no synchronous child process sits on the main process; one survey per folder runs at a time; the handler surveys the tree the page last read instead of reading it again from the library; and the forest reading draws the tree at once with the last survey, surveys at most every 10 s, redraws only when the survey changed, and converges on a change in between. Measured on the Mint box (same instrument both sides, 14 packages / 416 files): each later survey 59-77 ms before, 5-7 ms after; event-loop delay max 27-31 ms before, 19-29 ms after (first run only). Survey calls go from one per tree re-read to at most one per 10 s. Laptop re-measure is increment_e3e497427b8b.

fields.objective: Surveying a project's code costs milliseconds on a change and never stalls the main process, with the survey allowed to lag the checkout (ADR-0836 D2).

fields.body:
**Measured (2026-10-01, main daf9ece, Cloud SQL):** 14.2 s from launch to ready. The first `changes-since` returned 29.7 MB and the first `lines-since` 22.4 MB, each read twice (3.1-5.4 s each), because two live readings start at cursor 0: the forest reading (packages/forest/src/render/forest-reading.ts over packages/arc-surface/src/live-reading/live-reading.ts) and the sessions list's own (packages/forest/src/view/sessions-list.tsx). Each then polls `changes-since` and `lines-since` every 2 s independently, and on each change each reads the 412 KB project tree. The page keeps every change and line ever read (`history.push`, `lines.push` in apps/desktop/src/renderer/renderer.ts; `lines = [...lines, ...news.lines]` in the sessions list) and re-derives `workStates(lines)` and `forestScene(tree, history, ...)` over all of it: page heap about 590 MB.

**Breakdown.**
1. One shared live reading per page: one `changes-since` + `lines-since` ask per tick and one tree read per change, fanned out to the forest, the sessions list, the knowledge core and the arc surface. Red test first: two subscribers, one ask per tick.
2. A bounded start: the first read takes a recent window (or starts from a kept cursor and kept reading), and what needs older history fetches it lazily, showing what it has meanwhile (ADR-0836 D2, D4). Decide the window from what each consumer actually uses (drill-down's history, work states, session rows), measured, not guessed.
3. Derived state is kept incrementally: work states and session lines folded as news arrives, not recomputed over the whole history per poll; old lines dropped once folded.

**Waits on** "Background reads are batched" (both rewrite the sessions list's `onNews`). **Write fence:** packages/arc-surface/src/live-reading/, packages/forest/src/render/forest-reading.ts (coordinate with the code-survey lane's change there by merging main first), apps/desktop/src/renderer/renderer.ts, the sessions list's reading wiring, packages/knowledge-core's reading wiring, and the library's changes/lines read if a bounded variant is needed.

**Done when** tests pin 1-3, and the PR states before/after: time to ready, first-read bytes, page heap, and asks per tick.

fields.body:
**Found 2026-10-01 by the laptop re-measure (increment_e3e497427b8b).** Since #396 (main ab53761; the laptop's app restarted into it at 05:26Z), the desktop page reaches data-state "error" two seconds after opening with "The projects could not be read: Cannot assign to read only property 'projectTree' of object '#<Object>'", and draws no forest. Cause: `joinedReads` (packages/arc-surface/src/live-reading/page-reading.ts) returns `Object.assign(Object.create(reads), { projectTree })`. Over the real `window.storytree`, which Electron's contextBridge exposes with read-only (non-writable) properties, assigning to an inherited read-only property throws in strict mode. The lane's tests and captures used a plain stand-in bridge, whose properties are writable, so they passed.

**Breakdown.** 1. Red: `joinedReads` over a reads object whose properties are read-only, as the context bridge makes them, returns joined reads that answer (one tree read shared by concurrent asks). 2. Green: define the joined `projectTree` as an own property (`Object.defineProperty`), which an inherited read-only property does not block, keeping the prototype link so class-based reads keep their methods. 3. Re-run the laptop harness to confirm the page reaches ready.

fields.body:
**Measured 2026-10-01 on the laptop (re-measure, increment_e3e497427b8b), main ab53761 plus the #400 hotfix, Cloud SQL library, harness sampling main-process event-loop lag every 50 ms.** Main-process stalls of 5.6 s, 11.8 s and 7.0 s, at 68 s, 136 s and 191 s, once a minute; 4.3 s on a second run. In the same windows session-window reads took up to 8.9 s and context readings up to 9.0 s. Every other main-process stall was under 100 ms.

**Cause.** apps/desktop/src/main/main.ts runs `reads.lookAround()` every 60 s (packages/app/src/surfaces/reads.ts), which for each project runs the agent link's look as the app (`lookAsApp`). That look is synchronous on the main process: `execFileSync("git", ...)` per branch and per worktree in packages/agent-link/src/sessions/branch-states.ts and worktree-reaper.ts (this laptop has dozens of worktrees); `readdirSync` plus `readFileSync` of every Claude desktop session record (551 today) and a `DatabaseSync` read of Codex's sessions in app-records.ts; and sync stamp files in claims/merges.ts.

**Breakdown.**
1. Red first: while the look runs, the main process still answers another read promptly. Name the behaviour, for example "a read asked during the look answers within 100 ms" with a stand-in look that is slow.
2. Take the look off the main thread: run it in a worker thread or Electron utility process, or make its git and file work asynchronous and yield, whichever keeps the agent link's hooks (which run the same look from a short-lived process) unchanged in behaviour. Its result may be stale (ADR-0836 D2): the sessions list shows the last look while the next runs.
3. Do less per look: reuse unchanged answers (records by mtime, branches by ref), and never run two looks at once.

**Write fence.** packages/agent-link/src/sessions/{branch-states.ts, worktree-reaper.ts, app-records.ts} and their tests; packages/agent-link/src/claims/merges.ts only for the stamp; packages/app/src/surfaces/reads.ts's `lookAround`; the `lookAround` interval in apps/desktop/src/main/main.ts. Not the status line, the board or claims.ts (the `fanouts` lane, increment_30663b79cabd).

**Done when** tests pin 1 and the PR states before/after main-process stall maximum during a look, measured relatively on the box with the same instrument both sides. The laptop re-measure confirms it.

fields.body:
**Measured 2026-10-01 on the laptop (re-measure, increment_e3e497427b8b): main ab53761 plus the #400 hotfix, Cloud SQL library, CPU profile of the page over ~100 s.** After the globe stopped rebuilding on every poll, long frames are rare (page 3-6% blocked, longest 155-322 ms, no script attribution). But the page's main thread was idle only ~10% of profiled time. three.js `getParameters` took 34.9 s self, `getProgram` 13.4 s, the vertex-array `needsUpdate` 5.6 s, `getProgramCacheKeyParameters` 1.1 s: shader program parameters are re-derived on draw after draw, in many sub-50 ms tasks. The globe redraws continuously while the knowledge core animates (packages/knowledge-core/src/view/globe-points.tsx: the traversal glow's `useFrame` calls `invalidate()` every frame, and the replay does while replaying), so the cost is paid every frame. Hover and click events still present in 32-64 ms where they could take one frame.

**Likely causes, to confirm, not assume.** In three.js `setProgram`, a program is re-derived when a material's version changed (`needsUpdate = true`, or a clone made per frame: see `SessionIslandEmphasis`'s per-frame traverse in packages/forest/src/view/session-emphasis.tsx) or when one material is drawn by objects that differ in what its program depends on (vertex colours or alphas, instancing, clipping, fog, morph), so it flips program on every draw. Count `getProgram` calls per frame with the renderer's `info.programs` and a wrapped `getProgram`, by object name, to find which.

**Breakdown.** 1. Red first: a frame of an animating globe with nothing else changing re-derives no program (count from the renderer). 2. Fix the materials that flip or re-version: separate materials per object variant, no per-frame clones, and no `needsUpdate` unless the thing it guards changed. 3. Optionally cap the animation's redraw rate where motion allows (ADR-0836: smooth over exact). Pictures before and after must match.

**Evidence.** The profile is at `mint:[home] (summarise it with `RUN=... node prof.mjs`; function names are unminified, from apps/desktop/dist/renderer/renderer.js).

**Write fence.** packages/forest-world/src (materials, canvas), packages/knowledge-core/src/view/globe-points.tsx, packages/forest/src/view/session-emphasis.tsx and the globe view files under packages/forest/src/view. Not packages/agent-link (the `lookaround` lane) and not the sessions list.
fields.title: An animating globe reuses its shader programs every frame

outcome.note: Landed in PR #404. Cause confirmed by counting: three.js draws see-through, double-sided materials in two passes and sets needsUpdate before each, so every island ground and coast, pathway halo, coast tint, territory, file circle, selection ring and the glass re-derived its program twice a frame. Flat marks now draw in one pass (forceSinglePass); the glass is two fixed-side groups, far face then near. The knowledge core's moving lines now rewrite their GPU buffers in place instead of making new ones every frame. Measured on the Mint box (headless Chromium, software GL, same instrument on both builds, actual desktop page, two sessions animating): forest view went from 70 programs re-derived per frame to 0; gl.render went from 4.16-4.59 to 2.74-3.30 ms per frame; page idle went from 90-91% to 93-94%; GPU buffers created per frame went from about 5 to 0. Before and after stills are pixel-identical. Contract 5.4 on The canvas pins it. Not done: capping the redraw rate (breakdown item 3), not needed now that a frame only draws. The laptop re-measure is increment_e3e497427b8b.

fields.body:
Two instruments exist only in PR prose and scratch folders, and each lane rebuilds them (friction_19040467294d; #391 and #398 used different seeds).
1. **Read latency:** page reads over the throwaway test Postgres, seeded (25 arcs x 8 increments, questions), with each pg query delayed by a fixed amount and counted; median of 5.
2. **The desktop harness** (laptop re-measures increment_e3e497427b8b and increment_7e90c8c56f89): a second Electron instance with an isolated STORYTREE_HOME (settings.json, machine.json, project-choice.json copied), via playwright-core's _electron. It records IPC handler times, main-process event-loop lag, Event Timing, Long Animation Frames and a CPU profile over a scripted idle, hover, click and toggle run. `ELECTRON_EXE` and `APP_DIR` overrides; 2 s click timeouts. Copies today: `mint:[home],analyze,prof}.mjs`.

The product behaviour these protect is ADR-0836 (no noticeable lag), so they are measurement tools in packages/dev-loop, run by hand at an increment boundary like `pnpm test-ratio`, never a gate (ADR-0623). Land them with a one-paragraph how-to in the dev loop's notes.
fields.title: Keep the lag instruments in the repo

outcome.note: Landed in PR #450. The arc's two lag instruments are kept in packages/dev-loop as capability 8, Lag instruments (contract 8.1 pins the read instrument), run by hand, never a gate. pnpm lag:reads seeds one fixed project (25 arcs x 8 increments, a question each; 5 stories x 3 capabilities x 2 contracts; 40 log lines) into a throwaway Postgres, delays and counts every pg query, and prints each library/log read the page's reads are made of with its query count and median time, plus relatedNotes fired 5 ms into arcViews (Mint, 20 ms/query: projectTree 5 q / 42 ms, arcViews 3 / 22, click during arcViews 13 / 37). It times the library directly, not the frame's pageReads (which add one listProjects query each), because ADR-0847 bars the dev loop from depending on the frame. pnpm lag:desktop is the laptop harness (second Electron instance on a throwaway home with copied settings; IPC, main lag, Event Timing, LoAF, CPU profile over idle/hover/click/panel/sessions/toggle; --analyze reprints). Not run on the Mint box: Electron cannot start there (no display, no xvfb; headless ozone segfaults), so its first run is the laptop re-measure increment_7e90c8c56f89. The headless stand-in-bridge captures stay in packages/forest's evidence folders, which the capability's founding book points to.

fields.body:
Left by the foldlines lane (increment_d551be57d611). The page reading now holds the log as a LogFold (packages/agent-link/src/readings.ts) plus only the lines a surface reads one by one (claimed, released, landed, closed, merged, subagent-started, note-read): 940 lines, 0.34 MB, against 27,202 lines, 14.9 MB on main, measured on the real library's dump.

What is left: the kept reading in IndexedDB (packages/arc-surface/src/live-reading/kept.ts, pageKeptReading) still writes every thinned line as it arrives (`kept.add(added)` in page-reading.ts heard()), so the store grows with the log and every next start reads the whole of it back (about 14 MB, 27k lines) and folds it again before letting it go. Breakdown:
1. Keep the fold, not the lines: make LogFold's state serialisable (a plain snapshot: per-session aggregates, holders, branch states, app records and words, machines, last seen; Sets and Maps as arrays) with a from-snapshot constructor; red first: a fold restored from its snapshot and fed the rest reads the same as one fed every line.
2. The kept reading keeps, per piece, the thinned changes and only the one-by-one lines, plus the fold's latest snapshot (one record, overwritten), and the overlap check keeps working on the last line seq (keep the last line whatever its kind, for the check).
3. Measure next-start heap and time to ready with the page-memory instrument ([home], README inside; scripts assume /tmp/foldlines, copy them there).
Changes (7.3 MB held, 4,300 after thinning) are the other half of what is held; out of this increment's scope.

fields.title: First builds on a new user's laptop: TodoMVC, then Conduit over many sessions
fields.intent:
**Prove storytree across a long horizon with real builds that the laptop's own agents do, judged by official test suites rather than criteria we make up.** Owner, 2026-10-02: "yes, park this in an arc then drive, i imagine we would do babysitting of the agents from here, but let the laptop agents do the work." Follows question_6d10bcae0b9d ("maybe a website or something basic or maybe rebuild an existing open source project") and the setup arc's first-build acceptance (increment_44bd7a583f32 on arc_cfc7db517fae).

**Who does what.** The laptop's Claude Code and Codex build, each in its own project folder, prompted the way a vibecoder would prompt them. The supervising session, on the owner's dev laptop, babysits: it starts each laptop session over SSH (process_81a7122f6849), answers turns the way a user would, takes screenshots of the app, reads the project's library, grades the build off the laptop and records friction. It never edits the build itself. A storytree defect a build exposes is parked on the arc that owns it (usually arc_cfc7db517fae), fixed on its own pull request, and retested on the next release.

**What gets built (research pass, 2026-10-02).**
1. Warm-up: TodoMVC (spec https://github.com/tastejs/todomvc/blob/master/app-spec.md; official Cypress suite, 9 features), in both agents. This is increment_44bd7a583f32 on the setup arc, and it gives two projects to switch between.
2. The long build: RealWorld "Conduit", a small Medium.com clone (https://github.com/realworld-apps/realworld). Frontend first against the public demo API (api.realworld.show), one page group per fresh session (feed, then sign-in, then articles, then comments, then profiles, follows and favourites). Graded by the official Playwright suite (specs/e2e, element names fixed by SELECTORS.md). Claude Code leads; Codex follows a step behind in its own folder. A backend graded by the official Hurl API collection (specs/api/hurl) is a stretch, decided at the end.

**Why these (research digest).** Long-horizon benchmarks measure three things: task length in human time (METR: frontier about 12 hours at 50% success, Mar 2026), chains of dependent features where earlier ones must keep passing (Web-Bench: 20 dependent tasks per project, about 2K lines; Vals' VCB 1-100 scores consecutive green iterations), and coherence across context resets (Anthropic's long-running harness posts, Nov 2025 and Mar 2026: a feature list, a progress file and git, one feature per session; failures are building everything at once, declaring victory early and leaving state undocumented). All of them rest on a precise spec the agent can check itself against and on end-to-end behaviour tests; agents that test themselves score higher (Vibe Code Bench, r=0.72). TodoMVC and Conduit are the two candidates with a public spec and official suites that run with only a browser on the laptop. Their fame (models have seen them) matters for measuring a model, not for testing storytree's experience; an original spec is the move if we later measure storytree's lift on an agent. 7GUIs (a 7-step ladder, no official tests) and Tetris (Guideline spec, no tests) were the runners-up.

**How a build is scored.** Grading runs off the laptop (copy the build back, run the official suite on the dev laptop or the Mint box), so the laptop stays Node-less unless an agent installs Node itself, which is recorded. Per session: the official suite's result, with every earlier test kept as a regression (count consecutive increments that land fully green, as VCB 1-100 does); how quickly a fresh session finds its place from the library rather than by re-reading code; whether the project's library holds the plan, claims, landings and health the agent did (the owner, 2026-09-30: "test its able to build"); the forest and arc surface in screenshots; and every friction a first user would feel, timed.

**Known hazards.** The official suites find elements by fixed names (TodoMVC's `.new-todo` and the rest; Conduit's SELECTORS.md), so the spec handed to the agent includes them. Conduit's demo server is shared: a failure caused by it is separated from the agent's. The laptop has no Git: storytree claims work without it, but its workspaces need it, so how the agent copes is itself a finding.
fields.endState: Closed when, on the reset Git-less Windows x64 laptop: (1) Claude Code and Codex each built TodoMVC in their own project over several turns, graded by the official TodoMVC suite (increment_44bd7a583f32 on arc_cfc7db517fae); and (2) Conduit's frontend, built by the laptop's agents over at least five fresh sessions one page group at a time, passes the official RealWorld end-to-end suite against the demo server (failures caused by the shared server set aside with evidence), with the forest drawing the build's stories as they land, the project's library holding the plan, claims, landings and health the agent reported, and each fresh session finding its place from the library. Every friction a first user would feel is recorded with evidence and routed. Whether to go on to a Conduit backend graded by the Hurl API suite is decided by the owner at the end.

fields.body:
First Conduit session in each agent: a new empty folder, the prompt a vibecoder would write ('build me a blogging site like Medium, matching this spec: <realworld frontend spec and SELECTORS.md>; start with the home page showing the articles from the demo server'). The agent should plan the whole site as stories and build only the first. Also builds the grading: a kept script that copies a laptop build back and runs the official e2e suite on it. Method for every Conduit increment (see the arc intent): the supervising session starts FRESH sessions on the laptop (process_81a7122f6849), Claude Code first in its Conduit folder, then Codex in its own, a step behind; it prompts and answers the way a vibecoder would, never edits the build, and never hands the agent the test suite to run (the agent may write its own tests). After each session: copy the build off the laptop and grade it with the official RealWorld Playwright suite (specs/e2e, SELECTORS.md names) against the demo API, keeping every earlier area as a regression; read the project library (plan, claims, landings, health as reported); screenshot the forest and arc surface; time how long the fresh session took to find its place; record friction with evidence. A storytree defect is parked on its owning arc, fixed on its own pull request, and retested. Evidence under packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build/.

**Carried from the TodoMVC warm-up (increment_44bd7a583f32, 2026-10-02; evidence packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build).**
- Grade the grader first: TodoMVC's official suite at its pinned Cypress (15.14.2) fails 3 and skips 2 of 29 for any app (a removed spy `reset` call; aliases reused across a reload), so 24/29 was the ceiling. Before grading Conduit, run the RealWorld suite against a known-good implementation and record its own ceiling.
- Codex planned coarsely (1 story, 1 capability, 2 contracts) where Claude Code planned 1 story, 5 capabilities, 14 contracts. Conduit's several pages are where the forest should show the difference; record each agent's plan shape per session.
- Count Codex's approval-review refusals of check_setup (increment_aada58eb5fe4).
- Note whether the health wording has changed (increment_ef066f718a63) before judging what the user sees on the cards.
- Check for headless Edge processes the agents' own test runs leave behind (one from 2026-10-01 was still running; this round left none).
- Both agents ran without Git; neither installed it. Codex fetched a portable Node and Cypress into %TEMP% (about 250 MB) to run the official suite itself; Claude Code ran its tests in headless Edge with no Node.
- Turn harness: packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build/harness (turn.ps1 with -Fresh for a new session, start-task.ps1, appshot.ps1 captures the app window without a restart); grader: first-build/grade.

fields.title: Build a Conduit backend next, or stop the folder-only build here?
fields.stakes: Decides whether the laptop spends several more agent-hours extending the folder-only Conduit build with a server of its own, or moves straight on to the GitHub test (arc_5a044e04cba7). The answer closes this arc either way: it is the last item its end state leaves to you.
fields.context:
What is done: two complete frontends (plain HTML/JS, no build step) that talk to the public demo API, each passing every official end-to-end test; both libraries hold the whole plan and every landing; evidence in packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build/conduit.md and review.md.

What a backend would mean: the agent builds its own API server (users, articles, comments, profiles, tags) with a database, graded by the official Hurl collection (13 files) instead of the public demo API. On this laptop that means Node or Python plus a database, which the agent would have to install (Codex already fetched a portable Node; Claude Code wrote a PowerShell web server rather than install anything). Rough size: comparable to the frontend again, so 5 or more sessions per agent.

What it would add for storytree: a second, server-side layer of stories in the same project (does the forest show a frontend and a backend that depend on each other?), and a longer horizon (10+ sessions in one project). What it would not add: anything about Git, branches, workspaces or pull requests; that is the separate GitHub arc you asked for, which is ready to start.

Analogy: the frontend is a shop front on a rented building (the demo API). A backend is building the warehouse behind it. It tests whether the builders can keep going on a bigger site; it does not test whether they can work with a site manager's paperwork (the GitHub arc does). Where it breaks: unlike a warehouse, the backend can be graded on its own with the API tests, so it is not all-or-nothing.
fields.options:
A. Stop here: close this arc on the 139/139 result and start the GitHub arc next. 
B. Backend now: park Conduit 7+ increments for a backend in each agent's project, graded by the Hurl collection, before the GitHub arc.
C. Backend later, inside the GitHub test: build the backend in the GitHub project (arc_5a044e04cba7) as its later parts, so the long horizon and the pull-request workflow are tested together.
fields.statement: Both laptop agents built the whole Conduit frontend (the RealWorld Medium.com clone) over five fresh sessions, and both pass the official suite 139/139. The arc's end state left one call to you: go on to a Conduit backend, graded by the official API test collection (Hurl), or stop here?
fields.recommendation: Non-binding: C. The folder-only build has answered its question (storytree carries a five-session build with fresh sessions and no chat history). The backend's value is the longer horizon, and pairing it with Git and pull requests tests both at once instead of repeating the folder setup. A is the cheaper choice if you would rather keep the GitHub test to two parts.

fields.title: A first user's build on GitHub: Git, workspaces and pull requests on a fresh repo
fields.intent:
**A first user's build on GitHub, the other half of the first-build test.** Owner, 2026-10-02, asked whether the first-build test had a fresh GitHub repo (it had none: arc_424dae58bf1b's builds live in plain folders on a Git-less laptop, and every increment there closed "no git repo, so no PR"), then: "yes add that, maybe a fresh arc since its a separate test".

**What it tests.** The path arc_424dae58bf1b deliberately leaves out: a user whose agent installs Git, puts the project on GitHub, works in branches and storytree workspaces (which need Git), and lands each part through a pull request on a fresh private repository under the owner's account. That is how storytree builds itself and how many vibecoders work (GitHub sync), so it exercises storytree's workspace, claim-by-branch and landing-by-pull-request habits in a user's project, which a folder without Git never reaches.

**How.** Same laptop, same method as arc_424dae58bf1b (process_81a7122f6849; harness and graders in packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build): the laptop's agent does the work from a user's prompts; the supervising session babysits and grades off the laptop. The user asks for Git and GitHub in plain words ("put this on GitHub") rather than the supervisor installing anything. What gets built is Conduit (the RealWorld Medium.com clone) from the same requirements file, so the official suite grades it and the results compare directly with the folder-only builds.

**Owner steps.** The GitHub sign-in on the laptop (`gh auth login` shows a device code the owner approves in his browser) and his OK to create the repository on his account, both asked for at run time.
fields.endState: Closed when, on the reset Windows laptop, a fresh storytree project lives in a new private GitHub repository the laptop's agent created at the user's request, with Git installed by the agent; at least two Conduit parts were built in fresh sessions, each in its own branch or storytree workspace and landed through a merged pull request; each part passes the official RealWorld suite through its area; the project's library records each increment closed with its pull request; and every friction a first user would feel on this path (Git install, sign-in, branches, workspaces, pull requests, merging) is recorded with evidence and routed.

The agent installs Git (winget) and the GitHub CLI if it needs them; the owner does the GitHub sign-in on the laptop (gh auth login device code, approved in his browser) and confirms creating the repository, at run time. Record: time and prompts for each install, what the agent asked the user, what check_setup said before and after Git existed (it notes git as optional, ADR-0751), and whether storytree's workspaces now work in the project. Copy conduit-requirements.md in as the user's spec. Harness: packages/app-setup/evidence/first-build/harness.

fields.intent:
**Storytree's new opening for first-time visitors: chapter 1, then a guided tour of the real globe.** The owner opened this arc on 2026-10-02 (ADR-0857, decision_850c55d937c6), splitting it off the website arc (arc_a5b72bd96bd9), which keeps its own remaining work. The direction is settled in four decisions:
- ADR-0841: chapter 1 opens the site, and chapter 2 explores the real system.
- ADR-0852: chapter 2 is a guided camera tour of the real globe that replays real activity, built by extending the app's own controls.
- ADR-0853: the problem statement and the four principles.
- ADR-0857: five explainer chapters on a busy globe, each ending with comparisons; free play with a waitlist exit; chapter 1 lands first.

The playable mock is at https://claude.ai/artifact/38vgSpzXj2uFKdyU3Vjp43. How its globe ran from a saved reading, and the pitfalls met, are in pattern_95a3f23edd49. Codex lanes on the Mint box build it.

The ordered lane stopped there, with no snapshot changes and no owner question. Claims released; supervisor successors remain responsible for resuming.
