- It has one fixed prompt, "Build me a shopping website", and one Run button: no typing and no other tasks. Agents spawn agents until all twelve wait on the visitor; the lead agent concedes in about 22 seconds and offers "Show me the better way". The counter reads "12 agents · 12 waiting on you · 0 answered".
- The four reversals: it is a first screen the page can scroll past; sound stays off until turned on; returning visitors open at chapter 2 (or today's globe until the tour lands) with Replay, remembered in localStorage wrapped in try/catch; "I'll keep babysitting" brings three more agents, and the lead asks again.
- The turn collapses every window into one point, and the page's globe grows from it. Until the tour lands, that is today's forest section.
- Without script, or with reduced motion, it shows a still of the peak and the finale's words, then the page.

Tests in a real browser prove the behaviour: one tap plays to the finale with no other input; skip, scroll and Escape always reach the page; reduced motion and no-script never animate; the turn changes no address; sound is silent until turned on; a returning visitor opens past chapter 1. fields.body:
Chapter 2's tour, on the website (ADR-0852, ADR-0853, ADR-0857). It is built on the saved snapshot, the app's controls and the research increments. Port the behaviour from the mock (https://claude.ai/artifact/38vgSpzXj2uFKdyU3Vjp43), not its code.

**Opening.** The busy globe with everything on, slowly turning, with the problem in three beats, "There's no in-between.", then the four principles.

**Explainer menu.** Play all is the default, and any explainer can be picked alone. Each step is a camera move, the surfaces it needs, and at most four lines, each shown only after the one before has had time to be read (about 2.6 words a second at 1×).

**The 24 steps of the shaped outline**, a starting point:
1. Story nodes: "storytree breaks up your codebase into stories". 1.1 one island per story; 1.2 rows by what depends on what; 1.3 roads, which run one way; 1.4 an island grows with its code.
2. Capability nodes: "Stories are broken up into capabilities". 2.1 territories sized by code; 2.2 contracts, promises a test can check; 2.3 each file on the capability its tests trace to; 2.4 unclaimed code; 2.5 health, and who said so. The red-then-green and checked-health partial notes live here.
3. Knowledge graph: "Storytree remembers things using a knowledgegraph". 3.1 about 950 notes inside; 3.2 the kinds of note and what each is for; 3.3 shelves; 3.4 links, no loops, and loose notes at the centre; 3.5 ghosts; 3.6 agents pull only what the task needs, and the librarian keeps it honest.
4. Sessions: "Storytree visualises agents working through sessions". 4.1 the dated recording; 4.2 claims and colours; 4.3 unplanned work still shows; 4.4 context and the nudge (Claude Code only, partial); 4.5 what one session read, in order.
5. Arcs: "In Storytree work is planned using arcs". 5.1 intent and end state; 5.2 increments and their bars; 5.3 waits, and questions only the owner can answer; 5.4 who decides what.

Each explainer ends with its comparisons from the research increment.

**Controls, always there:** pause, speed (0.75×, 1×, 1.5×), Next, skip to free play, replay, and show everything (the tour waits while it is on). Each step has "why it exists" with two or three decisions; the tour waits while it is open.

**Accessibility:** it reads well at 390 px. Without WebGL it shows a still and the words still play. Reduced motion gives jump cuts. Every claim matches 0.3 as shipped (ADR-0798 D3).

Tests prove the behaviour; the look lands with its pictures.

The website's saved snapshot (the website story's Saved snapshot capability, capability_88dfe8ee2706) grows to carry what the tour needs (ADR-0852 D4, which widened ADR-0802). Stay in packages/website and read through the other stories' public exports; the recipe and its pitfalls are in pattern_95a3f23edd49.
- Land: each island's territories, files and imports, from forestScene with readCodeSurvey, plus the story places that planetLayout needs.
- The plan: story and capability titles, descriptions and health.
- Knowledge: the story, capability and note changes, keeping only title, number, status, frontCoverOf, links, supersedes and story.
- The arc board: arcViews and holds. Trim closed arcs, but keep every question's text fields, because the arc surface reads them.
- A dated recording: one window of activity lines, of the kinds session-started, session-ended, session-named, subagent-started (without its task), note-read, claimed, released, landed, closed, merged and closed-out. Keep each line's project field. Drop folder, machine, transcript, branch and task.

Redact home-folder paths and cloud project ids, and fail the refresh on anything that looks like a credential. Load it lazily: storytree's own came to 1.3 MB. Contracts with tests: a refreshed snapshot never carries a folder, machine, transcript, branch or task field; a home-folder path never survives; each line keeps its project; the recording window is the one asked for.

The app's globe gains the tour's controls as its own (ADR-0852 D5). The website reuses them through public exports and copies nothing (ADR-0798 D4).
- Camera stops: turn to a story, a capability, a file or the core, and zoom by framing, animated over a given time. Turn the globe the way PlanetView already does, with focusRotation(turnToIsland(direction), camera.quaternion). Add a sideways view offset, so a card beside the globe covers nothing it points at.
- Per-surface visibility: the sea, island grounds, roads, nameplates, territories (plain or health-coloured), file circles, the knowledge core and session tints.
- Exports: the forest view's public entry (and the knowledge core's and arc surface's views) gives the website the globe, its controls, and where a story, capability, file or the core sits on screen, for pointers.

The mock drove these from outside (pattern_95a3f23edd49). Here they become the app's own. Contracts with tests.

fields.body:
Research for ADR-0857 D4. For each explainer, find how other systems and coding-agent harnesses handle that surface, and why storytree does it differently. No product code. Name real products, and source and date every claim; keep it fair, since the site is public.
- Story nodes: how a codebase is pictured. Covers folder trees, dependency and architecture maps, and what agents see.
- Capability nodes and health: coverage reports, code-health and hotspot tools, quality gates, scorecards, and spec-driven agent tools.
- Knowledge graph: instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files), the harnesses' own memories, and memory layers or knowledge-graph services for agents.
- Sessions: each harness's own session views, and multi-agent dashboards and orchestrators.
- Arcs: issue trackers, spec and task tools for agents, and agents' own plan files.

Write the findings into the library as one research artifact, linked to ADR-0857 (decision_850c55d937c6). Give each explainer three to five comparisons, with sources and dates, and a two-line "why storytree differs" grounded in decisions. If any competitor does one of storytree's surfaces better, raise a question on this arc for the owner, saying what it does better and offering adopt, adapt or set aside, before the tour's copy is written. If web research is not available to the session, say so as residue and stop.

- See the sessions list and replay the recording.
- Look inside the knowledge core and pin a note to read it.

An exit hatch in the bottom-right corner lets visitors join the waitlist. Its target and wording come from the waitlist arc, which a separate session began shaping with the owner on 2026-10-02 (that session was cut from session 0488e44a). Opened 2026-10-02 by the owner, reviewing the chapter 2 mock (increment_9f0bb95f40b1 on the website arc arc_a5b72bd96bd9; his feedback is resteer_b43561a188eb): "We should replace the install with a waiting list - probably deserves a separate arc - cut a fresh session to shape this with me." and "The ending should be a freeplay mode where the user can get exposed to the full UI (arcs, sessions etc) and click around, bottom right corner is the exit hatch to join the waitlist."

Shaping with him, 2026-10-02 (in progress): what joining promises, what the form asks for and says, where sign-ups are kept and who reads them, whether the install command leaves the whole site, what the tour's "skip to install" becomes, and how the waitlist is measured and when it ends. Each settled fork is recorded as a decision linked from here.

Not this arc's: the tour's redesign itself (five explainers, free play), which stays on the website arc; the trusted circle's own invitations and welcome note, which stay on the first-users arc arc_2b919de0d372.
